books.title: Ships of Discovery
books.art_why: These are historical ships and voyages from long before photography, so drawings are needed.

pages.text: Introduction People often settle along rivers, lakes, and seas. Long ago, people who lived near large bodies of water were curious about what was beyond the horizon. They also thought that traveling over water might be easier than traveling over land. These thoughts led to someone making a simple boat. As boats and ships became more practical, people were able to travel farther from home. New types of boats were an improvement over the previous boats. They often were safer, carried more cargo, and were more comfortable. Up until about 150 years ago, boats were the main means of carrying goods and people from place to place. Let’s look at how boats were used to explore the world and how they have changed over time.
pages.brief: People stand along a riverbank, lake shore and sea coast beside simple boats, looking toward the distant horizon. A small early boat rests on the water while sturdier boats appear nearby, showing how people used rivers, lakes and seas to travel and to carry goods and people from place to place.

pages.text: Egypt AFRICA Nile River Early Years The oldest record of sea travel comes from Egypt. More than 6,000 years ago, Egyptians took to the water. They built boats by carving out the trunks of trees. But the Egyptians were not the only people to make boats from trees. Many other cultures that looked for ways to cross the water also carved boats from trees. These were sturdy boats, but they couldn’t carry very much.
pages.brief: On the Nile River in early Egypt, boat builders carve a long boat from a tree trunk. Workers shape the sturdy wooden craft beside the water, while other people from different cultures carve similar tree-trunk boats nearby, preparing to cross rivers and lakes with only a small amount of cargo.

pages.text: Over time, people wanted to move larger things over waterways. They wanted to build boats to carry many people. They also wanted to be able to carry food, animals, and other items to trade. Canoes made from oak trees were good boats for crossing a lake or going down a river. However, they didn’t work as well for carrying large things. Imagine trying to row a canoe across a lake with six sheep crammed around you. The space just wasn’t big enough. dugout canoe Humans have always been driven to improve things. So it was natural that long ago people looked for ways to build bigger, faster, and safer boats. People also realized that they needed better boats to explore places far from their homeland.
pages.brief: A rower struggles in an oak canoe on a lake, with six sheep crammed around him, showing how little space the canoe has. Nearby, a larger dugout canoe rests by the shore while people look for ways to build bigger, faster and safer boats for trade and exploration.

pages.text: The next step in boat building was using wooden beams to make a frame. The frame was then covered with wooden planks or bark from trees. Some cultures even used animal skins stretched over the frame. These boats were bigger and more streamlined and able to hold more cargo. The Egyptians were the first to cover a wooden frame with long, flat pieces of wood to create a hull, the outer shell of a boat. Some of their boats were as long as 21.3 meters (70 ft). The Egyptians were also the first to use sails. Sails reduced the need for people to row the boats. Some larger boats used both rowers and sails.
pages.brief: Boat builders stretch birchbark and animal skins over a wooden frame to make a canoe, while Egyptian shipwrights cover a long wooden frame with flat planks to form a hull. A large Egyptian boat with a sail and rowers moves on the water, showing how sails reduced the need for rowing.

pages.text: Greek ship Soon, the Greeks and other peoples around the Mediterranean Sea were building large boats powered by sails. About 3,000 years ago, sailing ships were built with two masts, each one carrying a sail. The addition of a second mast made ships easier to steer and also made them much faster. Five hundred years later, the Greeks developed a ship with four sails. Some of the fastest ships at the time were built for battle. Some warships had as many as three levels of rowers on each side. These larger ships also allowed people to travel to and explore distant places. During this period, exploration and trade moved beyond the Mediterranean Sea.
pages.brief: Greek sailors steer a large sailing ship across the Mediterranean Sea, its two masts carrying sails that make it faster and easier to control. Nearby, a warship has three levels of rowers on each side, while other sailing ships carry traders and explorers beyond the Mediterranean toward distant places.

pages.text: The Polynesians In the South Pacific, groups of Pacific Island peoples were building boats that could sail in the open ocean. Over 3,500 years ago, these people were traveling east, well beyond the islands where they lived. They also explored areas off the Asian mainland. These Polynesian sailors built a boat that was an early version of the modern catamaran. They took two canoes and connected them using large wooden poles. A deck was then built to span the poles. These boats were usually about 15 to 18 meters (50–60 ft) long. The central deck held masts for sails and had enough space for several people and their supplies during a long voyage. Polynesian catamaran.
pages.brief: Polynesian sailors build an early catamaran in the South Pacific by connecting two long canoes with large wooden poles and a central deck. The deck holds masts, sails and supplies for a long voyage, and several people prepare to set out across the open ocean toward islands far beyond their homes.

pages.text: These early boats provided a means of safe travel from one island to another. The Polynesians settled each new island they discovered. By the beginning of the year 1000 ce, they lived on nearly every island they could find in the Pacific Ocean. Their new homes included Hawaii, New Zealand, and Rapa Nui (Easter Island). The Polynesians were skilled sailors. They became so familiar with the ocean that they could tell their location by the size and shape of the waves. They could easily travel great distances by going from island to island. The Polynesians grew to accept sea travel as a way of life. PACIFIC OCEAN ASIA Hawaiian Islands Easter Island AUSTRALIA New Zealand Routes of Polynesian expansion.
pages.brief: Polynesian families settle on Pacific islands, with Hawaii, New Zealand and Rapa Nui among their new homes. Skilled sailors travel between islands in canoes, reading the size and shape of the waves to find their way, while the open Pacific stretches around them as sea travel becomes a way of life.

pages.text: The Vikings More than 1,300 years ago, a group of people in another part of the world began to build larger boats. These people were the Vikings. They lived in the northern part of Europe. The Vikings were well known as warriors and conquerors, and they were accustomed to traveling over water. By the year 700, they were sailing boats that were better than any others on the ocean. The boats they built, called knarrs (kuh- NARS), were used mostly for trading. These boats were up to 16.5 meters (54 ft) long and 4.5 meters (15 ft) wide. Because they were flat bottomed, the knarr boats could carry heavy loads. They were also stable and could travel safely across the open ocean. Vikings were willing to travel into the unknown to conquer new lands. They were the first Europeans to visit North America.
pages.brief: Viking traders load cargo onto a broad, flat-bottomed knarr in northern Europe. The sturdy wooden ship, about 54 feet long and 15 feet wide, sits low in the water, ready to carry heavy goods safely across the open ocean as Viking warriors and explorers travel into unknown lands, including North America.

pages.text: Vikings also built warships known as longships. It often was difficult to tell if a longship was coming or going because it looked the same in the front and in the back. Using this design, Viking attackers could easily change direction. Longships were able to travel as fast as 15 knots. A knot is a way to measure speed on water. Some of the larger longships carried as many as 200 warriors. The combination of large, speedy, easy- to-handle ships and a fierce fighting spirit made the Vikings tough to defeat. The Vikings ruled the ocean for nearly three centuries.
pages.brief: A Viking longship speeds across the water with rows of warriors aboard, its front and back shaped alike so attackers can change direction easily. Some larger longships carry as many as 200 warriors, and their speed and easy handling help the fierce Vikings rule the ocean for nearly three centuries.

pages.text: Age of Discovery Until the 1400s, most sailors still kept close to their home waters. But with the coming of the Age of Discovery, things changed dramatically. Every European sailing country wanted to find new lands. The race was on, and the Americas were the prize. Shipbuilders had to find ways to build faster and safer ships. In the 1400s and 1500s, sea explorers used small, sturdy ships known as caravels. These ships had three masts to carry sails. This design made the ships fast and easy to steer. Caravels had square sails on the front and the middle masts and a triangular-shaped sail on the back mast. Consider the Conquered What impact did these discoveries have on the people already living in these places? Too often, the impact was a tragic one. Christopher Columbus, Hernan Cortes, and other Europeans who led these expeditions often exploited both the land and people they found. Their motive was usually greed. Before long, ships would also be used to carry people across oceans and enslave them far from their homes.
pages.brief: European shipbuilders launch a small, sturdy caravel with three masts, square sails on the front and middle masts, and a triangular sail on the back. In the 1400s and 1500s, explorers race to find new lands, while people already living in the Americas face exploitation and enslavement by arriving Europeans.

pages.text: Christopher Columbus sailed three of these ships. The largest was 27.4 meters (90 ft) long and 9.1 meters (30 ft) wide. Compared to modern ocean liners and cargo ships, caravels were tiny. But even though they were quite small, the explorer Ferdinand Magellan set out to sail five caravels around the world with a crew of 260 sailors. Almost three years after they began the trip, one of Magellan’s ships and eighteen of the original crew members made it around the world. Magellan was not one of the survivors. He was killed somewhere in the Philippine Islands.
pages.brief: Christopher Columbus’s three small caravels sail together, the largest only about 90 feet long and 30 feet wide. Far across the ocean, Ferdinand Magellan’s five caravels set out with 260 sailors; almost three years later, one ship and eighteen crew members complete the journey around the world, while Magellan is killed in the Philippine Islands.

pages.text: The Chinese While European explorers were sailing the world, the Chinese had also taken to the sea in another part of the world. They were skilled sailors. Their most famous explorer, Zheng He, traveled in a fleet of sixty-two ships that were much larger than European ships. His largest ship was so big that it could have held all three of Columbus’s ships on its deck. This huge ship was 121 meters (400 ft) long and 45.7 meters (150 ft) wide. In addition to the sixty-two main trading ships, more than a hundred smaller support boats were in the fleet. ASIA China PACIFIC OCEAN AFRICA INDIAN OCEAN AUSTRALIA Route of Chinese exploration and trading.
pages.brief: Chinese explorer Zheng He stands on the deck of an enormous ship in a fleet of sixty-two trading ships and more than a hundred smaller support boats. The largest Chinese ship, about 400 feet long and 150 feet wide, could hold all three of Columbus’s ships on its deck as the fleet sails from China toward Africa.

pages.text: Chinese junk These Chinese explorers sailed all the way to Africa to trade. However, war with their Asian neighbors caused the Chinese to turn their attention away from exploration. Do You Know? Christopher Columbus’s entire crew was about 90 sailors on three ships. The Chinese explorer Zheng He had more than 162 ships and 30,000 sailors on one of his voyages.
pages.brief: A Chinese junk sails on the Indian Ocean, carrying traders who travel all the way to Africa. In the background, Chinese leaders turn their attention from exploration because of war with Asian neighbors. Nearby, Columbus’s three ships carry about 90 sailors, while Zheng He’s 162 ships carry 30,000 sailors on one voyage.

pages.text: Later Years As sea exploration continued, the Spanish led the way. By the 1500s, European ship designs had improved. The newest ships, called galleons, were larger, faster, and more comfortable. These vessels were as long as 42.7 meters (140 ft), but were still small compared to the Chinese ships. Many of them had nice, comfortable living quarters. Galleons were capable of serving both as trading vessels and warships. Because of their size, galleons were able to carry many cannons on board, making them dangerous in battle. galleon.
pages.brief: Spanish shipbuilders finish a large galleon in the 1500s, with comfortable living quarters and many cannons mounted on board. The vessel is about 140 feet long, larger and faster than earlier European ships, and it can serve both as a trading ship and as a dangerous warship as Spanish explorers lead the way at sea.

pages.text: In the late 1700s, British captain James Cook undertook some of the greatest explorations of his time. On his first ship, Endeavour, Cook sailed around the world. His ship was only 32 meters (105 ft) in length. It was smaller than many other ships and had a shallow hold, sitting only 4.3 meters (14 ft) deep when fully loaded. Cook was an intelligent explorer and a great sailor who also knew how to keep his crew healthy. He made them eat certain foods, such as limes and cabbages, to remain free from disease. Until Cook’s time, up to one-half of the crew on a long voyage would die of scurvy or other diseases. Cook knew his success as an explorer depended on keeping his crew healthy. Endeavour.
pages.brief: British captain James Cook stands on the deck of Endeavour as it sails around the world. The ship is only 105 feet long and sits just 14 feet deep when fully loaded. Cook makes his crew eat limes and cabbages to stay free from disease, knowing that healthy sailors are key to a successful voyage.

pages.text: Conclusion By the middle of the 1800s, sailors had explored and mapped most of the world’s coasts. As people settled farther from their homelands, better ships were needed to move people and supplies great distances. Fast ships called clipper ships carried people across oceans in a matter of days. Some of these ships had as many as thirty- five sails. In only a few years, however, the steam engine would replace wind power, ending the age of sailing ships. clipper ship When we look back at some of the ships used by early explorers, we have to admire the skill of the people who designed those ships of discovery. Setting sail into the unknown helped create the world we know today.
pages.brief: By the middle of the 1800s, sailors have explored and mapped most of the world’s coasts. A fast clipper ship with as many as thirty-five sails carries people across oceans in days, while a steam engine appears nearby, ready to replace wind power and end the age of sailing ships.

books.title: Living in Deserts
books.art_why: Suggested by keyword and covers traditional desert communities and historical ways of life.

pages.text: A Tuareg woman makes food outside her home in the Sahara. Demanding Deserts Dictionary definitions describe deserts as dry lands that can support little to no life. Desert landscapes can be very different, though. A desert can have trees and cacti. A desert can even have rocky mountains. Deserts usually aren’t dry all the time. Streams and rivers pass through some deserts, although they might remain dry for a long time. Many kinds of animals also live in the desert.
pages.brief: A Tuareg woman prepares food outside her home in the Sahara. The surrounding desert is dry land that supports little life, yet it may have trees, cacti, rocky mountains, and streams or rivers that stay dry for long periods. Many kinds of animals also live there.

pages.text: All deserts have something in common. Compared with the rest of the world, deserts are arid places. They usually get less than 25.4 centimeters (10 in.) of rain or snow each year. Deserts tend to have dry soil and not much plant life. Although some deserts can get very cold, most deserts are sunny and hot. Palm trees near an oasis in the Sahara in Egypt (top left); flowers in sand dunes in Australia (bottom left); running water in the Sonoran Desert (top right); the world’s largest salt flat, in Bolivia (bottom right)
pages.brief: Deserts are arid places with dry soil and little plant life, getting less than 25.4 centimeters of rain or snow each year. Most are sunny and hot, though some get very cold. Palm trees stand near an oasis in Egypt’s Sahara, flowers grow in Australian sand dunes, water runs in the Sonoran Desert, and Bolivia’s largest salt flat spreads out.

pages.text: Children run together in India’s Thar Desert. Five of the seven continents have hot deserts. Some deserts are small, but others are huge. Let’s take off and jet around the world. We will learn about some of the world’s deserts and the people who have called them home for thousands of years. People who live in the desert survive by adapting to their surroundings. They find food, water, and shelter, as in any other place on Earth. For people who live in desert areas, though, the desert isn’t just about getting by. The desert is so much more than that. It is home and a way of life.
pages.brief: Children run together in India’s Thar Desert. Hot deserts are on five of the seven continents, some small and some huge. People have called deserts home for thousands of years, adapting to their surroundings to find food, water, and shelter. For desert peoples, the desert is more than a place to survive; it is home and a way of life.

pages.text: The Tohono O’odham and the Sonoran Desert The Sonoran Desert stretches for 310,800 square kilometers (120,000 sq. mi.) across the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. Months may pass without any rain. Summer days can reach 49º Celsius (120ºF). Winter nights can dip below freezing, however. It rains more in the Sonoran Desert than in any other desert in the world! The Tohono O’odham (toe-HOE-noh OH-eh-dom) are Indigenous people who live in the Sonoran Desert. Tohono O’odham means “desert people.” The Sonoran Desert California New Mexico Arizona PACIFIC OCEAN Mexico NORTH NORTH AMERICA AMERICA More than 2,500 native plants grow in the Sonoran Desert, more than in any other desert in the world.
pages.brief: The Sonoran Desert stretches across the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. Months may pass without rain, summer days can reach 49°C, and winter nights can dip below freezing. More than 2,500 native plants grow there. The Tohono O’odham, whose name means desert people, live in this desert.

pages.text: For hundreds of years, people from Europe and the United States have taken land that the O’odham lived on for thousands of years. Today, the land where many O’odham live is divided among four groups. One is the Tohono O’odham Nation. The others are the O’odham people at the Gila River Indian Community, the Ak-Chin Indian Community, and the Salt River (Pima Maricopa) Indian Community. All four groups speak the O’odham language, but there are differences from tribe to tribe. O’odham people live in towns and cities, and on reservations. Francine Jose shows baskets made by her family long ago.
pages.brief: For hundreds of years, people from Europe and the United States have taken land where the O’odham lived for thousands of years. Today the land is divided among four groups: the Tohono O’odham Nation, Gila River Indian Community, Ak-Chin Indian Community, and Salt River (Pima Maricopa) Indian Community. Francine Jose shows baskets made by her family long ago.

pages.text: Over time, as more of their land was taken, the O’odham began to lead more modern lives. However, the O’odham people fought to keep their traditions over the years. Most O’odham include aspects of their traditions in their modern lives, such as farming, cooking traditional recipes, and basketmaking. Saguaro Fruit Harvesting The saguaro (suh-WAR-oh) cactus is an important part of O’odham culture. Each spring, beautiful flowers bloom on the cactus. Large red fruit then ripens in mid-June. The O’odham harvest the fruit from the tops of the giant cacti, which can reach upwards of 22 meters (75 ft.), using special tools. They turn the fruit into wine for their New Year ceremony in early July. An O’odham woman harvests saguaro fruit around 1907 (left). Today, O’odham still use traditional tools to harvest the fruit (right).
pages.brief: As more land was taken, the O’odham began leading more modern lives, but they kept traditions such as farming, cooking traditional recipes, and basketmaking. In spring, saguaro cactus flowers bloom; large red fruit ripens in mid-June. O’odham harvest fruit from giant cacti with special tools; an O’odham woman harvests saguaro fruit around 1907, and today O’odham still use traditional tools.

The Bedouin and the Sahara The Sahara stretches across northern Africa for 8.6 million square kilometers (3.3 million sq. mi). It is very hot and dry in the Sahara. Bedouin (BED-oo-in) people live in the Sahara and beyond. Because little rain falls in the Sahara, Bedouin have traditionally been nomadic. The Sahara Desert Morocco Tunisia Western Sahara Algeria Libya Egypt Mauritania Mali Chad Sudan Niger EUROPE EUROPE ATLANTIC OCEAN AFRICA AFRICA AFRICA In some parts of the Sahara, it rains less than 25 millimeters (1 in.) per year!
pages.brief: Bedouin children prepare to race their camels. The Sahara stretches across northern Africa, very hot and dry, and in some parts it rains less than 25 millimeters per year. Bedouin people live in the Sahara and beyond. Because little rain falls there, Bedouin have traditionally been nomadic.

pages.text: Homes in this Bedouin village in Egypt’s Sahara have walls made out of dried plants (top). The inside of this Bedouin home in Oman is colorful (bottom). Bedouin are animal herders who roam the desert during the rainy winter. Traditionally, they moved from oasis to oasis and also dug wells for water. Bedouin returned with their herds to farmland during the dry summer.
pages.brief: Homes in a Bedouin village in Egypt’s Sahara have walls made of dried plants; inside a Bedouin home in Oman, the walls are colorful. Bedouin are animal herders who roam the desert during the rainy winter, moving from oasis to oasis and digging wells for water. They return with their herds to farmland during the dry summer.

pages.text: Umm Sayhoun is a Bedouin village in Jordan. Traditional Bedouin homes were low, black, portable tents, called bayts, made out of goat hair or sheep’s wool. Bayts protect people from the sun, wind, and blowing sand. For the past hundred years, different countries have been taking over the land where Bedouin have lived for thousands of years. Many Bedouin are no longer nomadic. Instead, they live in houses and apartments in villages and cities. A Bedouin mother smiles with her son inside their home in Oman.
pages.brief: Umm Sayhoun is a Bedouin village in Jordan. Traditional Bedouin homes were low, black, portable tents called bayts, made from goat hair or sheep’s wool to protect people from sun, wind, and blowing sand. Countries have taken over Bedouin land. Many Bedouin now live in houses and apartments. A Bedouin mother smiles with her son in Oman.

pages.text: ASIA ASIA The Gobi Desert INDIAN OCEAN Mongolia China The Gobi is called a rain shadow desert. Mountains block rainy weather that would have let plants grow there. Mongolian Nomads of the Gobi The Gobi stretches for 1.3 million square kilometers (500,000 sq. mi.) from southern Mongolia to northern China, in Asia. Mongolian nomads live in the Gobi. Traditionally, they roamed the Gobi’s sand dunes and rocky mountains in cold, windy weather, herding horses, sheep, goats, cattle, and camels. A Mongolian woman herds her animals in the Gobi.
pages.brief: The Gobi stretches from southern Mongolia to northern China in Asia. It is called a rain shadow desert because mountains block rainy weather that would let plants grow. Mongolian nomads live in the Gobi. Traditionally, they roamed its sand dunes and rocky mountains in cold, windy weather, herding horses, sheep, goats, cattle, and camels. A Mongolian woman herds her animals.

pages.text: A Mongolian boy runs outside his family’s ger in the Gobi. Traditionally, home in the Gobi was a round tent or yurt covered in felt, called a ger. Inside, people were kept safe from cold nights and other weather. Fewer and fewer Mongolian nomads are left today. Harsh winters killed the herds of thousands of families. Changes in government also made life difficult for herders. Over the past thirty years, almost half a million nomads moved to the capital of Mongolia to look for work and food. Many brought their gers with them.
pages.brief: A Mongolian boy runs outside his family’s ger in the Gobi. Traditionally, home was a round tent or yurt covered in felt, called a ger, keeping people safe from cold nights. Fewer Mongolian nomads are left today. Harsh winters killed herds, government changes made life difficult, and almost half a million nomads moved to the capital for work and food.

pages.text: A Way of Life Each desert has different challenges, but the Indigenous peoples who live there have always found their own solutions. In the past, people who lived in the desert relied only on what they could find around them. Today, much has changed, and many people lead modern lives in the desert. However, some continue to live as their ancestors once did, and many continue to celebrate the traditions of their desert communities. Life in the desert is as demanding as it is rewarding. The people who make the desert their home have deep respect for their surroundings. They use its offerings while also honoring its power and beauty. A man walks a camel along a busy street in the United Arab Emirates.
pages.brief: Each desert has different challenges, but Indigenous peoples have always found their own solutions. In the past, people relied only on what they could find around them; today many lead modern lives in the desert. Some continue as their ancestors did and celebrate desert traditions. A man walks a camel along a busy street in the United Arab Emirates.

books.title: Australia
books.art_why: The book includes historical events before photography, so drawn scenes suit the whole book.

pages.text: Welcome to Australia The official name of Australia is the Commonwealth of Australia, but Australians call their land “Oz.” It is a place so unique, it might have come from a fantasy story rather than real life. Australia is the world’s largest island. Australia is the only country that is also a continent. In fact, it is the smallest and flattest continent. Australia has beautiful beaches and amazing wildlife. It is also a country with a fascinating and troubling history. The first European colony on Australia was a group of prisoners sent from Great Britain. Colonization greatly impacted the island’s Indigenous peoples. Australia is located in the southern half of Earth, so it is south of the equator. This means that it has the opposite seasons of places north of the equator. When it is winter in North America, for example, it is summer in Australia. June through August is winter in Australia. Read on to learn more about the country, the continent, and the island called the land “Down Under.”
pages.brief: Australia appears as the world’s largest island and the only country that is also a continent, surrounded by ocean, with beaches and native wildlife. A southern-hemisphere view contrasts Australia’s seasons with North America’s, while a small historical scene recalls the first British prisoners arriving.

pages.text: Tirhatuan Wetlands Conservation Reserve in Melbourne, Australia The Land Australia covers 7,692,024 square kilometers (2,969,907 sq. mi.) of land. The Indian Ocean borders Australia on the west and south. The Pacific Ocean surrounds the northern and eastern edges. Australia has three main areas: the Western Plateau, the Central Lowlands, and the Eastern Highlands. The Western Plateau covers over half of Australia. It is a flat, dry desert area with hot weather. Scientists have found the world’s oldest rocks in the Western Plateau. Dry grasslands are found in the Central Lowlands. There, it is hot all year during the day but can be very cold at night. The Great Dividing Range is part of the Eastern Highlands. It is home to rivers, valleys, and Australia’s highest mountains.
pages.brief: A wide view of Australia shows the Indian Ocean bordering the west and south and the Pacific Ocean around the north and east. The flat, dry Western Plateau holds old rocks; the Central Lowlands have dry grasslands; the Great Dividing Range rises with rivers, valleys and high mountains. Tirhatuan Wetlands Conservation Reserve in Melbourne is shown as a wetland scene.

pages.text: Some of Australia’s habitats include desert, grasslands, rainforests, and heathlands. Heathland areas are usually coastal, with low plants covering the ground. Northern Australia has a tropical climate, while the southeastern and southwestern areas are mostly mild. The middle of the country is mainly desert. Most areas in Australia have very few people living in them. Today, around ninety percent of Australians live in cities, mainly along the coasts. In Australia, most cities are located long distances from one another. Canberra is Australia’s capital city. Sydney is its largest city, with a population of more than five million. desert heathlands.
pages.brief: A land of habitats appears: desert, grasslands, rainforest and coastal heathlands with low ground plants. The tropical north, mild southeast and southwest, and desert middle are visible. Most people live in cities along the coasts, with Canberra as capital and Sydney as the largest city.

pages.text: Australia’s huge, dry inland area is known as the Outback, and few people live there. The Outback has enormous deserts and some mountainous regions. The landscape seems to stretch on forever. Rain may not fall there for years at a time. “Towns” in the Outback are typically made up of just a few buildings and are spread far apart. Some residents of the Outback live and work on enormous ranches called stations. Other people work in mining and oil production. Do You Know? Australia has over twenty thousand species of plants and animals. Eucalyptus, or gum trees, are Australia’s most common tree.
pages.brief: The huge, dry Outback stretches across inland Australia with enormous deserts and mountainous regions. Rain is absent for years. A few small towns of scattered buildings sit far apart, while residents work on enormous ranches called stations or in mining and oil production. Eucalyptus gum trees stand in the dry landscape.

pages.text: The People Thousands of years ago, Australia was home to many Indigenous peoples. Some think that around one million Indigenous peoples lived in Australia, while others think the number is lower. After the British colonized the continent, it was changed forever. Today, Australia is a nation with more than 25 million inhabitants. In 2020, around 91 percent of Australians were white and 7 percent were Asian. Less than 3 percent were Indigenous peoples.
pages.brief: Indigenous peoples are shown living across Australia thousands of years ago, before British colonization changed the continent forever. A modern crowd of more than 25 million Australians reflects the page’s mix of white, Asian and Indigenous inhabitants.

pages.text: History Two distinct groups are considered Indigenous Australians—Aboriginal peoples from the mainland of Australia and Torres Strait Islanders. After fifty thousand years of living in Australia, the lives of Indigenous peoples came to a stark halt in the seventeenth century. Europeans began to explore and colonize their land. The British saw Australia as a way to solve the problem of overcrowding in British prisons. In 1788, a settlement arrived in Australia from England with around 759 prisoners (568 men and 191 women). The settlement also had 200 soldiers and 40 wives and children of the soldiers. They lived in tents and ate native animals as well as food sent from England. A commander places the British flag in Sydney.
pages.brief: Aboriginal peoples and Torres Strait Islanders are shown as Indigenous Australians. In 1788 a British settlement arrives in Sydney with prisoners, soldiers, wives and children living in tents and eating native animals and food from England. A commander places the British flag in Sydney.

pages.text: Before the British colonized the land, Indigenous people belonging to more than 500 different groups lived in Australia. They had their own distinct languages and cultures. Between 1788 and 1798, about 90 percent of Australia’s Indigenous population was killed. Some died during violent encounters with the British and others from diseases brought by the colonizers. Indigenous peoples continually fought for their lands. They kept their cultures, languages, and traditions. By 1901, the population of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples had dropped to about 117,000. However, it has since risen to around pre-colonization numbers. The Stolen Generation Between 1910 and the 1970s, the Australian government took tens of thousands of children from Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander families. The children were adopted by white Australians and were forced to stay away from their indigenous cultures and traditions. The impact on these children, known as the “Stolen Generation,” is far-reaching. Indigenous people still struggle to recover from the terrible experience. Members of the Stolen Generation gathered when the Australian Prime Minister apologized to Indigenous Australians in 2008.
pages.brief: More than 500 distinct Indigenous groups with their own languages and cultures are shown before British colonization. Later, members of the Stolen Generation gather as the Australian Prime Minister apologizes in 2008. Indigenous peoples are shown fighting for their lands and keeping traditions through immense loss from violence and disease.

pages.text: Wildlife Australia’s history also affected its wildlife population. As cities have expanded, natural areas have grown smaller. This is making habitats and food scarce for some animals. The continent’s isolation and harsh conditions make it an ideal home for some animals. Animals found nowhere else on Earth live in Australia. Many of Australia’s mammals are marsupials, such as kangaroos and wallabies. These animals give birth to tiny babies that must live in a pouch or pocket on its mother’s body to continue to develop. Most marsupials disappeared long ago on other continents (South America still has some). But Australia’s isolation allowed many types of marsupials to thrive. Scientists aren’t exactly sure why. This baby kangaroo, or joey, is around four weeks old.
pages.brief: A mother kangaroo carries a tiny joey, about four weeks old, in her pouch while wallabies stand nearby. City expansion shrinks natural areas, making habitats and food scarce. Australia’s isolation and harsh conditions let marsupials such as kangaroos and wallabies thrive, though most marsupials disappeared on other continents.

pages.text: The platypus is an animal unique to Australia. It has four legs, fur, and beady eyes. It also has a tail like a beaver’s, a duck’s bill, and webbed feet. Adult males have venomous spurs on their back ankles. Although a platypus is a mammal, females lay eggs. One of Australia’s most extraordinary places is the Great Barrier Reef, which is located off the coast of northeastern Australia. It is the largest coral reef system in the world. Over 1,500 types of fish, 2,000 kinds of coral, and other sea creatures, sea plants, and birds live there. Climate change, fishing, coastal construction, and pollutants are all major threats to the reef. Many people are working to save the Great Barrier Reef. Bleached coral are likely to die, but they can still survive. A platypus uses its beak to hunt along the sea floor. Coral Bleaching When reef water gets too warm due to climate change, coral react by casting out the algae that live on them. Then the coral change color to all white and begin to starve.
pages.brief: A platypus with fur, beady eyes, a duck’s bill, beaver-like tail and webbed feet hunts along the sea floor. Offshore northeastern Australia, the Great Barrier Reef teems with fish, coral, sea creatures, plants and birds. Some coral is bleached white, and people work to save the reef from climate change, fishing, coastal construction and pollutants.

pages.text: Punamii-unpuu (Mitchell Falls) Things to Do The Sun is usually shining in Australia. Many Australians like to go to the beach and spend time out on the water. Some typical activities include swimming, surfing, snorkeling, scuba diving, and boating. Australia’s largest bay is Shark Bay. It is on the western part of the island and home to an incredible array of wildlife. The western area’s Kimberley region has breathtaking gorges, rocky shores, waterfalls, rivers, and beaches. Bondi Beach, in the southeast near Sydney, is one of the world’s most famous beaches.
pages.brief: Under a bright sun, Australians swim, surf, snorkel, scuba dive and boat in the ocean. Shark Bay on the western side holds abundant wildlife. The Kimberley region shows gorges, rocky shores, waterfalls, rivers and beaches, while Bondi Beach near Sydney appears as a famous southeast beach.

pages.text: Uluru A three- or four-day train journey across the entire continent takes visitors through Australia’s different habitats. They can witness breathtaking sights, such as the rocky peaks and gorges of the Flinders Ranges in the Outback. Trips to explore the Outback never disappoint. Visitors hike, discover wildlife, and swim in wild water holes. Uluru, the world’s largest monolith, or single rock, is a sacred site of the Anangu peoples. It is located about two hundred miles west of Alice Springs, in a region called Red Centre. Sydney is an important destination in Australia. Visitors enjoy the city’s harbor and the Sydney Harbor Bridge, the largest steel arch bridge in the world. They also take in the beauty of one of the most famous modern buildings, the Sydney Opera House. The Sydney Opera House has millions of roof tiles.
pages.brief: A train crosses the continent through different habitats, passing rocky peaks and gorges of the Flinders Ranges in the Outback. Visitors hike, discover wildlife and swim in wild water holes. Uluru, a huge single rock sacred to the Anangu peoples, rises in the Red Centre. Sydney’s harbor, Harbour Bridge and Opera House appear.

pages.text: Down Under Australia’s isolated location has allowed it to develop in many unique ways. The island is celebrated for its natural beauty. It is also known for being the world’s biggest island and the only country to also be a continent. Much about the land Down Under, from its unique creatures to its incredible landscapes, is unlike any place else on Earth. Many Australians enjoy surfing the waves along the country’s beautiful beaches.
pages.brief: Australia’s isolated island continent is celebrated for natural beauty, unique creatures and incredible landscapes unlike anywhere else on Earth. It is the world’s biggest island and the only country that is also a continent. Australians surf the waves along beautiful beaches.

books.title: Giant Insects
books.art_why: A giant-insect guide with a prehistoric reconstruction and scale illustrations, matching the suggested keyword check.

pages.text: Insects Are Everywhere! Every time you step outside your door, you probably look right past hundreds— even thousands—of insects. Scientists estimate that there are around ten quintillion (10,000,000,000,000,000,000) insects alive on Earth at any given time. So far, they have identified over 900,000 different insect species —about 80 percent of all the world’s animal species. They think that two to thirty million more species remain undiscovered or unidentified. It’s no surprise that many people are glad most insects are small. This wasn’t always the case, though. Hundreds of millions of years ago, before dinosaurs walked on Earth, insects were already buzzing around. Using fossil evidence, we know these insects were similar to modern insects—they each had three body sections, six legs, and often two sets of wings. They were a bit different in other ways, though. These critters were titans!
pages.brief: A person steps outside a door and into a world of insects, with hundreds or thousands of tiny insects scattered in the air. In the background, ancient insects with three body sections, six legs, and two sets of wings buzz before dinosaurs, showing the giant titans of long ago.

pages.text: This drawing shows what a Meganeura might have looked like. The prehistoric Meganeura looked like a dragonfly. However, it had a wingspan of well over 30 inches (72.2 cm). Scientists think insects grew so huge partly because back then, Earth had more oxygen in the air. Over hundreds of millions of years, the amount of oxygen dropped from about 35 percent to today’s 21 percent. As a result, the insects adapted, evolved, and became smaller. A few insects, however, have remained the giants of their world. These beasts spark many people’s curiosity, and hopefully they’ll spark yours as well. You’re about to set out on a bug- hunting adventure around the world. You might call it a giant insect safari. You’ll pass by billions of smaller insects as you search the globe for these huge monsters. You’ll have the chance to see them with your own eyes and learn some fascinating details about them. Prepare your pack—you’re about to head out. Get ready to be surprised!
pages.brief: A large Meganeura, looking like a dragonfly with a wingspan well over 30 inches, flies through prehistoric air. Around it are smaller insects, showing how insects became smaller as oxygen dropped. A traveler prepares a pack for a giant insect safari around the world.

pages.text: Giant Darner Dragonfly: The Speed Demon Your journey starts by a slow-running stream in the southwestern United States. You hear the buzzing of a giant darner dragonfly. It uses its 5-inch (12.7 cm) wingspan to zip through the warm air at speeds of over 35 miles per hour (56.3 kph). These insects are so good at turning that they can completely shift direction in a split second. That’s when you catch a glimpse of one. This insect’s speed and ability to move come in handy as it hunts mosquitoes and other small insects. The dragonfly lands on your arm, but you have nothing to worry about. The giant darner dragonfly is harmless. You look at it just long enough to see the shimmering wings and black, blue, and green 5-inch (12.7 cm) body before it takes off again. As you walk through the tall grass on your way to your next destination, you see flashes of other dragonflies—giant darners and their smaller cousins. You wish them good hunting. Giant darner dragonflies live near streams like this one in the southwestern United States.
pages.brief: By a slow-running stream in the southwestern United States, a giant darner dragonfly zips through warm air with shimmering wings and a black, blue, and green body. It hunts mosquitoes, turns in a split second, and lands on a person's arm. Tall grass and smaller dragonfly cousins are nearby.

pages.text: (12.7 cm) female giant darner dragonfly male giant darner dragonfly.
pages.brief: A female giant darner dragonfly and a male giant darner dragonfly are shown close together. The two insects have long bodies and shimmering wings. They rest side by side, showing the female and male forms of this dragonfly species.

pages.text: Titan Beetle: The Pencil Breaker You’ve arrived in the steamy Amazon rainforest. It’s dark, and you can hear the tapping of rain on the leaves overhead. Something flies through the beam of your flashlight. At first, you think it’s a bird. You look closer and see it’s a 7-inch (17.8 cm) titan beetle—the biggest beetle in the world. This nocturnal creature was attracted to your light. As you watch it crawl its way through the dead leaves and dirt, you see the thick mandibles on its head. They’re strong enough to snap through a pencil. You’re tempted to find a stick to see if the titan beetle can break it. When you get near, though, it hisses and you back off. Like many beetles, this one has only a few weeks to live as an adult. It doesn’t have time to mess with you—it needs to find a mate. Though it can fly, it’s too heavy to take off from the ground. It uses its powerful, spiny legs to climb a tree and launch itself from a branch. You duck as it flies toward your face. Laughing, you continue your journey. titan beetle.
pages.brief: In the dark, steamy Amazon rainforest, a 7-inch titan beetle crawls through dead leaves and dirt. Its thick mandibles are open near a pencil. A person with a flashlight watches as the beetle hisses, climbs a tree with spiny legs, and launches from a branch toward the person's face.

pages.text: (17.8 cm) titan beetle taking off from a branch.
pages.brief: A titan beetle takes off from a branch. Its hard shell and spiny legs are visible as it spreads its wings, launching into the air. The beetle is about 7 inches long, the biggest beetle in the world.

pages.text: Giant Water Bug: The Toe Biter The afternoon in Thailand is hot and humid. You stop to look into a clear, cool-looking freshwater pond. The idea of dangling your aching feet in the water is tempting, but then you see the giant water bug. You recognize it because this insect is found in bodies of fresh water all around the world. It’s about 5 inches (12.7 cm) long. It clings to an underwater plant while holding a minnow in its powerful front legs. It eats by using its strong jaws to force digestive juices into the struggling fish. Then it sucks out the remains. You see a few other giant water bugs. One must be a male, as it has round eggs stuck on its back. After mating, the female giant water bug glues the eggs there for safety until they hatch. Another giant water bug tries to catch a tadpole and misses. These bugs will eat pretty much anything they can overpower, including frogs, snakes, and even baby turtles. Their bite isn’t dangerous to people. Even so, you remember one of the local people saying they have one of the most painful bites of all insects. She said this just before taking a big, crunchy bite out of a grilled giant water bug. The water may look perfect, but you decide not to stop.
pages.brief: In a clear freshwater pond in hot, humid Thailand, a giant water bug clings to an underwater plant while gripping a minnow in its front legs. Nearby, a male carries round eggs on his back, and another water bug reaches for a tadpole. A person at the pond holds a grilled giant water bug.

pages.text: N Where they live Putting the Bite on Insects: People have been eating insects since prehistoric times. Over 1,000 types are eaten in many parts of the world. They include water bugs, cockroaches, ants, dragonflies, and grasshoppers.
pages.brief: A world map shows lands where giant insects are found. Beside it, people gather and eat insects such as water bugs, cockroaches, ants, dragonflies, and grasshoppers, a practice that goes back to prehistoric times and continues in many parts of the world.

pages.text: Goliath Beetle: The Heavyweight You’re back to walking through a rainforest. You’re not surprised since most of Earth’s insects live in rainforests. This time you’re in Central Africa. The rainy season has made the air feel heavy and thick. You hear a shuffling sound and look around. You find a female Goliath beetle using her head to dig in the soil. She’s making a safe place to lay her eggs. You take a moment to examine the patterns on her shell. Another beetle buzzes by and lands on a tree. It’s a male Goliath beetle. You can tell by the Y-shaped horns on the front of his head. He’s almost 5 inches (12.7 cm) long; the female is smaller. These beetles didn’t get their name for their length. They earned it for being the heaviest insects in the world. This male looks as if he will weigh in near the top of the range at over 3.5 ounces (100 g). The Goliath beetle is big but harmless. It eats the waste that falls to the forest floor. You think about getting the male to climb on your arm, but you change your mind when another male shows up. If you wait, the two males may fight each other using their impressive strength and horns. The smaller male flies away quickly, though. That means it’s time for you to move on, too.
pages.brief: In a rainy Central African rainforest, a female Goliath beetle uses her head to dig in the soil, making a safe place for eggs. A male with Y-shaped horns lands on a tree. He is almost 5 inches long and very heavy. The female is smaller, and another male flies away.

pages.text: (12.7 cm) female Goliath beetle male Goliath beetle.
pages.brief: A female Goliath beetle and a male Goliath beetle are shown. The male has Y-shaped horns on the front of his head and is larger. The female is smaller. Both have patterned shells and are among the heaviest insects in the world.

pages.text: African Driver Ant: The Ultimate Army You’re about to leave the African rainforest when you come upon what looks like a dark stream running across the ground. You move closer, but not too close. Millions of African driver ants march along the ground. In the center, you see the small worker ants. They aren’t much bigger than the ants you see at home. Along the edges, the soldier ants, each almost 1 inch (2.5 cm) long, form a wall. Their large mandibles point outward to protect the ants within. These insects are on the hunt, so they’re very dangerous. Though blind, they find their way easily using touch, smell, and chemical signals. Colonies can have over twenty-two million ants (the largest colonies of any insect on Earth), and they’re all hungry. Millions upon millions of ants swarm in search of food. They eat pretty much any animal they can overpower—including people. a column of African driver ants.
pages.brief: Millions of African driver ants march across the ground like a dark stream. Small worker ants fill the center, while larger soldier ants with outward-pointing mandibles form a wall along the edges. The blind ants hunt using touch, smell, and chemical signals. They swarm in search of food and can overpower animals, including people.

pages.text: You decide to follow the ant column to see if you can find the nest. Against a large rock, you see a dark wall of movement. The ants have formed a temporary nest made out of living ants. As you watch, this nest begins to break up. They must have exhausted the food supply of the area. The ant column carries away food, millions of eggs, and the queen. At over 2 inches (5.1 cm) long, she is the largest ant on Earth. She can lay up to two million eggs each month. Despite the amazing sight, you start to notice a few ants crawling in your direction and decide it’s probably best to get out of there. 1 inch (2.5 cm) larger soldier ants protecting the smaller worker ants.
pages.brief: Against a large rock, African driver ants form a temporary nest made of living ants. The nest begins to break apart as the column carries away food, millions of eggs, and the queen, the largest ant on Earth at over 2 inches long. A person notices ants crawling toward them and moves away.

pages.text: Madagascar Hissing Cockroach: The Noisy Pet It’s a lovely day in tropical Madagascar as you walk through the forest. You decide to sit down on a log beside a slow-moving stream. When you do, the log moves—and something hisses. You look down to see you’ve upset a colony of Madagascar hissing cockroaches. Each about 2 to 3 inches (5.1–7.6 cm) long with a shell of black and dark orange, they crawl back into the shade of the log. It’s too early for them to be out. At night, this colony would be crawling along the forest floor, looking for fallen fruit and dead plants. Unlike most species of cockroaches, the Madagascar hissing cockroach can’t fly, and the females give birth to live young instead of laying eggs. You reach out and touch a cockroach. It’s a male by the look of the long horns on its head. It hisses, pushing air out through small holes along its body, and then spits. You laugh because these insects are gentle and harmless. In fact, you have a friend who keeps a number of them as pets. You’d like to stay and watch, but it’s time to move on. Besides, you can watch your friend’s cockroaches. a pet Madagascar hissing cockroach.
pages.brief: In a tropical Madagascar forest, a person sits on a log beside a slow-moving stream and upsets a colony of hissing cockroaches. The black and dark orange insects crawl into the shade. One male with long horns hisses, pushing air through small holes, then spits. The gentle cockroaches are harmless and can be kept as pets.

pages.text: Madagascar hissing cockroaches 2–3 inches (5.1–7.6 cm)
pages.brief: A colony of Madagascar hissing cockroaches is shown close together. The insects have black and dark orange shells and measure about 2 to 3 inches long. Several cockroaches crawl over one another as they gather in a group.

pages.text: Wetapunga: The God of Ugly Things On Little Barrier Island off the coast of New Zealand, you hunt through the trees in search of the endangered wetapunga, or giant weta. These strange cricketlike insects’ name means “the god of ugly things” in the native Maori language. They have lived on these islands for millions of years. Over the last few hundred years, however, they have almost been wiped out due to the introduction of rats and mice, which eat the slow wetapunga. As the Sun begins to set, you find a wetapunga hiding among the leaves of a tree. It looks like a cross between a cricket and a grasshopper, only much bigger. The largest one ever found was about 4 inches (10.5 cm) long and 2.5 ounces (70.9 g). This one looks to be almost that big. It crawls slowly along the branch, nibbling on leaves. It will spend almost its entire life in trees. You could catch it if you wanted, as these insects can’t fly or jump, nor do they kick or bite. You decide to leave it alone since you have to run back to town. A group that is trying to bring back wetapungas plans to release a number of them into the wild, and you want to be there. giant weta.
pages.brief: On Little Barrier Island off New Zealand, a giant weta hides among the leaves of a tree at sunset. The endangered, cricketlike insect crawls slowly along a branch, nibbling leaves. It cannot fly or jump. Rats and mice have nearly wiped out these slow insects, but a group plans to release more into the wild.

pages.text: 4 inches (10.5 cm)
pages.brief: A female giant wetapunga is shown alone. The cricketlike insect is about 4 inches long, with a heavy body and long legs. It is the female form of the giant weta, an endangered insect from New Zealand.

pages.text: Queen Alexandra’s Birdwing Butterfly and Atlas Moth In a rope chair high above the ground, you look around at the forest canopy of Papua New Guinea. Lush green surrounds you for miles. Then you see a flash of blue rise up. It’s a male Queen Alexandra’s birdwing butterfly flapping its shimmering blue-green and brown wings, which span almost 8 inches (20.3 cm). You look around for a female but don’t find one. Females would be larger, with a 12-inch (30.5 cm) wingspan of a lighter shade of brown. Other than in zoos, this rare species can only be found in the wild in Papua New Guinea, and only in the forest canopy. You watch in awe as the male feeds on a flower and flutters away. On your way down, something else catches your eye. You stop and pull yourself closer to a branch where an atlas moth sits, its wingspan 11 inches (27.9 cm) wide. The hooks on the ends of its wings remind you of this moth’s other name: the snake head moth. The Queen Alexandra’s butterfly lives up to three months or more and feeds regularly. However, the atlas moth lives only a few weeks and never feeds. You’ve seen this species before, as it’s fairly common throughout Southeast Asia, but it’s still an impressive sight.
pages.brief: High in a rope chair above the forest canopy of Papua New Guinea, a person watches a male Queen Alexandra's birdwing butterfly with shimmering blue-green and brown wings. Nearby, an atlas moth rests on a branch, its wings 11 inches wide. The butterfly feeds on a flower while the moth, which never feeds, stays still.

pages.text: (20.3 cm) male Queen Alexandra’s birdwing butterfly 11 inches (27.9 cm) atlas moth.
pages.brief: A male Queen Alexandra's birdwing butterfly is shown with a wingspan of almost 8 inches, its wings shimmering blue-green and brown. Beside it rests an atlas moth with an 11-inch wingspan. The moth's wingtips have hooks that remind people of a snake's head.

pages.text: Chan’s Megastick: The Hidden Wonder Your final stop brings you to the London Natural History Museum. You’ve come to view the world’s longest insect: Chan’s megastick. One of only six found in the world so far (all of them in Borneo), this one is the longest. The whole insect, with its legs extended, stretches 22 inches (55.9 cm) under the glass. The body alone is 14 inches (35.6 cm) long. 22 inches (55.9 cm) It really does look like a plain old stick, which might explain why scientists didn’t discover it until 2008. Like other stick insects, this species is believed to hide within the forest canopy while it feeds on leaves. 14 inches (35.6 cm) Chan’s megastick.
pages.brief: At the London Natural History Museum, Chan's megastick lies under glass. With its legs extended, the world's longest insect stretches 22 inches; its body alone is 14 inches long. It looks like a plain stick. This species was not discovered until 2008 and is believed to hide in the forest canopy while feeding on leaves.

pages.text: As you leave the museum, you begin to wonder how many new species of insects you passed during your travels. They might be heavier than a Goliath beetle, stronger than a titan beetle, or more dangerous than a colony of driver ants. The only way to know is to keep learning, keep exploring—and keep your eyes open. three-horned beetle peacock katydid with wings flared.
pages.brief: A person leaves the museum and wonders how many new insect species were passed during the journey. Nearby are a hickory horn devil caterpillar, a giant stag beetle, a three-horned beetle, and a peacock katydid with wings flared. The scene invites keeping eyes open for more insects.

books.title: Woods of Wonder
books.art_why: Old-growth forests, parks, and animals exist in the real world today.

pages.text: Woods of Wonder.
pages.brief: A wide view of a wondrous woodland, with many trees and branches standing throughout the forest. The inviting scene suggests a place full of wonder, where the reader can imagine exploring among the many trees.

pages.text: Oh, That’s Old! Imagine you’re in a dark, lovely forest. Trees with trunks wider than cars tower overhead. Smaller plants soak up what little light they can find. Pine needles and other dead leaves cover the ground. Like something out of a fairy tale, an old-growth forest is a place of wonder and mystery.
pages.brief: Inside a dark, lovely old-growth forest, trees with massive trunks tower overhead while smaller plants soak up weak light. Pine needles and dead leaves blanket the ground. The scene feels like a fairy tale, full of wonder and mystery.

pages.text: Some old-growth forests look like this scene. Others look very different. Some have only one type of tree, while others have many. Some have trees that seem to touch the sky. Others have trees shorter than a house. Because of all these differences, scientists do not have one definition for an old-growth forest. However, they have found some things that many old-growth forests share. Many scientists agree that an old- growth forest must be at least 150 years old. The trees within the forest might be many different ages, though, including large trees, both living and dead (or dying). Standing dead trees, called snags, and fallen trees provide food and shelter for different animals, plants, and fungi. Looking up in an old-growth forest can make you dizzy!
pages.brief: A varied old-growth forest with some areas of one tree type and others mixed, tall trees and shorter trees. Large living trees stand with dead snags and fallen logs, providing shelter for plants and fungi. Looking upward, the canopy rises dizzily high.

pages.text: Forest Levels Canopy Tall trees like pines, maples, and oaks Understory Small trees and bushes Forest floor Grasses, mosses, ferns, and logs The forest’s canopy should have more than one layer. Fallen trees make holes in the canopy where young trees can find sunlight to grow. Old-growth forests are some of the most beautiful and interesting places on Earth. By studying and taking care of them, we can learn a lot.
pages.brief: A forest shown in layers: tall pines, maples, and oaks form a multi-layered canopy; small trees and bushes fill the understory; grasses, mosses, ferns, and logs cover the forest floor. A gap left by a fallen tree lets sunlight reach young trees growing below.

pages.text: United States Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks in California together cover more than 1,353 square miles (3,504 sq km). They hold more than 300 square miles (777 sq km) of old-growth forest, made up mostly of coniferous trees. Among these are giant sequoias, found only in California. These huge trees are among the oldest on Earth. They can live for more than 3,000 years. A giant sequoia known as the General Sherman Tree is the largest tree in the world.
pages.brief: In Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks in California, enormous giant sequoias tower among coniferous old-growth forest. One especially massive sequoia, the General Sherman Tree, stands as the largest tree in the world, surrounded by other huge trunks.

pages.text: The Pacific fisher lives in the parks’ old-growth forest, under the thick canopy. It hunts birds and small mammals. Its favorite meal is porcupine. Because its habitat is limited to old-growth forests, some states are taking steps to protect it. Sequoia vs. Redwood Giant redwoods and giant sequoias both grow in California. They have the same color bark. Both are huge, but they’re different. Giant redwoods are the tallest trees in the world. They can reach up to 378 feet (115 m)! Giant sequoias are the largest. At up to 40 feet (12 m) in diameter, a sequoia can grow almost twice as wide as a redwood. Redwoods grow best in fog. Sequoias need dry heat for their cones to open. Redwoods grow near sea level. Sequoias grow at 5,000 to 7,000 feet (1,524 to 2,134 m).
pages.brief: A Pacific fisher moves beneath the thick canopy, hunting birds and small mammals in old-growth forest. In California, giant redwoods and giant sequoias stand as huge trees with the same bark color; redwoods are tallest, while sequoias are widest.

pages.text: Across the United States in North Carolina and Tennessee, Great Smoky Mountains National Park covers more than 800 square miles (2,072 sq km). Almost all of the park is forest. Old-growth forests only make up about a quarter of the park. Deciduous trees make up most of the old-growth forests in this area.
pages.brief: In Great Smoky Mountains National Park across North Carolina and Tennessee, forest covers almost all the land. A smaller old-growth area within the park is filled mostly with deciduous trees, their broad leaves making up the woodland.

pages.text: Northern flying squirrel The endangered Carolina northern flying squirrel makes its home here. These small mammals don’t really fly. They use skin attached to their front and back paws to glide. They mostly eat fungi but may also eat fruits and nuts. Without the old-growth forest, these animals would vanish. Tough, Not Tall Not all old-growth forests have towering trees. In some harsh places with wild and icy winds, pines, spruces, and other coniferous trees grow short and twisted. These trees are called Krummholz, a German word meaning “crooked wood.” They are only about 6 feet (1.8 m) tall, but don’t let their size fool you: Some are one thousand years old.
pages.brief: A Carolina northern flying squirrel glides between trunks using skin between its paws, then feeds on fungi, fruits, and nuts. Nearby, in a harsh windy place, short twisted coniferous pines and spruces called Krummholz grow only about six feet tall, though some are a thousand years old.

pages.text: A Japanese beech tree reaches for the sun in Shirakami-Sanchi, Japan. Japan In the northern part of Japan is Shirakami- Sanchi. It’s one of the last old-growth forests in East Asia. Made up mostly of beech trees, the area covers just 65 square miles (170 sq km) of the mountains. Forests like this one once covered most of northern Japan, but people have cut many down.
pages.brief: In Shirakami-Sanchi in northern Japan, a Japanese beech tree reaches toward the sun. This small mountain old-growth forest, made up mostly of beech trees, is one of the last in East Asia, though forests like it once covered much more of northern Japan.

pages.text: Shirakami-Sanchi has no trails or buildings, and animals in the area are protected. The forest is home to the Japanese serow. This goatlike animal is only found here and in two other small areas in Japan. More than 2,100 types of insects and 87 types of birds live in the forest. These include the black woodpecker, which is endangered in Japan. Japanese serow Black woodpeckers.
pages.brief: In a protected Shirakami-Sanchi forest with no trails or buildings, a goatlike Japanese serow stands among the trees. An endangered black woodpecker clings to a trunk nearby, sharing the old-growth woodland with many insects and birds.

pages.text: Fallen trees like this fir can nurse along other plants in this old-growth forest in the Caucasus of Russia. Russia Russia’s Western Caucasus area stretches about 1,062 square miles (2,750 sq km) from the Black Sea to the Caucasus Mountains. The area has many different plants and animals. Coniferous trees make up most of the forests.
pages.brief: In the Western Caucasus of Russia, a fallen fir tree lies on the forest floor, nursing other plants along its trunk. The old-growth forest stretches from the Black Sea to the Caucasus Mountains, with coniferous trees making up most of the woodland and many plants and animals living there.

pages.text: Snow leopards Different kinds of endangered animals make these forests their home. Some scientists think that a few endangered snow leopards live here. Scientists sometimes find signs of the large cats, such as paw prints and droppings. The endangered wisent has also been brought back into the forest. Wisents are European bison.
pages.brief: In the Caucasus forest, a snow leopard moves among the trees; scientists sometimes find its paw prints and droppings. A European bison called a wisent has also been brought back into the woodland, where endangered animals make their home.

pages.text: Conclusion Old-growth forests often have very complex ecosystems. They may have been supporting life for hundreds or thousands of years. Governments, national parks, and other groups protect many of these places. However, other old-growth forests, both small and large, are in danger. Human actions can damage or destroy these delicate environments. Once gone, the beauty and scientific information that these old-growth forests hold may be lost forever. Laws prevent logging in some old-growth forests but not others. People continue to debate how much protection is enough.
pages.brief: A complex old-growth ecosystem stands with many layers of life, supported for hundreds or thousands of years. Around it, people discuss protection as some forests are guarded by laws and parks, while others face damage from human actions and the risk of being lost.

books.title: Owls Overhead
books.art_why: Owls, their habitats, and the people who study or photograph them exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Tawny owl Flying in the Moonlight It’s a quiet, moonlit night, and you walk along a dirt path on the edge of town. Suddenly, a shadow crosses your path, but you hear no sound. You look up as a dark shape glides over you and disappears into the nearby trees. It’s an owl—one of more than two hundred different species of owls that live around the world. They come in many sizes and live on every continent except Antarctica.
pages.brief: On a quiet moonlit night, a person walks along a dirt path at the edge of town. A dark owl glides silently overhead, crosses the path as a shadow, and disappears into nearby trees. The scene suggests one of more than two hundred owl species living around the world.

pages.text: Eyes for the Night Many of the adaptations that help owls survive also make them seem mysterious. For instance, most owls hunt at night. As a result, they don’t have to compete with daytime hunters such as eagles, hawks, and falcons. Like most birds, owls can’t move their eyes in their sockets. Instead, owls must turn their heads to track a moving object. Owls are able to rotate their heads almost all the way around—280 degrees. They can even turn their heads upside down. Burrowing owl Northern hawk owl.
pages.brief: At night, a burrowing owl and a northern hawk owl are shown. One owl turns its head far around, almost all the way, to track something moving because its eyes cannot move in their sockets. It can even turn its head upside down while hunting in the dark.

pages.text: An owl’s pupils are small in bright light (top) and large in low light (bottom). Owls’ big eyes are an adaptation, too. These birds can’t see in total darkness. However, their pupils—the black circles in the center of their eyes—can grow large to let in more light. Their large pupils let them see better in low light than most animals. In fact, when light is low, tawny owls see as much as one hundred times better than humans.
pages.brief: A close view compares an owl's pupils in bright light and low light. In bright light the pupils are small; in low light they grow large, letting in more light. The owl's big eyes help it see better in darkness, as much as one hundred times better than humans.

pages.text: The hairlike feathers on owls’ faces help them react to things they touch. Some owls even have these feathers on their feet! As good as their night vision is, owls can’t see things close to their faces. Instead, hairlike feathers work like feelers to help owls react to things they touch, sort of like a cat’s whiskers. Pellets! Owls can’t chew or grind their food. Instead, they often swallow small prey whole. They can’t digest the unwanted parts of the animals. Teeth, claws, and small bones, stuck together with bits of fur or feathers, end up in the gizzard. That’s a part of their stomach with strong muscles that roll those parts into small balls, called pellets. A few hours after they eat, owls cough up a pellet. Scientists look through the pellets to learn what owls eat. Owl pellet.
pages.brief: An owl's face and feet show hairlike feathers that work like feelers. Nearby, an owl pellet lies on the ground after being coughed up. It holds teeth, claws, small bones, fur, and feathers. A scientist examines the pellet to learn what the owl ate.

pages.text: Owl skull Owls have very large ears, which are hidden under feathers. Some owls have thin skin that covers the ears’ openings. Upper ear Lower ear Even Better Ears To hunt, however, most owls rely on their hearing. Most owls have huge ears, with one higher than the other. The higher one hears sounds from above, while the lower one hears sounds from below. Their flat, round faces help funnel sounds to their ears. By moving the feathers around their faces, owls can send more sound to one ear or the other. Doing this helps them locate prey.
pages.brief: A close view of an owl skull shows large ear openings hidden under feathers, with one ear higher than the other. Beside it, an owl's flat, round face funnels sounds toward the ears. The owl can move face feathers to send more sound to one ear or the other.

pages.text: Owls, such as this barn owl, often crush their prey with their strong feet and sharp talons. The grip of some owls can be ten times stronger than a human’s grip. Their hearing is so good that they can hear bugs in grass or mice in snow. In fact, owls have better hearing than any other group of birds. Great gray owls can hear a mouse hidden under 18 inches (46 cm) of snow. Once they’ve located their prey, they can dive under the snow to grab a meal. Barn owls can hear a mouse moving 90 feet (27 m) away and catch one in complete darkness. They have the best hearing of any animal ever tested.
pages.brief: A barn owl grips prey with strong feet and sharp talons. The owl's hearing is so good it can hear bugs in grass or mice under snow. A great gray owl can dive beneath deep snow after a hidden mouse, while a barn owl can catch a mouse in complete darkness.

pages.text: Silent Hunters Many animals that owls hunt also have excellent hearing. So if an owl wants to eat, it must attack by surprise. The soft feathers that cover owls’ bodies allow them to fly silently. A great horned owl will sit high on a tree branch, watching until the time is right to attack. A skillful hunter, it feeds on many kinds of animals, even skunks and snakes. In Florida, one great horned owl tackled a 6-foot (2 m) indigo snake and won. It also eats birds, including eight other owl species. In fact, many large owls eat small owls. Great horned owls are excellent hunters. They can even catch another bird in flight.
pages.brief: A great horned owl sits high on a tree branch at night, watching for the right moment to attack. Its soft feathers let it fly silently. The skillful hunter feeds on many animals, including skunks, snakes, and birds, and it can even catch another bird in flight.

pages.text: Elf owl Snowy owl While most owls hunt only at night, snowy owls hunt mostly during the day. That’s because summer nights in the Arctic are so short. The tiny elf owl hunts during the day as well, feeding mostly on insects. The main diet for most owls, though, is small mammals—lots of them. A hungry great gray owl may eat 1,400 voles in a year. In its lifetime, a barn owl may eat 11,000 mice!
pages.brief: In daylight in the Arctic, a snowy owl hunts while summer nights are short. The tiny elf owl also hunts by day, catching insects. Most owls eat small mammals, though: a great gray owl may eat 1,400 voles in a year, and a barn owl may eat 11,000 mice in its lifetime.

pages.text: A barn owl lives up to its name by raising its young in a barn. Where Owls Live Some owls can live in many different habitats. The great horned owl lives in swamps, forests, prairies, mountains, and deserts. Barn owls live under bridges as well as in caves, empty houses, church towers—and barns, of course!
pages.brief: A barn owl raises its young inside a barn, living up to its name. Elsewhere, a great horned owl may live in swamps, forests, prairies, mountains, or deserts. Barn owls also live under bridges, in caves, empty houses, church towers, and barns.

pages.text: An Owl’s Housekeeper Screech owls in Texas hunt snakes. However, they bring one kind of snake back to their nest alive: the blindsnake. They let it go inside the nest, where it eats the maggots that feed on the dead animals stored there. The snake becomes a housekeeper! Some owls require a special habitat, though. Burrowing owls live mostly on the prairie and nest underground, using old burrows dug by mammals. When open spaces are hard to find, they move to cemeteries and golf courses, and even near airport runways.
pages.brief: In Texas, a screech owl brings a live blindsnake to its nest. The snake eats maggots that feed on dead animals stored there, acting as a housekeeper. On the prairie, burrowing owls nest underground in old mammal burrows, and when open spaces are scarce they use cemeteries, golf courses, or areas near airport runways.

pages.text: Spotted owls can only survive in old-growth forests. By 1994, 80 percent of their former habitat had been destroyed by logging. To protect the spotted owl, loggers cut down fewer trees, but barred owls have since taken over spotted owl habitat. Today, they outnumber spotted owls in the northwestern United States.
pages.brief: A spotted owl perches in an old-growth forest. In the background, logged trees show that much of its former habitat was destroyed. A barred owl sits nearby in the same northwestern forest; barred owls have taken over spotted owl habitat and now outnumber spotted owls in the northwestern United States.

pages.text: Owl Sounds Owls aren’t always silent, nor do they all hoot. They use different sounds to call a mate, warn of danger, or claim an area. Each species has its own calls that set it apart from other owls. A great horned owl can bark like a dog and meow like a cat. Barn owls don’t hoot—they scream. Their strange cry and ghostly appearance once made some people think of barn owls as bad luck. Photographers take pictures of a great gray owl, the largest species of owl in the world. Owls Are Out There It’s rare to see an owl, but they’re out there. If you’re in the country and want to spot one, try going out at dawn or dusk. Listen for their calls. If you stay out late enough, people might think you’re an owl—a night owl, that is.
pages.brief: At dusk, a great gray owl, the largest owl species, perches while photographers take its picture. Nearby, a barn owl opens its beak in a scream. The countryside scene suggests people listening for owl calls at dawn or dusk, and maybe staying out late as a night owl.

books.title: Forests on Fire
books.art_why: Historic fire scenes and forest cycles are shown as reconstructed views.

pages.text: Forests on Fire.
pages.brief: A dense forest stands with flames rising through the trees, while smoke fills the sky above. The fire moves through the forest, showing a forest on fire, with no people present and the landscape dominated by burning trees and drifting smoke.

pages.text: The 1988 Yellowstone fires set two world records. They were the most expensive, costing taxpayers $120 million; and they burned the most acres in a single day—165,000. Yellowstone on Fire Yellowstone is America’s oldest national park and one of its best loved. With its hot, dry summers and close-packed lodgepole pines, the park is no stranger to forest fires. Until 1988, the park’s largest fire on record covered 25,000 acres. At more than 2.2 million acres, Yellowstone is big enough to handle such fires now and then.
