During the summer of 1988, though, the park saw a set of huge fires. Most of the fires were started by lightning. Careless people started others. Some fires started in forests outside the park and burned their way in. Firefighters tried to control the fires caused by people from the start, but other fires were allowed to burn. Then on July 14, winds up to 80 miles per hour (129 kph) swept in. Many park visitors were ordered to leave. In their place, 25,000 firefighters from all over the country came in to fight the fires.
pages.brief: In Yellowstone National Park, close-packed pines stand under a hot, dry summer sky. Lightning strikes and small fires start among the trees, while firefighters in gear arrive from all over the country. Strong winds sweep through as park visitors leave, and many firefighters move in to fight the flames.

pages.text: Yet the fires were just getting started. Every afternoon, high winds sent embers high into the sky. They landed and started more fires. On August 20, fierce winds caused 165,000 acres to burn in just one day—a day that came to be known as Black Saturday. Firefighters fought the flames for nearly two months. By September 11, rain and early snow finally came to the rescue, dampening fires that thousands of firefighters could not. By then, 44.5 percent of the park had burned. Including the forests surrounding the park, 1.2 million acres—an area nearly the size of the state of Delaware—had burned. Do You Know? One square mile equals 640 acres. The 1.2 million acres that burned in 1988 are equal to 1,875 square miles (4,856 square km). Viewing the devastation, many observers criticized the park’s decision to let the natural fires burn. They described the park as “ruined.” Those fires raised many questions. Was Yellowstone ruined? When does it make sense to let a wildfire burn? Does a wildfire serve any purpose except to destroy?
pages.brief: High winds lift glowing embers into the sky above burning forest, and flames spread across a vast landscape on Black Saturday. Firefighters battle the flames for nearly two months. Rain and early snow fall at last, dampening the fires while burned forest stretches across the park and surrounding woods.

pages.text: Costs of Fire Forest fires are often destructive and sometimes deadly. In the case of severe forest fires, superheated gases can reach 1,600°F (871°C). Blasts of heat have cracked boulders in half and melted chainsaws. Types of Fire There are three types of forest fires: ground fires, surface fires, and crown fires. A ground fire travels low to the ground and sometimes underneath it. It feeds on ground fuel and rarely shows a flame. You might walk right over it and not even know it’s there. A surface fire stays low but burns hotter, burning trees and brush. When it grows fierce enough, it turns into a crown fire. Crown fires are the big fires. They can travel 10 miles (16 km) per hour. Flames can reach up to 300 feet (91 m). A single forest fire can include all three types of fires.
pages.brief: A forest fire is shown in three layers: a low ground fire creeping beneath the forest floor, a hotter surface fire burning brush and trees, and a towering crown fire racing through treetops with flames reaching high. Nearby, a cracked boulder and a melted chainsaw show the intense heat.

pages.text: Number of Fires and Acres Burned in the United States Key Recently, although the number of total fires in the United States has decreased, the total number of acres burned has increased. In five to fifteen minutes, a fire can release as much energy as an atomic bomb. Less severe fires can destroy property, homes, and the lives of humans and other animals. When fire has burned the plants that hold the ground in place, the landscape becomes more vulnerable to flooding and landslides. Smoke from big fires causes pollution and breathing problems. Even hundreds of miles away, the sky turns brown and smells of smoke. Nationwide, wildfires burn millions of acres each year. The United States spends more than $1 billion to fight them.
pages.brief: Across the United States, wildfires burn millions of acres each year. A powerful fire releases enormous energy, while smoke turns the sky brown hundreds of miles away. Burned slopes lose plants that hold the ground, leaving the landscape open to flooding and landslides, with homes and wildlife at risk.

pages.text: Do You Know? Lightning strikes 8 million times around the world each day. Every year in the United States, lightning is the cause of an estimated 17,400 fires. Causes of Fire In the United States, the western region has the most forest fires. This part of the country has many forests and hot, dry summers during which lightning is common. Lightning is the leading natural cause of wildfires. People start many forest fires, too, but usually not on purpose. Many are accidents, possibly started by a campfire that wasn’t put out properly. Some are even less direct, such as a spark from a passing train’s wheels igniting dry grass or nearby woods. Most fires go out by themselves. Usually only a few acres burn, and some of those fires never even touch trees. Of course, a few fires grow huge.
pages.brief: In the western United States, hot, dry summers and many forests make lightning a leading cause of wildfire. A strike flashes above the trees while a campfire left smoldering and a spark from a passing train threaten dry grass. Most small fires fade on their own; a few grow huge.

pages.text: Early firefighters in South Dakota use sand to manage a fire. Sand can put out a fire, help slow it down, or stop it from spreading. People and Fire Forest fires are nothing new, but attitudes toward them have changed over time. The Europeans who settled the West in the 1800s fought them at every turn. Until then, fires and forests had managed to find a balance. Nobody fought the wildfires, in part because nobody owned the forests. When Yellowstone became a national park in 1872 and for a long time after, both visitors and the people who ran the park continued to see fire as destructive. The early caretakers of national parks and forests thought that putting out fires was just good stewardship. In 1935, the U.S. Forest Service established a rule about putting out all fires the day after they started. This all sounded sensible at the time. After all, putting out fires protects the forest. Right?
pages.brief: Early firefighters in South Dakota use sand to manage a fire, slowing it and stopping it from spreading. In the western forests, settlers and early park caretakers fight every fire, believing that putting out fires protects the forest and is good stewardship.

pages.text: Jeff Henry holds a picture he took during the 1988 Yellowstone fire. He’s standing by new trees in 2008 in the same spot where he took the photograph of the historic fire twenty years before. Adapted to Fire Actually, many forests are equipped to survive forest fires. In fact, fire often benefits the native plants and animals in these forests. Fire fights invasive plants and kills harmful insects. Ash from the burned plants, which is rich in nutrients, dissolves back into the soil. Fire can improve habitat for wildlife by replacing dark, crowded stands of trees with open, sunny vistas and helping grass grow, which provides food for animals.
pages.brief: Jeff Henry stands beside young trees in 2008, holding a photograph he took during the 1988 Yellowstone fire in the same spot. Around him, open, sunny ground and fresh grass show how fire can clear crowded stands, return nutrients to the soil, and improve habitat for wildlife.

pages.text: For thousands of years, fire has been one of the forces that have shaped certain forests—not just lodgepole forests, but other kinds as well. Fire burns the forest here and there until it has cycled through the entire landscape. Burned areas become grassy meadows that eventually grow new trees. Together, these different areas create a system of food and shelter for many species. Different forests complete this cycle in different spans of time. One type of forest might take a thousand years, while another type may only take a hundred years. In these forests, many plant species are adapted to fire. The very trees that burned in Yellowstone offer a great example because some lodgepole pines need fire to reproduce. Fire allows the pinecones to open and release their seeds. Without fire, the cones just sit and wait. Within a month of Yellowstone’s 1988 monster fire, snow covered the park. When the snow melted the following spring, it watered the roots and seeds that had survived underground. Nutritious grasses sprouted from the charred earth, attracting elk and deer. Wildflowers bloomed the next spring and summer. As it turned out, the burned park wasn’t ruined after all.
pages.brief: A burned Yellowstone landscape becomes a grassy meadow, then new trees grow. Lodgepole pinecones open after fire and release seeds onto charred ground. Snow melts into the soil, nutritious grasses sprout, and elk, deer, and wildflowers return to the burned park.

pages.text: Fire removes undergrowth to allow light to reach the forest floor and foster the growth of new plants. Too Much Fuel Many people can find it hard to adapt to fire. Everyone knows fire is dangerous and can cause great damage. People’s view of the forest can vary greatly. Some may see the forest only as a source of wood, grass for cattle grazing, or a beautiful spot to pitch a tent—not as an ecosystem that sometimes needs to burn. Viewed that way, it seems only logical to put out forest fires. Yet not letting fires run their course can cause a problem for forests and people alike. Without fire, needles, brush, and logs build up over time. Once a fire does start, the built-up debris on the forest floor causes the fire to become more severe. Too much fuel can make a fire almost impossible to control.
pages.brief: Fire clears undergrowth so light reaches the forest floor and new plants can grow. In a crowded forest, needles, brush, and fallen logs pile up over time. When a fire starts in this built-up fuel, it burns hotter and becomes almost impossible to control.

pages.text: Many severe forest fires have burned across the West in recent years. While other factors, such as climate change, have also played a role, most forest experts agree that these severe fires are caused by too much fuel on the ground—and stamping out so many wildfires is to blame. Fighting fires is also expensive. Since 1960, the annual cost to federal, state, and local governments to fight wildfires has grown from less than $100 million to more than $3.3 billion. This huge expense takes money away from programs that clear trees and brush in high-risk areas— programs that would prevent, or at least reduce, the scope and severity of fires.
pages.brief: Severe fires burn across the western United States, fed by too much fuel on the forest floor. Firefighting costs grow from less than $100 million to more than $3.3 billion a year. The expense takes money from programs that clear trees and brush in high-risk areas.

pages.text: Too Many People So why not let some of these fires burn? In some remote places, that’s possible. The trouble is, there aren’t as many remote places as there once were because people keep moving in. Since 1990, areas near U.S. wildlands are being developed at a rate of 2 million acres per year. That’s about three acres per minute. Between 1990 and 2008, 10 million homes were built in U.S. wildlands near urban areas. Many are at high—or very high—risk of wildfire. It’s no surprise, then, that more homes are burning. In the 1960s, about 200 homes a year were lost to wildfires. By the 2000s, an average of 2,700 homes burned in wildfires each year. In California alone, wildfires destroy an average of 700 homes every year. That state spends $165 million each year on homes lost to or damaged by wildfire. California spends millions more trying to keep those homes from burning in the first place. Letting fires burn near these homes is risky. Yet we now know that it’s also risky if none of these fires are allowed to burn.
pages.brief: Homes spread into wildlands near forests, where people build at high risk of wildfire. More houses stand close to trees and brush, and more homes burn each year. Firefighters face a hard choice: letting fires burn near neighborhoods is risky, yet stopping every fire is risky too.

pages.text: Visitors to Yellowstone can witness the natural cycle of trees growing out of the ashes of the massive fire in 1988. Rethinking Fire When a wildfire burns, it’s hard to remember that something so destructive is also so productive. Yellowstone is living proof that it is. After the 1988 Yellowstone fire, dead gray stands of lodgepole pines covered the mountains for miles. Today, those trees’ seedlings form lush stands of young trees that grow taller every year. Someday, their offspring will do the same— thanks to fire. Wildfire serves a role in nature. People need to consider that role. In some cases, we might do well to stand back and let the fire do its work.
pages.brief: Visitors to Yellowstone see young trees growing from the ashes of the 1988 fire. Dead gray lodgepole pines once covered the mountains; today lush stands of young trees grow taller each year. Their offspring will someday do the same, showing that wildfire has a role in nature.

books.title: Animal Discoveries
books.art_why: Real animals exist today; no named famous person.

pages.text: Animal Discoveries.
pages.brief: A bright, inviting photograph shows a varied collection of animal life from around the world in natural habitats, arranged to suggest the wonder of discovery and the many creatures still unknown; no single species dominates the scene.

pages.text: The Bonaire banded box jellyfish’s scientific name is Tamoya ohboya. The name was chosen in a contest. The winner said most people would say “Oh boy!” when seeing the jellyfish. Introduction If you wanted to find a new animal species, where would you look? You might look in remote corners of the globe. You might also look under a microscope to see how one species is different from another. Scientists discover more than 15,000 animal species each year. That’s 1 percent of the more than 1.5 million species we know about already. At the same time, species are dying out at record rates around the globe. For this reason, when we do stumble on a new species, it is an important discovery.
pages.brief: A Bonaire banded box jellyfish drifts in clear blue water, its striped tentacles trailing; a scientist peers through a microscope nearby, while the vast ocean and remote corners of the globe suggest where new species might be found.

pages.text: Monkey Mania In 2007, a new species of monkey was found in the forests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The lesula has large eyes and is shy and quiet. The first one found by scientists was being kept as a pet. lesula monkey The Caquetá titi monkey lives in the Amazon jungle with about twenty other species of titi monkey. The Caquetá is known for its bushy red beard. It doesn’t have a white bar on its forehead as other titi monkeys do. Its babies purr like cats. Only around 250 Caquetá titi monkeys are alive today, meaning the species is endangered. Caquetá titi monkey.
pages.brief: Two monkey species are shown: a lesula with large eyes sits quietly in a forest of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, while a Caquetá titi monkey with a bushy red beard clings to a branch in the Amazon jungle, its baby nearby.

pages.text: The Matang narrow-mouthed frog lays its eggs in pitcher plants. The tadpoles grow in the liquid inside. Freaky, Fabulous Frogs The Matang narrow-mouthed frog is the size of a pea. It was discovered on Borneo, an island in Southeast Asia, in 2010. It turns out that scientists had seen these frogs before but thought they were the young of a different species. Then they heard the frogs calling. Since only adult frogs make calls, they realized that these tiny frogs must be full-grown.
pages.brief: A pea-sized Matang narrow-mouthed frog sits beside a pitcher plant on Borneo, where its eggs and tadpoles develop inside the plant’s liquid; nearby, scientists listen as adult frogs call, proving the tiny frogs are full-grown.

pages.text: The long-nosed tree frog is also known as the spike-nosed tree frog. A herpetologist discovered the long-nosed tree frog in 2010 while exploring the Foja Mountains of New Guinea. The area is so remote that it has been called the “Lost World.” This tree frog is known for its long, unique nose. When the male frog calls, its nose points up like a spike. When the frog is done calling, its nose falls. No one knows why. The frog has another name: the Pinocchio frog. The herpetologist spotted it sitting on a bag of rice in his campsite.
pages.brief: A herpetologist in a remote New Guinea campsite spots a long-nosed tree frog sitting on a bag of rice; the male frog’s long nose points upward like a spike as it calls in the Foja Mountains.

pages.text: When the blossom bat feeds on nectar, it also helps pollinate the flower, which can then make seeds to grow new plants. Furry Finds Another find during the 2010 Foja Mountains trip was the blossom bat. Although bats are mammals, this one has been called the “hummingbird of the bat world.” It uses its long tongue to drink nectar from the flowers of rainforest trees. During a 2005 expedition to another island— Madagascar—researchers found Goodman’s mouse lemurs. Not much bigger than mice, these tiny lemurs jump around in the trees at night. In the daytime, they sometimes sleep in empty birds’ nests. Do You Know? Lemurs are only found in Madagascar. Goodman’s mouse lemurs.
pages.brief: A blossom bat hovers at a rainforest flower, its long tongue reaching for nectar, while nearby on Madagascar a tiny Goodman’s mouse lemur leaps through trees at night; by day it may sleep in an empty bird’s nest.

pages.text: Sazima’s tarantulas are only found in the tabletop mountains of Brazil. These mountains have a different climate than the surrounding area. Interesting Invertebrates Scientists estimate that vertebrates—animals with backbones—make up only 3 percent of all species. The remaining 97 percent of animal species known to scientists are invertebrates— animals without backbones. Sazima’s tarantula has a special beauty. Its dark blue body almost glows. This fantastic arachnid has an extremely limited habitat, only living high in the mountains of Brazil.
pages.brief: A Sazima’s tarantula with a dark blue, almost glowing body rests high in Brazil’s tabletop mountains, a habitat with a climate unlike the surrounding area; other invertebrate animals without backbones are suggested in the shadows around it.

pages.text: Like most insects, planthoppers go through stages of development. This young planthopper is just beginning to develop wings. The “troll-haired” planthopper was discovered in 2013 in the rainforests of South America. It may not be good-looking, but at least it has good hair. The wild hair isn’t hair at all, but instead waxy secretions from the insect’s belly. When a predator attacks, the “hair” breaks off, and the planthopper can jump to safety. That’s what scientists think, anyway, but they aren’t sure.
pages.brief: A young “troll-haired” planthopper with wild, waxy hair-like secretions on its belly clings to a rainforest leaf in South America, its wings just beginning to develop; a predator approaches as the fragile “hair” prepares to break away.

pages.text: The Gorgon’s head starfish is named for the Gorgons from Greek mythology. These creatures had hundreds of snakes on their heads instead of hair. Underwater Wonders Scientists discovered the Gorgon’s head starfish in 2010 in the Atlantic Ocean, about half a mile (800 m) beneath the surface. The Gorgon’s head, a species of basket star, has five curly, branching arms that split off from its body. The five arms include as many as five thousand tips. The tips help it find food floating by in the water. It also uses its arms to walk along the ocean floor and to protect itself.
pages.brief: Deep in the Atlantic Ocean about half a mile below the surface, a Gorgon’s head starfish spreads five curly, branching arms with thousands of tips; the basket star uses them to catch floating food, walk along the ocean floor and protect itself.

pages.text: Scientists were able to identify the walking bamboo shark as a new species because its coloring differs from that of other bamboo sharks. Since Earth’s oceans are so huge, large parts have yet to be explored. However, that’s not the reason it took until 2013 to discover the walking bamboo shark. Like most sharks, the walking bamboo shark is no threat to humans. It lives off the coast of Indonesia. Scientists discovered it because its coloration differs from that of other bamboo sharks. This new species is thought to reach about 30 inches (80 cm) in length. It uses its fins to push itself along the ocean floor in search of food. The wiggling movement makes it look as though the shark is walking.
pages.brief: Off the coast of Indonesia, a walking bamboo shark uses its fins to push itself along the ocean floor, its wiggling movement making it look as though it is walking; the shark’s distinct coloration sets it apart from other bamboo sharks.

pages.text: Hiding in Plain View In 2013, researchers discovered that for more than a hundred years, olinguitos (oh-lin-GEE- tohs) had been identified as the wrong species. These mammals, which look like teddy bears, leap through trees at night. The smallest member of the raccoon family, the olinguito can be found in Ecuador and Colombia. It is the first species of this type to be discovered in the Americas in thirty- five years. Mistaken Identity Humans may encounter an unidentified species for years while mistaking it for a familiar species. This often happens because the two species look the same, at least on the outside. These are called cryptic species. They are only found to be distinct when scientists study their genetic code. As DNA technology is used more and more, reports of distinct new species are on the rise.
pages.brief: A small olinguito that looks like a teddy bear leaps through trees at night in Ecuador or Colombia; scientists compare its genetic code with similar mammals, revealing that this cryptic species had been mistaken for a familiar one for more than a century.

pages.text: Finding new species of birds is almost as rare as finding new mammals. In 2009, researchers discovered the Cambodian tailorbird near the city of Phnom Penh. Tests showed that this tailorbird was a separate, new species. Besides studying its DNA and feathers, scientists studied its pretty song. While all tailorbirds warble, no two species sound quite the same. Sure enough, the song of the Cambodian tailorbird sets it apart from all the rest.
pages.brief: Near the city of Phnom Penh, a Cambodian tailorbird perches and sings its pretty song; researchers study its feathers and DNA, and its unique warble helps confirm it is a separate new species from all other tailorbirds.

pages.text: Number of Species Discovered by Type 2000–2009 2 Plants: 23,604 3 Arachnids: 12,751 4 Fungi: 11,984 5 Crustaceans: 7,070 6 Mollusks: 5,949 7 Bacteria: 4,417 8 Fish: 3,587 9 All other: 18,351 What’s Next? Scientists continue to amaze us by finding new species. Experts agree that most have yet to be discovered. However, those animals we have discovered bring some problems to light. For example, many species have tiny populations. Human activity causes many species to face small and shrinking habitats. Yet each new discovery is also cause for hope. It can bring a renewed effort to save and even restore a habitat. Doing this can save the animals that live there, both those we know about and those we don’t know about…yet.
pages.brief: A wide array of life forms—plants, arachnids, fungi, crustaceans, mollusks, bacteria and fish—are shown in a natural setting, while scientists work to protect a shrinking habitat; the scene suggests both the many discoveries still to come and the hope of restoring places where known and unknown animals live.

books.title: Mexico
books.art_why: Mexico's places, wildlife and people exist today and can be photographed, and this is a country survey rather than a life of one famous person.

pages.text: Mexico United States Baja Peninsula Gulf of California Gulf of Mexico Mexico Yucatán Peninsula PACIFIC OCEAN Mexico City NORTH AMERICA Belize Honduras SOUTH AMERICA Guatemala El Salvador Where Is It? In the southern part of North America lies the country of Mexico. It is found between the United States and the countries of Belize and Guatemala. West of Mexico is the Pacific Ocean. On the eastern coast is the Gulf of Mexico. The Gulf of California divides the main land area of Mexico from the Baja (BAH-hah) Peninsula. Mexico also includes some islands. These lie along the east and west coasts.
pages.brief: Mexico seen from above: the country stretches south from the United States, with Belize and Guatemala to the southeast. The Pacific Ocean lies west, the Gulf of Mexico east, and the Gulf of California separates the long Baja Peninsula from the mainland. Small islands dot the east and west coasts.

pages.text: A monument to war heroes greets visitors as they enter Chapultepec Park (bottom). The park includes history museums (top left) as well as lakes (top right). Mexico City, one of the oldest cities in North America, is the capital of Mexico. It sits in a basin surrounded by mountains and is home to more than nineteen million people. Mexico City contains many beautiful parks. Chapultepec (chah-pool-te-PEK) Park is the largest. It contains a zoo, gardens, fountains, museums, lakes, and forests.
pages.brief: The entrance to Chapultepec Park in Mexico City, where a tall stone monument to war heroes greets visitors. Beyond it spread the park's lakes, gardens, fountains, forests, zoo and history museums, the largest park in one of North America's oldest cities, set in a mountain-ringed basin of more than nineteen million people.

pages.text: People Thousands of years ago, Indigenous peoples lived on the land that is now Mexico and built amazing civilizations. Then, Spanish explorers came to Mexico in 1517. By 1521, the Spanish had colonized Mexico. As a result, about two thirds of modern Mexico’s people are mestizos (mes- TEE-zohz). This means they are the descendants of both Indigenous and European ancestors. The other third of the population consists of Indigenous peoples, Spanish descendants, and other people who have come to the country. Today, Mexico has a population of more than 120 million people. Most Mexicans speak Spanish. More people speak Spanish in Mexico than any other country in the world. Some people speak Indigenous languages. Most of the population lives in cities. More than three fourths of Mexico’s people live in cities.
pages.brief: A crowded city street in Mexico, people walking past shop fronts. Most are mestizos, descended from both Indigenous peoples and the Spanish who colonized the land from 1521; others are Indigenous, of Spanish descent, or newcomers. Most Mexicans speak Spanish, and more than three fourths live in cities.

pages.text: Mexico is rich in natural resources such as oil and silver. It exports tons of coffee, sugar cane, and cotton throughout the world each year. The country is also famous for its art and artists. Painting, sculpture, and dance have a long and rich history in Mexico. Do You Know? Mexico is famous for its large paintings called murals. One of its most famous muralists was Diego Rivera. In this famous mural, he shows the Zapotec and the Mixtec, two Indigenous groups of ancient Mexico, at work making jewelry from gold and precious stones such as jade and turquoise. The mural, along with many others, is in the National Palace in Mexico City.
pages.brief: Inside the National Palace in Mexico City, a huge mural by Diego Rivera covers the wall. It shows Zapotec and Mixtec craftspeople at work, shaping gold, jade and turquoise into jewellery. Visitors stand below, looking up at the painted figures.

pages.text: Mexico’s Landforms Sonoran Desert Copper Canyon Chihuahuan Desert Baja Peninsula Gulf of California Sierra Madre Oriental Mountains Mexican Plateau Gulf of Mexico Yucatán Peninsula PACIFIC OCEAN Mexico Mexico City Pico de Orizaba Sierra Madre del Sur Mountains Land Mexico has many mountain ranges, and some mountains are also volcanoes. The highest mountain is a volcano 5,700 meters (18,701 ft.) high named Pico de Orizaba (PEE-koh day OR- ee-SAH-bah). Mountains run along the west, east, and south. Mexico also has canyons that reach amazing depths. Copper Canyon in northern Mexico is known for being larger than the Grand Canyon. The center of the country is a plateau. The raised, flat land makes it ideal for building roads and towns. Most people live in this area.
pages.brief: A wide view of Mexico's landforms: mountain ranges run along the west, east and south, with a raised flat plateau in the centre where most people live. In the north, Copper Canyon cuts deep into the land, and the volcano Pico de Orizaba rises highest of all.

pages.text: Two peninsulas, the Baja and the Yucatán, jut into the ocean. The Yucatán Peninsula is made of limestone that has dissolved away over thousands of years in some places. The result is spectacular caves, including underground caves filled with water called cenotes (sih-NOH-teez). The Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts stretch across northern Mexico. The Sonoran Desert has more types of plants than any desert in North America. Warm, wet rainforests cover parts of southeastern Mexico. These forests are home to many different types of plants and animals. Mexico’s coastal lowlands contain lagoons, marshes, and swamps. Past the eastern coast lies the Caribbean Sea. Mexico does not have many lakes and rivers, but one is very well known because it forms the border between Mexico and the United States. Mexicans call this river the Rio Bravo del Norte, which means “wild river of the north.” People of the United States call it the Rio Grande.
pages.brief: A still pool of water deep inside a limestone cave on the Yucatán Peninsula, ringed by rock. Above ground the scene shifts to the Sonoran Desert, thick with more kinds of plants than any other North American desert, then to warm wet rainforest in the southeast and coastal lowlands of lagoons and marshes.

pages.text: History The earliest people in Mexico were Indigenous peoples. One of the most well known groups is the Mayan people. The Maya built great cities, temples, and pyramids without the help of the wheel or animals. They also created beautiful works of art, studied the stars and planets, and developed a calendar. Visitors to Mexico can see El Castillo (kahs-TEE-yoh), a pyramid built by the Mayan people long ago. In the early 1300s, the Aztec people arrived in central Mexico. They built their capital city on an island in a lake. The Aztec were also known as the Mexica, and from that name comes the name Mexico. The site of the Aztec capital city, Tenochtitlán (tay-nohch-teet-LAHN), would become Mexico City. The Aztec built a huge empire. In 1519, the Spanish explorer Hernán Cortés arrived in the Aztec capital. Within two years, he and his followers had taken over the land and conquered the Aztec people.
pages.brief: El Castillo, the stepped stone pyramid the Maya built long ago without wheels or animals, stands in a clearing; other Maya temples and city ruins rise among trees. Later the Aztec built their capital on an island in a lake, until Spanish explorer Hernán Cortés arrived in 1519 and conquered them.

pages.text: Pancho Villa (left) and Emiliano Zapata (right), were the leaders of the Mexican Revolution. In 1521, Mexico became a Spanish colony. It remained a colony until 1821, when the people fought and won a war to be free from Spanish rule. In the century that followed, many people were poor farmers who struggled to survive. Wealthy Europeans owned 95 percent of the land. Farmers and workers had few rights and little money. During the Mexican Revolution (1910–1920), the people rose up and changed the government. Mexico became a democracy, which helped to improve daily life for people who were poor. Today, Mexico is still a land of extremes. There are two main social classes, the rich and the poor, with a very small middle class.
pages.brief: Pancho Villa and Emiliano Zapata, leaders of the Mexican Revolution, stand side by side. Around them are the poor farmers and workers who had few rights and little money, while wealthy Europeans owned almost all the land. Their uprising changed the government and Mexico became a democracy.

pages.text: Although the jaguar is active during the day, it hunts mainly at night. Animals Many different types of animals live in Mexico. The jaguar plays an important role in the stories, songs, and prayers of Mexico’s ancient Indigenous peoples. It lives mainly in the rainforests of Mexico. The largest of all the cat species in North America, it can measure about 2 meters (6 ft.) in length. It has black spots and a roar that sounds like a loud cough. Unlike many other cats, the jaguar likes to swim, play, and hunt in water. Its main source of food is the peccary, a small, wild member of the pig family. Sadly, the jaguar is in danger of extinction; however, many people are trying to save them.
pages.brief: A jaguar moves through the rainforest, black spots dappled over its coat. Largest of North America's cats at about two metres long, it likes water, swimming and playing in it, and hunts peccaries at night. Its roar sounds like a loud cough. Ancient Indigenous peoples told stories about it.

pages.text: The sacred bird of the ancient Maya and the Aztec, the quetzal (keht-SAHL) lives in the rainforests of Mexico. Like many types of birds, the male is brightly colored, and the female is plainer in appearance. The male’s head and chest are bright golden green. Its back is blue, its belly is red, and its tail feathers can be more than 1 meter (3 ft.) long. The bright colors of the male quetzal help it attract a mate. In the mountains of Mexico lives the red-knee tarantula. This large, hairy spider is named for the reddish-orange patches on its leg joints. The legs of this large spider span 15 cm (6 in.). It grows very slowly, and the female spider can live to be thirty years old. The ends of the red-knee tarantula’s legs can detect vibrations, smells, and tastes.
pages.brief: A male quetzal perches in the rainforest, golden-green head and chest, blue back, red belly, tail feathers trailing more than a metre. Nearby in the mountains a red-knee tarantula rests, large and hairy, reddish-orange patches at its leg joints, its legs spanning fifteen centimetres.

pages.text: Mexico’s Copper Canyon is a popular tourist site, although it is difficult to reach. A train takes visitors through the area. Conclusion Mexico is a country of diversity. It has modern cities and ancient ruins. Deep canyons lie within high mountains. Dry deserts and wet rainforests cover the land. Its long history and natural beauty fascinate people around the globe. If you were to visit Mexico, what would you want to see first?
pages.brief: A train carries visitors through Copper Canyon, the vast gorge deeper and larger than the Grand Canyon, difficult to reach but popular with tourists. Beyond it lie modern cities beside ancient ruins, high mountains, dry deserts and wet rainforests, all within one country.

books.title: Brazil
books.art_why: Brazil is a real country that exists today, so photographs of its cities, people, land and animals are possible; it is not a book about a named famous person.

pages.text: Brazil Guyana Venezuela Suriname French Guiana Colombia ATLANTIC OCEAN Peru São Luis Brazil Brasília Bolivia PACIFIC OCEAN Rio de Janeiro São Paulo ATLANTIC OCEAN Paraguay NORTH AMERICA Argentina SOUTH AMERICA Uruguay Where Is It? Brazil is the largest country in South America and covers nearly half of the entire continent. It is almost as large as the entire United States. The western half of Brazil shares a border with many smaller countries. These countries include Venezuela, Colombia, Peru, Bolivia, Paraguay, Argentina, and Uruguay.
pages.brief: A view of the South American continent from high above, with Brazil spreading across nearly half of it. Smaller countries sit along Brazil's western edge, and the Atlantic Ocean lies to the east. Brazil's enormous size is set beside the whole United States for comparison.

pages.text: To the east of Brazil is the Atlantic Ocean. The country’s coastline is more than 7,400 kilometers (4,600 mi.) long. The capital of Brazil is Brasília (bruh-ZIL-yuh), which is located near the middle of the country. However, Brasília wasn’t always the capital. The larger city of Rio de Janeiro (REE-oh DAY zhuh- NAIR-oh), located on the east coast of the country, was the capital until 1960. The government decided to build a new capital city farther inland. Although it is still new, Brasília is growing quickly. More than two million people live and work there. Many people work for the government, since the city is Brazil’s political center. Brasília is filled with many modern buildings.
pages.brief: Brazil's long Atlantic coastline stretches out of sight, waves breaking on the sand. Inland, near the middle of the country, the modern capital city of Brasília rises with its new buildings, where government workers do their jobs. Farther east on the coast sits the larger, older city of Rio de Janeiro.

pages.text: People More than two hundred million people live in Brazil, and eight out of every ten people live in cities. The country has several large cities, including São Paulo (SOW POW-low), the largest city in South America. Many people in Brazil work in service industries, such as construction, banking, education, and healthcare. Large hotels and restaurants line many of the country’s beaches, providing work for people living along the coast. Other Brazilians work in factories, making cars, airplanes, and steel. Many of these factories are located around São Paulo. In the countryside, people work in mining and farming. Brazil is a leading producer of minerals such as iron ore, tin, and even gold. Brazil’s farmers grow much of the world’s coffee on huge plantations. They also grow oranges, cassava, and soybeans. Some farmers raise hogs and chickens, and ranchers raise cattle. Brazil grows the most popular type of coffee, called Arabica.
pages.brief: Busy city streets in São Paulo, South America's largest city, where people work in banking, education, construction and healthcare. Factories around the city build cars, airplanes and steel. Along the coast, hotels and restaurants line the beaches. In the countryside, farmers tend huge coffee plantations and ranchers raise cattle.

pages.text: Futebol Many Brazilians enjoy watching and playing soccer, which they call futebol (FOOT-bohl). Brazil has won the World Cup, the world’s largest soccer tournament, more than any other country. The country’s most famous soccer player—Pelé—is known around the world. Pelé led his team to victory in the World Cup in 1958, 1962, and in 1970. Pelé Brazilians come from many different backgrounds. Some are descended from the Native peoples who first lived there. Others are descendants of people from Angola, the Congo, and other African countries, who were enslaved and brought to Brazil to work on plantations and in mines. Many others are descended from people who came to Brazil from far-away countries such as Portugal, Spain, Germany, and other places in Europe. In fact, Brazil was a colony of Portugal for three hundred years, and the main language in Brazil is Portuguese (POR-chuh-geez).
pages.brief: A soccer stadium packed with cheering fans as Brazil's team plays, recalling the World Cup victories led by the famous player Pelé. Nearby, a street scene shows Brazilians of many different backgrounds — descendants of Native peoples, of Africans brought to Brazil, and of families from Portugal, Spain and Germany.

pages.text: Land Many rivers flow through Brazil, making the soil rich and good for growing crops. However, one river clearly stands out. The Amazon River is one of the widest and longest rivers in the world, flowing for at least 6,400 kilometers (4,000 mi.) through northern Brazil. Its waters feed the vast Amazon basin, which covers nearly half of Brazil and about 7 million square kilometers (3 million sq. mi.). The largest tropical rainforest in the world, the Amazon rainforest, is also located here. Brazil is so large that it includes five main regions. The landforms in each region are so different that they are like separate countries. The north and southeast regions include highlands. In the north, the Guiana highlands consist of steep mountains and deep valleys. In the southeast, hills and low mountain plateaus make up the Brazilian highlands.
pages.brief: The wide water of the Amazon River winds through dense green rainforest in northern Brazil, its waters spreading across a vast basin that covers nearly half the country. Farther north, steep mountains and deep valleys rise in the Guiana highlands, while hills and low mountain plateaus make up the highlands of the southeast.

pages.text: Brazil’s Landforms Guiana Highlands ATLANTIC OCEAN Amazon River Amazon Basin Brazil Brazilian Highlands Brasília Pantanal Wetlands PACIFIC OCEAN Coastal Lowlands ATLANTIC OCEAN Brazil’s long east coast makes up another region. It includes beautiful sandy beaches, which are some of the main attractions for tourists visiting the country. The Pantanal is located in central Brazil. It is one of the world’s largest freshwater wetlands and extends for thousands of miles around the tributaries of several different rivers.
pages.brief: Sandy beaches run along Brazil's long east coast, where tourists come to swim. Inland, the Pantanal spreads out as one of the world's largest freshwater wetlands, water winding around the tributaries of several rivers. Beyond it, highlands rise and the Amazon River cuts across the land.

pages.text: History The first known people who lived in Brazil were Native peoples such as the Guarani and Yanomami. Different groups of Native peoples still live in the rainforests and along the banks of the Amazon River today. In the early sixteenth century, Portugal conquered Brazil. The Portuguese enslaved many Native people and forced them to work on huge sugarcane plantations. Later, they enslaved people in Africa and brought them to work on coffee plantations and in diamond and gold mines. In 1822, Brazil became an independent country ruled by an emperor. Slavery ended in 1888. In 1889, the emperor at the time was forced by the military to step down, and Brazil became a republic. In a republic, the people usually choose their leaders, but this didn’t always happen in Brazil. Instead, the people were often led by dictators. After much turmoil, the country became a democracy in 1985.
pages.brief: Native peoples such as the Guarani and Yanomami live in the rainforest and along the banks of the Amazon River. Elsewhere, workers cut sugarcane on a huge plantation and dig in gold and diamond mines. An emperor rules the newly independent country, before a republic takes its place.

pages.text: Rio de Janeiro has the largest Carnaval celebration in Brazil. It is held in a special building called the Sambadrome. Celebrations Many holidays in Brazil are religious in nature. Most Brazilians belong to the Catholic faith, a religion that was brought to Brazil by the Portuguese. However, because Brazilians come from many different backgrounds, religious customs of other groups—such as Native and African peoples—are also followed. Carnaval is the largest and most popular holiday in Brazil. It is a four-day celebration leading up to Lent, which is the forty-day period in which Catholics prepare for Easter. During Carnaval, people crowd into Brazil’s streets for parades and dancing. Many people wear elaborate costumes with masks and headdresses.
pages.brief: A crowd packs into the Sambadrome in Rio de Janeiro for Carnaval, the biggest celebration in Brazil. Dancers in elaborate costumes with masks and tall headdresses parade past cheering people. In the streets outside, more crowds dance together during the four-day holiday leading up to Lent.

pages.text: Animals Brazil is home to the widest variety of life on Earth. The Amazon rainforest provides a home to more animals —and plants—than any other environment in the world. Colorful birds such as the toucan (TOO-kan) live there, as well as jaguars and ocelots (OS-uh-lotz). Slow-moving sloths hang from trees, and giant anacondas slither along the forest floor. Many different types of monkeys swing from the trees. In the Amazon River, meat-eating fish called piranhas (pi-RAH-nuhz) hunt in groups of one hundred or more. Large manatees swim through the water.
pages.brief: Inside the Amazon rainforest, a colorful toucan perches on a branch, a jaguar pads quietly below and an ocelot slips through the shadows. A sloth hangs slowly from a tree while monkeys swing through the canopy, and a giant anaconda slides along the forest floor. In the river, piranhas hunt in a large group.

pages.text: Other parts of Brazil, such as the Pantanal wetlands, also include unique animals. Storks and herons build nests in the Pantanal’s trees. Colorful parrots, such as the blue and yellow macaw, fly overhead. Deer and jaguar roam the land. Giant anteaters also live in the Pantanal. Sadly, some animals in the Amazon rainforest and the Pantanal could disappear from Earth forever. Every year, trees are cut down for timber and to clear land for farming. As a result, animals like the jaguar and the golden lion tamarin, a type of monkey, are losing their habitat. Many organizations are working together with the Brazilian government to keep this from happening.
pages.brief: In the Pantanal wetlands, storks and herons build nests in the trees while a blue and yellow macaw flies overhead. A giant anteater noses through the grass and a golden lion tamarin, a kind of monkey, clings to a branch. Nearby, felled trees lie on cleared ground.

pages.text: The large city of Rio de Janeiro is known for its many beautiful beaches. Conclusion Brazil is a country filled with life. The Amazon rainforest teems with more living things than anywhere else on Earth. The people in the cities and countryside have vibrant celebrations unlike any other. From its land to its animals and people, the vast country of Brazil has many things to learn about and explore.
pages.brief: The city of Rio de Janeiro stretches along the coast, its famous beaches curving beside the ocean, with forested hills rising behind the buildings. The wide view takes in a country full of life — crowded street celebrations, wildlife in the rainforest, and open land stretching in every direction.

books.title: France
books.art_why: The book includes ancient and medieval history, including cave art, kings, and the French Revolution, which cannot be photographed.

pages.text: France United Kingdom Belgium Germany English Channel Luxembourg Paris ATLANTIC OCEAN Dijon France Switzerland Limoges Bay of Biscay Italy Bordeaux Bayonne Toulouse Marseille Monaco Gulf of Lion EUROPE Spain Corsica ASIA AFRICA MEDITERRANEAN SEA Where Is It? France is the largest country in western Europe. To the northeast of France are Belgium and Luxembourg. To the east are Italy, Germany, and Switzerland, and to the south is Spain. The United Kingdom and Ireland lie across the English Channel to the northwest. France is bordered by water on two sides. To the west is the Atlantic Ocean, and to the northwest is the English Channel. To the southeast is the Mediterranean Sea.
pages.brief: A map of western Europe places France at the center, with Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, Switzerland, Italy, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Ireland around it. The Atlantic Ocean, English Channel, and Mediterranean Sea border France on different sides.

pages.text: Paris and the Eiffel Tower The capital of France is Paris, a city known around the world for its beauty. Millions of people visit Paris each year to see its famous landmarks. These sites include the Eiffel (EYE-ful) Tower, Notre Dame (no-truh DAHM) Cathedral, and the Louvre (LOO-vruh) art museum. A monument called the Arc de Triomphe (ARK du tree-OHMF) stands over one of the city’s main streets, the Champs-Élysées (SHAHM-zay-lee-ZAY). More than ten million people live in Paris. The city is France’s center for both business and culture. Paris is also considered one of the fashion capitals of the world. Arc de Triomphe The Louvre.
pages.brief: In Paris, visitors gather around the Eiffel Tower, Notre Dame Cathedral, the Louvre art museum, and the Arc de Triomphe above the Champs-Élysées. Crowds fill the busy city streets, showing Paris as a center for business, culture, fashion, and tourism.

pages.text: Paris and other cities are filled with restaurants and hotels for the more than eighty-two million tourists who visit France. People More than sixty-six million people live in France. Most people live and work in its cities and towns. Tourism is the largest service industry in France. In fact, France is the most visited country in the world! Many people work in hotels, restaurants, and museums that welcome these millions of visitors. Many French people also work in factories that produce goods such as cars, aircraft, and clothing. Other factories make chemicals and process food. Some people work in mines, digging resources such as coal out of the ground.
pages.brief: Tourists fill restaurants, hotels, and museums in French cities and towns. Workers serve visitors, while factory workers build cars, aircraft, and clothing, and make chemicals and processed food. In a mine, workers dig coal from the ground.

pages.text: Workers harvest grapes from a vineyard in France. The grapes are used mainly to make wine. More than half of the country’s land is used for farming. French farmers grow wheat, grain, sugar beets, and potatoes. Others raise animals, including cattle, hogs, and sheep. Some also grow grapes in vineyards. The majority of people in France are Roman Catholic. Others are Protestant, Muslim, or Jewish. The country’s main language is French, although people speak different dialects depending on the area.
pages.brief: Workers harvest grapes in a French vineyard, with rows of vines on a hillside. Nearby farmland holds wheat, grain, sugar beets, and potatoes, and farmers raise cattle, hogs, and sheep. The farm landscape stretches across the countryside.

pages.text: France’s Landforms Straight of Dover English Channel Seine River Paris Brittany Peninsula Loire Valley Paris Basin Loire River Jura Mountains France Bay of Biscay Mont Blanc Massif Central French Alps LIGURIAN SEA Cote d’Azur Pyrenees Mountains Gulf of Lion Corsica MEDITERRANEAN SEA Land France has many different landforms, including hills, forests, mountains, rivers, lakes, and beaches. France is mostly covered in flat plains and low, rolling hills. It also has high plateaus. The Seine (SEN) River runs through Paris, and, along with smaller rivers, drains the Paris Basin. The country is also known for its beautiful beaches, especially along the Mediterranean Sea.
pages.brief: A landscape view of France shows flat plains, rolling hills, high plateaus, forests, mountains, rivers, lakes, and beaches. The Seine River runs through Paris, and smaller rivers drain the Paris Basin. Mediterranean beaches lie along the coast.

pages.text: Mont Blanc, located in the French Alps, is the tallest mountain in western Europe. France has five different mountain ranges. The most well-known ranges are the French Alps and the Pyrenees (PEER-uh-neez). The French Alps are part of the larger Alps mountain range that runs through many countries. The French Alps lie along the border between France, Switzerland, and Italy. The Pyrenees lie along the border between France and Spain. A large plateau spreads across southern France. It has ancient mountains and volcanoes, which are no longer active, as well as deep river gorges. France also includes some islands. The largest is Corsica, which is located off the southern coast in the Mediterranean Sea.
pages.brief: Mont Blanc rises snow-capped in the French Alps, the tallest mountain in western Europe. The Pyrenees stretch along the border with Spain, while southern France holds a plateau with ancient inactive volcanoes and deep river gorges. Corsica island lies offshore in the Mediterranean Sea.

pages.text: France has a long history. Experts believe that early humans lived in what is now France nearly two million years ago. More than two thousand years ago, France was known as Gaul. The people who lived there were called Celts. Around 50 bc, the Roman Empire took over Gaul and ruled the land for about five hundred years. Around ad 400, German tribes took Gaul from the Romans. These German people were called Franks. They named the land Francia, which is how France got its name. For the next thousand years, powerful kings ruled France. In 800, a French king named Charlemagne (SHAR-luh-mayn) became leader of the Holy Roman Empire. This empire included France and parts of what are now Belgium, Germany, and Italy. However, the empire fell apart after Charlemagne died in 814. History Early humans painted animals on the walls of a cave in Lascaux (la-SKOH), France.
pages.brief: Early humans paint animals on a cave wall at Lascaux. Celts live in Gaul, Roman soldiers take over the land, and German Franks name it Francia. A king named Charlemagne leads the Holy Roman Empire, which includes France and nearby lands.

pages.text: From about 1066 to 1453, many wars were fought over the land of France. Most of these wars were between France and England. This began in 1066 when a group from Normandy, a region in France, invaded England. Another famous war between the two countries began in 1337 and lasted until 1453. Today it is known as the Hundred Years War. For hundreds of years, France was ruled by kings, many of whom treated the people poorly. In 1789, the people rebelled against the king and the French Revolution began. France became a republic in 1792, though the revolution would not end until 1799. The French overthrew two more leaders, setting up new governments each time. Today, France is a republic with a strong democracy. Louis XIV One of France’s greatest kings was Louis (LEW-ee) XIV. He ruled from 1643 to 1715, the longest a king has ever ruled in Europe. He fought many wars, expanded France’s borders, and built a lavish palace called Versailles (vehr-SEYE).
pages.brief: Medieval battles rage between France and England, including the Hundred Years War. A lavish palace at Versailles shows King Louis XIV, who ruled for a very long time. In 1789, French people rebel against their king during the French Revolution.

pages.text: On Bastille Day, veterans of France’s armed forces often lead the parades. Celebrations The French celebrate many different holidays. The French Revolution began on July 14, which is now known as Bastille Day. On that day in 1789, the French people stormed the Bastille, a prison in Paris. They took control of the building so they could set the prisoners free. Today, the French people celebrate their freedom with parades and fireworks. Mardi Gras (MAR-dee GRAH) is another popular holiday. Mardi Gras is a Roman Catholic holiday held about six weeks before the Easter holiday. Many cities and towns have huge carnivals with parades and floats. People dress in costumes and dance in the streets.
pages.brief: Veterans of France’s armed forces lead a Bastille Day parade as fireworks light the sky. A historical scene shows Parisians storming the Bastille prison to set prisoners free. At Mardi Gras, costumed people dance in the streets behind carnival floats.

pages.text: More than five hundred different kinds of cheese are made in France. Crêpes (KRAYPS), which are thin pancakes, and baguettes are also very common. France is famous for its food and cooking styles. Many French people consider good food to be one of the most important parts of life. One type of popular French cooking usually includes rich dishes made with butter, cream, eggs, and other flavors. The French enjoy many different types of fresh bread, and it is served at most meals. Breads are often sold as baguettes (ba-GETS), or long, thin loaves. France is also famous for its many different kinds of cheese. Many areas in France offer their very own type of cheese. baguettes Food.
pages.brief: A French table holds many kinds of cheese, thin crêpes, and long baguettes. A cook prepares rich dishes with butter, cream, and eggs. Fresh bread is served at most meals, and different areas make their own cheeses.

pages.text: The sidewalk cafes are popular in many parts of France. Conclusion France is a modern country with a long and interesting history. Its past is filled with powerful kings and empires. Today, France is the most visited country in the world. People travel from all over the world to see its beautiful cities, villages, and castles and to eat its rich foods. Vineyards and farms dot its rolling hills and plains. Delicious foods such as cheeses and fresh breads fill its shops. If you were to visit France, what would you like to see first?
pages.brief: People sit at a popular sidewalk café in a French town. Beyond the town, vineyards and farms cover rolling hills and plains, and a castle and village stand in the landscape. A shop displays cheeses and fresh breads for visitors.

books.title: Ancient Cliff Dwellers
books.art_why: The book is about ancient cliff dwellers who lived long before photographs, so the scenes must be reconstructed drawings.

pages.text: Colorado Utah Four Corners Arizona New Mexico.
pages.brief: A wide view of the Four Corners region, showing open land where Colorado, Utah, Arizona, and New Mexico meet. The scene is empty of people, with a simple crossing point in dry country and distant horizons under a clear sky.

pages.text: The Four Corners Mesa Verde National Park was founded in 1906. It is the first national park in the United States established to honor human accomplishments. It is located where the states of Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico meet. The park contains many cliff dwellings that are among the most striking examples of early human architecture in North America. The builders used great skill, creating these remarkable dwellings without the aid of modern tools or machines. Who lived in these structures? How did they live? Why did they make their homes in the cliffs? Why did they leave, and where did they go? Do You Know? Mesa Verde National Park is located in the Four Corners area. It is the only place in the United States where the corners of four states meet. The marker indicating the point is a tourist attraction.
pages.brief: Mesa Verde National Park: cliff dwellings built into a high cliff wall, with stone rooms and openings, surrounded by open mesa country. In the foreground, a simple boundary marker marks the Four Corners meeting point, with visitors nearby as a tourist attraction.

pages.text: Petroglyphs at Mesa Verde The early people who lived in the Four Corners area are called prehistoric because they left no written records. We know about them because we’ve found many remains of their culture buried in the ground. Mesa Verde is located in a high, flat desert surrounded by mountains. The arid, or dry, conditions at Mesa Verde are ideal for preserving skeletons, mummies, dwellings, tools, and trash piles. These remains have helped archaeologists to study the lives of the early people who lived in the area. Other remains include pictographs, or paintings on stone, and petroglyphs, or pictures carved in stone. Evidence Word Wise Mesa Verde is pronounced “MAY-suh VAIR-day.” Mesa, which is Spanish for “table,” also refers to raised, flat-topped land. Verde is Spanish for “green.”
pages.brief: A high, flat desert ringed by mountains at Mesa Verde. Archaeologists examine buried remains and dry ground, while a rock wall shows painted pictographs and carved petroglyph pictures. Skeletons, mummies, tools, and trash piles rest in the arid soil, preserved by the dry conditions.

pages.text: Paleo-Americans To understand the story of the cliff dwellers, we need to go back in time. Scientists know that at least 14,000 years ago, during the Ice Age, ancient people crossed a land bridge from northern Russia to Alaska in North America. Hundreds of years later, some of their descendants traveled far enough south to reach the Four Corners area. The first Four Corners people were called Paleo- Americans. They survived by hunting and gathering. Paleo-Americans used large spears to hunt huge herd animals, including elephant-like animals called mammoths and mastodons, and giant bison. They also gathered nuts, berries, and other wild plants. The Paleo-Americans did not have permanent homes. Instead, they moved from place to place following the animals they hunted. They camped in caves or built simple shelters.
pages.brief: Paleo-American hunters carrying large spears cross a cold land bridge from northern Russia toward Alaska during the Ice Age. Others travel south to the Four Corners area, where they hunt mammoths, mastodons, and giant bison and gather nuts and berries. They camp in caves or simple shelters.

pages.text: Archaic People When the Ice Age ended about 10,000 years ago, temperatures became warmer. This caused the extinction of many large animals and turned large grasslands into deserts. The Four Corners people had to adapt to these changes and find new ways to survive. Archaeologists call these people the Archaic people. Like their Paleo-American ancestors, the Archaic people were hunters and gatherers. But the animals they hunted were smaller and provided less meat than the ones their ancestors hunted. The Archaic people began to rely more on plants for food. The Archaic people made different tools from those of the Paleo-Americans. They made smaller spear points for hunting deer and bighorn sheep. They also made nets and traps for catching rabbits and birds. They used special tools for chopping and grinding roots, seeds, nuts, and wild plants. Early Tools The first grinding stones and bowls were made during the Archaic people’s time. Similar tools are still used now.
pages.brief: Archaic people in a warmer, drier landscape hunt deer and bighorn sheep with smaller spear points. Others set nets and traps for rabbits and birds, gather roots, seeds, and nuts, and grind them with stone tools and bowls. Large Ice Age animals are gone, and grasslands have turned to desert.

pages.text: Corn was an important part of the Ancestral Puebloans’ diet. Ancestral Puebloans By about 2,000 years ago, life in the Four Corners had changed in important ways. People had learned to grow their own food instead of relying on wild animals and plants. Agriculture changed their way of life. These people were called the Ancestral Puebloans. The earliest Ancestral Puebloans still relied mostly on hunting and gathering. However, growing their own food, such as corn and squash, on the open, flat land allowed them to feed a larger group of people. It also gave them a source of food they could depend on.
pages.brief: Ancestral Puebloans tend corn and squash on open, flat farmland under a bright sky. Some still hunt and gather wild plants, but the growing crops provide a dependable food supply for a larger group. Corn stands tall among the plants, showing its importance in their diet.

pages.text: Making Baskets As the Ancestral Puebloans grew more food, they found ways to store it. They began to use plant fibers and tree bark to make baskets. Some baskets held food, while others were woven so tightly that they could hold water. Because baskets could not be placed over a fire, the Ancestral Puebloans cooked by placing hot rocks into baskets filled with water. They also began making sandals from plant fibers. Yucca plant (right) and sandals made of yucca fibers (top) As the Ancestral Puebloans grew more crops and made more tools and baskets, they moved around less. Even as agriculture became more important to the Ancestral Puebloan way of life, they continued to hunt using spears and nets. During this time, they lived in caves along cliffs and canyon walls.
pages.brief: Ancestral Puebloans weave baskets from plant fibers and tree bark, some tight enough to hold water. A person places hot rocks into a water-filled basket to cook. Others make sandals from yucca fibers beside a yucca plant, while hunters with spears and nets work near caves along canyon cliffs.

pages.text: Pit houses could be from 9 to 25 feet (2.74–7.62 m) in diameter. The walls were made of branches and brush or grass covered in clay or mud. Over time, the Ancestral Puebloans relied more on agriculture to feed their growing population. By about 1,500 years ago, they grew beans in addition to corn and squash. Having a reliable food source from farming allowed them to stay in one place. They built temporary houses, called pit houses, near their fields. These houses were built on top of shallow pits dug in the ground. The sides and ceilings were constructed of tree branches, bark, and soil. Archaeologists think the Ancestral Puebloans were a peaceful people because no weapons of war have been found. Also, the location of their houses suggests that they did not feel threatened by enemies since houses built in the open are hard to defend.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of a circular pit house built over a shallow pit, with branch, bark, and soil walls, a smoke hole, entrance, and central fire pit. Nearby, Ancestral Puebloans tend corn, bean, and squash fields. The open houses sit near the fields, with no weapons of war in sight.

pages.text: Another important change during this time was the production of pottery. Although Ancestral Puebloans continued to make baskets, using clay pots allowed them to cook over an open fire. Clay pots also stored food better. The Ancestral Puebloans started using bows and arrows during this time, which was easier and more successful than spear hunting. These changes allowed the population to continue growing as food became more plentiful. They also used animal hair twisted with cotton string to make warm socks and leg coverings. Sometimes they also wove feathers and string made from yucca plants to make clothing. The first pottery of the Ancestral Puebloans changed their way of life. Cord made of yucca fibers and feathers Boot made of turkey feather yarn.
pages.brief: Ancestral Puebloans shape clay pots and set them over an open fire to cook, while others store food in finished pots. A hunter draws a bow and arrow. People make warm socks and leg coverings from animal hair and cotton string, and clothing from feathers and yucca cord, including a boot of turkey feather yarn.

pages.text: Pueblo Bonito Do You Know? Chaco Canyon, in northwestern New Mexico, was an important cultural center made up of 12 large pueblos. The largest was Pueblo Bonito. About 1,000 people lived there. Archaeologists think that Chaco Canyon was a trade center. Building Larger Houses Around 1,300 years ago, the Ancestral Puebloans were living in larger groups. They built rectangular houses completely aboveground. They used tree limbs and bark for a frame. Then they covered the wood with adobe (soil containing clay). Over time, they started building houses with sandstone blocks stacked and held together with adobe. The houses were built side by side, creating large buildings called pueblos. Pueblo is a Spanish word that means “town” or “village.” The Ancestral Puebloans also built underground circular structures called kivas. They were used for holding ceremonies.
pages.brief: A large aboveground pueblo of stacked sandstone blocks held with adobe rises in Chaco Canyon, with many rectangular rooms built side by side. About a thousand people live in Pueblo Bonito, the largest pueblo, and trade goods pass through the cultural center. An underground circular kiva is used for ceremonies.

pages.text: The Ancestral Puebloan culture thrived for several hundred years. The people developed new ways to help their crops grow. They built structures, such as dams and terraces, to manage water for their fields. Successful crops allowed them to feed their growing population. The types of pottery the Ancestral Puebloans made changed. They made everyday pottery that was used for cooking and storing food. Everyday pottery was gray with a rough outer texture that helped heat the food inside. They also made pottery that was rubbed and polished to create a smooth surface for decoration or trade. They decorated this pottery with complex, colorful designs using paint made from wild plants. An example of Ancestral Puebloans’ pottery.
pages.brief: Ancestral Puebloans build dams and terraces to manage water for their fields, where crops grow successfully. Others make gray everyday pottery with a rough outer texture for cooking and storage, and smooth polished pottery decorated with complex, colorful designs painted from wild plants.

pages.text: Moving to the Cliffs Around 900 years ago, the Ancestral Puebloans moved to ledges on cliffs and canyon walls. The cliff dwellings found at Mesa Verde and other places in the Four Corners area are typical of this time period. These houses were up to five stories tall. They provided housing for hundreds of people. The cliff dwellers used ladders and ropes to get to their homes. They also cut finger and toe holds into the rocks for climbing up the walls. About 600 cliff dwellings are located in Mesa Verde National Park. Cliff Palace is the largest. It had 217 rooms and 23 kivas. The smallest rooms may have been used for storage.
pages.brief: Ancestral Puebloans climb ladders and ropes to cliff dwellings built on ledges high in canyon walls. The stone homes rise up to five stories and house hundreds of people. At Mesa Verde, Cliff Palace is the largest cliff dwelling, with 217 rooms and 23 kivas, while smaller rooms store food.

pages.text: A Safety Issue? Some archaeologists think the Ancestral Puebloans were being attacked by other nations. They needed homes they could easily defend. Many cliff dwellings could only be reached with ladders. The people in them could pull their ladders inside, leaving their enemies no way to enter. Although this idea makes sense, there is little evidence that this was the reason for the move. Archaeologists were puzzled by the Ancestral Puebloans’ move from open areas to cliff dwellings. They think that as the Ancestral Puebloan population grew, more farmland was needed. Moving to cliff dwellings freed more flat land for growing crops. The Ancestral Puebloans also may have needed to create new fields to replace old fields that were overused and had lost the ability to grow food well. Another possible reason for the move might have been for warmth during winter. The weather was getting colder during this time. Most cliff dwellings face south or southwest, where the Sun’s rays could warm the rock walls of their homes.
pages.brief: Cliff dwellers pull their ladders inside a high stone home, leaving no way for enemies to enter. Below, archaeologists study the cliffs and open flat land. Other Ancestral Puebloans prepare new fields for crops as old soil wears out, while winter sunlight warms south-facing rock walls.

pages.text: Building Dwellings Building the cliff dwellings was a huge challenge for the Ancestral Puebloans. They didn’t have machines and used only stone tools. They were skilled at designing structures that made the best use of the space. The builders made walls from large stones chipped into shape and held together with adobe. They covered the walls with adobe, sometimes painting designs on the insides of the walls. Builders made upper floors by laying large wooden poles across the tops of walls and placing smaller poles across the beams. Next, a layer of sticks or bark was piled on. Then they added a thick layer of adobe to hold it together.
pages.brief: Ancestral Puebloan builders use stone tools to chip large stones into shape and set them with adobe. They cover walls with adobe and paint designs inside. For upper floors, they lay large wooden poles across walls, add smaller poles, sticks or bark, and a thick layer of adobe.

pages.text: Daily Life The Ancestral Puebloans probably spent most of their time outside working together in groups. Some cooked, ground corn, carried water, and made pottery and baskets. Others wove cloth, farmed crops, and hunted. Others made tools out of stone, wood, and plant fibers. Children worked alongside their parents, learning by watching and practicing. They also took care of turkeys and played. During the winter, some work was done inside the dwellings. Archaeologists think that rooms were used year-round for sleeping. Trade with other nations was an important part of Ancestral Puebloan life. The map below shows some of the items they traded and where the items came from. Mesa Verde Trading furs turquoise pottery shells corn salt beads cotton Mesa Verde Possible trade routes.
pages.brief: Ancestral Puebloans work together outside: cooking, grinding corn, carrying water, making pottery and baskets, weaving cloth, farming, hunting, and shaping tools. Children help their parents, learn by watching and practicing, care for turkeys, and play. Trade goods such as furs, turquoise, pottery, shells, corn, salt, beads, and cotton move along possible routes.

pages.text: The outside of a kiva (inset); The inside of a kiva (main) Spiritual Life Modern kivas are still used by the descendants of the Ancestral Puebloans. That is how we know they were used for religious ceremonies. They were probably also used for family gatherings, as guest rooms, and as workspaces in winter. People entered kivas with ladders. Each kiva had a fire pit in the center and a shaft providing fresh air. Half of the Mesa Verde kivas also had a small hole in the floor called a sipapu. The hole represented a doorway between the spirit world and the physical world. Archaeologists think that the Ancestral Puebloans believed that all living things have both a spirit self and a physical self. They also believed in life after death.
pages.brief: The inside of a circular kiva shows a central fire pit, a fresh-air shaft, and a small floor hole called a sipapu. People enter by ladder. A modern kiva outside view appears nearby. Ancestral Puebloans use kivas for religious ceremonies, family gatherings, guest rooms, and winter workspaces.

pages.text: Leaving the Cliffs Between 1280 and 1295, the Ancestral Puebloans left the cliff dwellings. They moved south to New Mexico and Arizona. No one knows for sure why they moved. Archaeologists think that the fact that the climate kept changing played an important role. It got colder, causing a shorter growing season for crops. Watering crops became harder because there were long periods of time with little or no rain. In addition, the soil may have been so overused that growing enough food became impossible. Perhaps by the time the Ancestral Puebloans left Mesa Verde, they had cut down most of the trees for firewood and for building pueblos. Hunters may have killed so many wild animals that the meat supply was gone. Some people think that enemy nations drove out the cliff dwellers. However, that is unlikely because there are no remains of other cultures at Mesa Verde after the Ancestral Puebloans left. Archaeologists find older remains deeper in the ground and newer remains closer to the surface. If enemies drove out the cliff dwellers, evidence of their culture would be found on top of the Ancestral Puebloan remains.
pages.brief: Ancestral Puebloans leave the cliff dwellings and travel south toward New Mexico and Arizona. Around them, colder weather, long dry periods, overused soil, cut trees, and scarce wild animals make life hard. Archaeologists study layers of remains in the ground, with older remains deeper and newer remains closer to the surface.

pages.text: Modern-Day Descendants When the ancient cliff dwellers left Mesa Verde, some moved south, settling along the Rio Grande in New Mexico. These are the ancestors of the modern Pueblo nations. Others moved to Arizona, eventually forming the Zuni and Hopi nations. Estella Loretto cleans a bronze statue. Today, members of these nations continue many of the traditions of the ancient cliff dwellers. Many Pueblo, Zuni, and Hopi people continue to farm and perform ceremonies. They still honor their connection with the land and the spirit world. They create exquisite pottery, jewelry, baskets, carvings, and weavings. Ray Tafoya is known for his pottery.
pages.brief: Modern Pueblo, Zuni, and Hopi people continue traditions of the ancient cliff dwellers. Some farm and perform ceremonies, honoring their connection with the land and spirit world. Estella Loretto cleans a bronze statue, and Ray Tafoya is shown with his pottery, alongside jewelry, baskets, carvings, and weavings made by descendants.

pages.text: Preserving the Past Follow these rules to preserve ruins and artifacts. 1. Look, but don’t take. It is against the law to keep artifacts. 2. Do not touch or draw on walls, petroglyphs, or pictographs. 3. Do not climb on walls. Many walls are easily damaged. An example of a damaged wall Protecting the Cliff Dwellings In the late 1800s, many people visited the cliff dwellings. Some photographed, drew, and described the sites, but others took artifacts from the dwellings to sell. Over time, people became concerned about protecting the cliff dwellings from damage and theft. The concern led to the creation of Mesa Verde National Park in 1906. The National Park Service protects the cliff dwellings while also letting visitors enjoy them. Educational exhibits at Mesa Verde and other sites in the Southwest teach people about the Ancestral Puebloan way of life.
pages.brief: Visitors at Mesa Verde stand near ancient stone walls and petroglyphs, following rules to look without taking artifacts, touching walls, or climbing on fragile ruins. A damaged wall shows the need for care. Park exhibits teach about Ancestral Puebloan life and National Park Service protection.

books.title: Earth's Water
books.art_why: Real-world science topic with observable water forms, so photos fit.

pages.text: Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: A wide view of planet Earth from space shows blue water across its surface, introducing Earth’s water. The scene shows Earth as a watery planet and sets up the book’s look at water in its many forms and places.

pages.text: Water Everywhere Water fills oceans, lakes, and ponds, and it flows in rivers, streams, and underground. It is even in the air. Frozen water exists on some parts of Earth as snow and ice.
pages.brief: Oceans, lakes, and ponds are full of water; rivers and streams flow across the land; water lies underground and is present in the air. In cold parts of Earth, snow and ice show frozen water.

pages.text: Water covers over two-thirds of Earth’s surface. Most of it consists of salt water in the oceans. Earth has much less fresh water, and many plants and animals depend on fresh water for survival. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: Earth seen from space has water covering more than two-thirds of its surface. Most of that water is salt water in the oceans, while much less fresh water exists. Plants and animals depend on fresh water for survival.
