pages.text: Some of this fresh water is aboveground, while other fresh water is groundwater underneath Earth’s surface. What are some ways you use Earth’s water?
pages.brief: A split view shows fresh water aboveground in visible places and groundwater underneath Earth’s surface. The scene presents both kinds of fresh water and leaves room to think about the many ways people use Earth’s water.

pages.text: Different Forms of Water Liquid water is the most common state of water on Earth. When you pour liquid water into a container, it takes the shape of that container. Liquid water is always moving, even if you can’t see it move. Water moves in rivers and streams due to currents —the constant flow of moving water. Lakes and ponds are often called standing bodies of water because the liquid water in them moves so slowly. Surface and underwater currents cause ocean water to move, with waves forming and crashing. Winds, the Moon, and the Sun affect the strength of ocean currents. Each of these containers holds four cups of water. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: Liquid water in containers takes the shape of each container, and four containers each hold four cups. Rivers and streams flow with currents, lakes and ponds move slowly, and ocean waves and currents are affected by winds, the Moon, and the Sun.

pages.text: Ice can be carved into many shapes. Not all water is in a liquid state. When liquid water gets very cold, it freezes and forms ice. Ice is another state of water— solid water. Ice can float on liquid water. People form ice into different shapes. You’ve probably made ice cubes to cool down a drink. Artists even carve ice sculptures.
pages.brief: When liquid water gets very cold, it freezes into solid ice, which can float on liquid water. People form ice into cubes to cool a drink, and an artist carves an ice sculpture into a different shape.

pages.text: Much of Earth’s frozen water is at the North and South Poles, the coldest areas on Earth. Huge masses of ice called glaciers, which are commonly found at the poles, store much of Earth’s fresh water. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: At the North and South Poles, the coldest areas on Earth, huge masses of ice called glaciers store much of Earth’s fresh water. The scene shows frozen water at the poles and glaciers holding fresh water.

pages.text: Some of Earth’s water is in an invisible state as a gas called water vapor. While it’s always invisible, water vapor is all around us. When it is hot outside, more water vapor fills the air than when it is cold outside. Humidity is the amount of water vapor in the air. On hot and humid days, the air feels thick with lots of water vapor concentrated in the air.
pages.brief: Invisible water vapor gas is all around us. On a hot day more water vapor fills the air than on a cold day; humidity is the amount of water vapor, and hot, humid air feels thick with concentrated water vapor.

pages.text: As this snowperson absorbs sunlight, the snow eventually heats up and melts into liquid water. Changing Water Earth’s water is constantly changing from one state to another. When frozen water is heated, it melts and becomes liquid water, and when liquid water is cooled, it freezes and becomes ice. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: A snowperson absorbs sunlight, heats up, and melts into liquid water. The scene shows frozen water changing to liquid when heated and liquid water changing to ice when cooled, as Earth’s water constantly changes from one state to another.

pages.text: Liquid water can become a gas, too. Have you ever seen a puddle of water dry up on a hot day? Energy from the Sun changed the liquid to a gas in a process called evaporation. Evaporation happens every day as the Sun beats down on Earth’s bodies of water. When water vapor in the air cools down, it changes from a gas to a liquid in a process called condensation. Energy from the Sun causes water to evaporate.
pages.brief: Energy from the Sun causes a puddle to dry up as liquid water evaporates into gas. Water vapor in cooling air condenses back into liquid, and the Sun’s energy drives evaporation from Earth’s bodies of water every day.

pages.text: Clouds drop water on the desert as rain. Clouds are made up of tiny drops of water formed by condensation. The tiny drops stick together, creating larger, heavier drops. If the drops become large enough, they fall as rain, snow, or another type of precipitation. Some rain and melted snow soak into the ground, becoming groundwater. Precipitation and groundwater fill rivers, lakes, streams, and ponds. Water evaporates from bodies of water around the world, and, later, it condenses and falls in other places on Earth. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: Clouds made of tiny condensed water drops stick together into larger, heavier drops and fall as rain over a desert. Rain and melted snow soak into the ground as groundwater and fill rivers, lakes, streams, and ponds, while water evaporates elsewhere and condenses to fall again.

pages.text: Water Is Important Rain keeps plants alive and allows them to grow. People and other animals require water to survive. We also use it for other purposes, such as fighting fires.
pages.brief: Rain falls on green plants and helps them grow. People and other animals need water to survive, and firefighters use water from a hose to fight a fire, showing different important daily uses of water.

pages.text: It is important to take care of Earth’s water. Human activities are the main cause of water pollution, although sometimes it occurs naturally. Littering and dumping trash lead to dirty and unusable water. Polluted water makes people, plants, and animals sick. Would you want to drink and play in polluted water? Earth’s Water 16 polluted not polluted.
pages.brief: Litter and dumped trash make water dirty and unusable, while human activities are the main cause of water pollution. Polluted water can make people, plants, and animals sick, and the scene contrasts polluted water with clean, unpolluted water.

books.title: Golf
books.art_why: The book includes early golf history and old equipment from before modern photography.

pages.text: Golfers spend many hours trying to improve their golf swing. Why Golf? If you compare golf to other sports, you may think that hitting a ball into a hole in the ground sounds fairly simple. Nothing could be further from the truth. To play well, golfers need patience, balance, focus, and lots of practice. Yet if golf is hard, why do millions of people love the sport? It’s played in beautiful places with rolling green land. It gives people the chance to learn, practice, and improve. Most of all, golf offers hours of fun and relaxation.
pages.brief: Several golfers practice their swings on a wide, rolling green course under open sky. One golfer stands ready with a club while others watch and adjust their own stance. The scene shows patience, balance, and focus as they spend hours trying to improve.

pages.text: Golf Hole fringe – an area around the green that has longer grass hole – marked with a flagstick putting green (“green” for short) water hazard – a stream or pond fairway bunker – a shallow hole in the ground that is usually filled with sand rough – an area that has trees, shrubs, and long grass teeing ground.
pages.brief: A golf hole shows the teeing ground at one end and a putting green with a flagstick at the far end. A fairway leads between them, with a sand-filled bunker, a water hazard, and rough areas of trees, shrubs, and longer grass around the green.

pages.text: Golf Clubs Golf clubs have heads of different shapes, depending on what they are used for. • Irons are used for shorter shots. • Woods and fairway metals are used to hit the ball long distances. • Wedges are used for short, high shots or to get the ball out of sand. • Putters are used to roll the ball once it is on the green. iron wood wedge putter Playing Golf Golfers use clubs to hit a small, hard ball into a hole using as few strokes, or swings, as possible. Sometimes the ball must travel a very long way to reach the hole. Sometimes it only needs to move a short distance. At other times, it must fly high in the air to get over long grass or other things. Golfers need to know how to make all these types of shots.
pages.brief: Four golf clubs rest side by side: an iron, a wood, a wedge, and a putter, each with a differently shaped head. Nearby, a golfer hits a small hard ball, showing a long shot, a short shot, and a high shot flying over long grass toward a hole.

pages.text: The sport is played on a golf course, which is a large area of land that is carefully mowed and trimmed to define the areas of the course. A golf course usually has nine or eighteen sections, or holes. Each section begins at the teeing ground, where golfers usually place their ball on a small peg called a tee. They hit the ball down the fairway—the area that leads to the small hole at the far end of the section. The area around the small hole is called the putting green, or simply the green. It almost always takes several strokes to get the ball there. However, lucky golfers sometimes get a hole in one. In golf, the word hole has two different meanings. One is the small hole into which golfers hit the ball (left). The other is each of the nine or eighteen sections of a golf course (right).
pages.brief: A large, carefully mowed golf course stretches across the land, with several sections marked out. At the teeing ground, a golfer places a ball on a small tee and hits it down the fairway toward the putting green. Far away, a small hole waits beside a flagstick.

pages.text: This hole is almost surrounded by water and rough, with a large bunker as well. Other holes might have fewer hazards. Golfers need to deal with hazards, which are parts of the course that they try to avoid. Getting a ball out of a hazard may take extra strokes, which is bad for a golfer’s score. One type of hazard is a sand-filled area called a bunker. Streams and ponds are other types of hazards. The rough— the area around each section, which usually has trees, bushes, and longer grass—can also present problems. water hazard bunker rough.
pages.brief: A golf hole sits almost surrounded by water and rough, with a large sand-filled bunker nearby. A golfer faces the hazards and prepares to hit the ball out. Trees, bushes, and longer grass edge the section, while a stream and pond threaten extra strokes.

pages.text: A golf game usually involves playing eighteen different sections, called holes. If a golf course has only nine holes, golfers often play the course twice. Each hole on a golf course has a number, called the par. If a hole has a par of four, golfers try to get the ball into the hole in four strokes or less. The number depends on the distance from the teeing ground to the hole. Most holes are three, four, or five par. Par for the course is the total of all the pars for the entire nine or eighteen holes. Golfers who play together in a small group compare their totals for the whole course. The player with the lowest score wins. Scoring a Par Five Hole A golfer’s score is based on the number of strokes compared to par. The sport has special names for scores. Name of Score Number of Strokes Hole in one One.
pages.brief: A small group of golfers walks together from one hole to the next on an eighteen-hole course. One player prepares to hit into the hole on a par-five hole while the others wait. Their scores are compared by strokes, and one lucky shot could be a hole in one.

pages.text: Golfers respect how much concentration it takes to play the game well. They stand back and stay quiet when another person is taking a swing. It can take between three and five hours to play a round of golf, or eighteen holes. People who golf just for fun often ride the course in golf carts. Professional golfers walk from one hole to the next. Helpers called caddies carry their clubs. Golfers wear shoes with spikes on the bottom for gripping the grass. Their clothing allows them to move easily when they swing a club. Some golfers wear a glove on one hand to help them grip the clubs better and avoid getting blisters.
pages.brief: A golfer stands quietly back while another takes a swing, showing concentration and respect. In the background, players ride golf carts along the course, while a professional walks with a caddie carrying clubs. The golfer wears spiked shoes, easy-moving clothing, and a glove on one hand.

pages.text: A Sport Is Born Scotland is the birthplace of modern golf. The game may have begun as long ago as the 1400s. It probably spread to England in the early 1600s and to India, Australia, and other British colonies soon after. By the late 1800s, golf was played in many countries around the world. old clubs Equipment has changed a lot over the years. The first golf balls and clubs were made of wood. In the early 1600s, people started using leather balls filled with feathers. In 1848, a new ball was invented. It was made of tree sap that was dried, heated, and shaped. Players began using metal golf clubs with the new balls. Modern golf balls with rubber cores first appeared in 1898. old ball modern ball Golf balls started to have dimples in the early 1900s. The dimples help the balls fly higher and farther.
pages.brief: In Scotland, early golfers play with wooden clubs and balls. Old wooden clubs and a feather-filled leather ball sit beside a modern dimpled golf ball with a rubber core. A metal club rests nearby, showing how equipment changed from wood and feathers to tree-sap balls and modern designs.

pages.text: A Global Game Because golf began in Scotland, the sport is most popular in countries where English is spoken. People in more than 130 countries around the world play the game. The United States has many more golf courses than any other country. However, compared to how many people live in each country, Scotland has the most golf courses. In addition to outdoor courses, many places have indoor digital simulators where people can improve their skills. Miniature golf is played both indoors and outdoors. Top Ten Golfing Countries.
pages.brief: A world map shows golfers in many countries, with the United States standing out for its many courses and Scotland for having the most courses compared to its population. Some players practice indoors on digital simulators, while others play miniature golf inside or outside.

pages.text: Who Plays Golf? More than sixty million people around the world play golf. In the United States, over twenty million people play each year. Programs exist for young people to learn the game and compete. Top men’s golfers compete in the U.S.-based Professional Golfers’ Association (PGA) Tour and the European Tour as well as several others. Top women’s golfers from around the world compete in the U.S.-based Ladies Professional Golf Association (LPGA) Tour. In addition, men and women each have several top professional tournaments, called majors. Winning a major earns a golfer respect, fame, and money. Only a small number of golfers earn a living by competing in golf tournaments. Golf competitions sometimes have wildlife hazards. The 2008 Women’s World Cup in South Africa was interrupted by baboons.
pages.brief: Many golfers of different ages play on courses around the world. Young players learn and compete in programs, while top men and women play in professional tours and major tournaments. At a South African competition, baboons wander onto the course and interrupt play.

pages.text: Tiger Woods Jack Nicklaus Patty Berg Golf Greats Jack Nicklaus is the top golfer in the history of the sport. He competed in important tournaments from 1961 to 2005 and won more than a hundred competitions. He won eighteen majors. Patty Berg was the top woman to ever play golf. As a professional, she competed from 1940 to 1962 and won sixty tournaments and fifteen majors. Tiger Woods may be the greatest golfer playing today. He has done better on the PGA Tour than any other golfer now playing.
pages.brief: Three golf greats are shown: Jack Nicklaus, Patty Berg, and Tiger Woods. Nicklaus stands with clubs after winning many majors, Patty Berg competes in a professional tournament, and Tiger Woods swings on the PGA Tour. Each has earned respect for outstanding play.

pages.text: Types of Golf Courses Golf courses are located in many different places. Some are like large, grassy parks with tall trees. Some are narrow strips of land along coastlines. In desert areas, courses often have cactuses and palm trees. Few players will ever experience golfing on the Moon, but anyone who is interested can find a way to play golf right here on Earth. All you need is a club and a golf ball. With lots of practice, young players will learn what millions of golfers already know: golf is out of this world! Alan Shepard swings a golf club at a ball on the Moon in 1971.
pages.brief: Golf courses appear in many places: a grassy park with tall trees, a narrow strip along a coastline, and a desert course with cactuses and palm trees. On the Moon in 1971, Alan Shepard swings a golf club at a ball while young players practice on Earth with a club and ball.

books.title: Deep in the Ocean
books.art_why: Real deep-ocean animals, scientists, ships, satellites, and diving equipment exist today; no named famous person is featured, so photographs suit.

pages.text: The small, deep ocean sea pig moves along the ocean floor. It eats tiny sea animals and microbes that live in the mud. Deep Underwater Imagine taking a voyage to the deepest part of the ocean. What types of things would you expect to see? Would it be dark or light? Would you see clearly or would the water be cloudy? Would it be warm or cold? Would you see familiar animals and plants or find strange and new ones?
pages.brief: A small sea pig moves along the muddy ocean floor in the deep ocean. It eats tiny sea animals and microbes that live in the mud. The deep underwater world around it is the setting for an imagined voyage to the deepest part of the ocean.

pages.text: Sunlight warms the shallow parts of the ocean down to 200 meters (656 ft) below the surface. Plants and animals that need sunlight and warm water live there, such as tiger sharks and many species of common dolphins. Deep in the ocean, other animals, including vampire squid, fangtooth fish, and viperfish, live in water that is cold and dark.
pages.brief: Sunlight warms the shallow ocean down to 200 meters, where tiger sharks and many common dolphins swim in warm, sunlit water. Farther down, in cold and dark water, vampire squid, fangtooth fish, and viperfish live where sunlight does not reach.

pages.text: Ocean Zones.
pages.brief: A wide view of the ocean is divided into broad depth zones, from the surface down to the deepest bottom. The layers are arranged one below another, showing the different parts of the ocean as separate zones. The scene focuses on the ocean itself, with no animals or people.

pages.text: Diving Deep in the Ocean The deep ocean, below 1,000 meters (3,281 ft), is freezing cold. The water pressure below 39.6 meters (130 ft) can harm you if you don’t have the right protective gear. Sport divers wear air tanks filled with a mixture of gases for safety. They also wear special dive computers that help them know how far down they are and how much air they have. Deep divers wear special hard diving suits to protect them from the water pressure. For really deep dives, groups of two or three scientists ride in a small submarine called a submersible. Some of these submersibles have robot arms that can collect samples of water, soil, and small animals underwater. sport diver 39 m (128 ft) 7–13°C (45–55°F) diving suit 609 m (2,000 ft) 4.5–7°C (40–45°F) submersible craft 6,096 m (20,000 ft) 0–2°C (32–35°F)
pages.brief: A sport diver wears an air tank and a dive computer while descending into cold deep water. Nearby, a deep diver wears a hard protective suit against water pressure. A small submersible carries two or three scientists, and its robot arm collects samples of water, soil, and small animals.

pages.text: Oceanographers Scientists who study the ocean are called oceanographers (oh-shuh-NOG-ruh-furs). They often live for months on a ship, working seven days a week, and also teach at colleges and universities. Some of them study what sea animals eat and where they live. Others study the ocean water itself. All of them have to understand biology, chemistry, geology, and physics. Biology is the study of living things. Chemistry is the study of what things are made of and how they react and change when they come into contact with other things. Geology is the study of rocks and soil and the processes that shape and change the Earth. Physics is the study of the natural laws, such as energy, force, and motion, that govern how things work.
pages.brief: Oceanographers live and work for months on a ship, busy seven days a week. Some observe what sea animals eat and where they live, while others study the ocean water itself. Their work brings together biology, chemistry, geology, and physics to understand living things, materials, rocks and soil, and natural laws.

pages.text: Using Satellites for Tracking Satellites up in space can help to track sea animals’ travels in Earth’s oceans. Scientists tag some animals with electronic sensors to study them. A satellite can track the signal from the tag attached to the animal’s fin or back. The signal shows when, where, and how the animal travels. These tags have been used to track some fish that have traveled up to 75,000 kilometers (46,602 mi). Scientists can use this information to predict the animal’s future movements. tag satellite.
pages.brief: A satellite circles high above Earth while a tagged sea animal swims in the ocean below. A small electronic sensor is attached to the animal’s fin or back, and its signal reaches the satellite. The tracking shows when, where, and how far the animal travels, helping scientists predict future movements.

pages.text: Counting the Sea Animals What types of animals live in the ocean? Where do they live? How many are there? Oceanographers studied and counted animals for ten years to discover the answers. They looked at all the world’s oceans from the North Pole to the South Pole. They counted everything they could find from the largest whales to the smallest organisms. The surprising report is called the Census of Marine Life. Released in 2010, it contains data from more than 540 different expeditions that began in more than eighty countries. Lionfish swim among coral sea fans. Their long, feathery spines can sting any predator that comes too close. Native to the South Pacific, lionfish were first spotted in United States’ waters in 2000.
pages.brief: Oceanographers count ocean animals from the largest whales to the smallest organisms across all the world’s oceans, from the North Pole to the South Pole. A lionfish swims among coral sea fans, its long, feathery spines held ready to sting any predator that comes too close.

pages.text: The leafy sea dragon blends in with the plants of its surroundings. Its eyes move independently of each other so it can look in two directions at once. The male sea dragon carries the eggs for the female and gives birth. The Census of Marine Life The study revealed new information and several surprises about extreme habitats. One surprise from the study was where things lived: everywhere —in all water levels and temperatures! Marine species lived in the hottest and coldest places. More than seventeen thousand species lived in deep places without light and some without oxygen. Another surprise was how many new species were discovered. More than twelve hundred new marine species have been described, and more than five thousand species are still waiting to be described. Scientists found one species of Jurassic shrimp that was thought to have gone extinct more than fifty million years ago.
pages.brief: A leafy sea dragon drifts among plants, blending in with its surroundings. Its eyes move independently, looking in two directions at once, and the male carries the eggs before giving birth. In the background, scientists study extreme ocean habitats where many new species, including a Jurassic shrimp, live.

pages.text: Over 2 kilometers (1.3 mi) deep in the ocean, giant tube worms live in the hot water that bubbles up from a lava pillar. Living in Hot and Cold Water The very cold Deep Ocean Zone has more than one million hot volcanoes in it. The water temperature at a volcano can be 400°C (752°F), which is hot enough to melt lead. Species such as eyeless shrimp, white crabs, giant tube worms, and many bacteria live in this very hot water. These animals use sulfur rather than sunlight to live.
pages.brief: Deep over two kilometers down, giant tube worms cluster around a lava pillar where hot water bubbles up. Eyeless shrimp, white crabs, and bacteria live in the same hot volcanic water, using sulfur instead of sunlight to survive. The water is hot enough to melt lead.

pages.text: Huge groups of Arctic and Antarctic animals were also found living in water that is close to or below freezing. Giant squid, Antarctic cod, and the lion’s mane jellyfish are some species that live under solid ice that is 700 meters (2,296 ft) thick. Many of these species slow down their movements to save energy so they don’t freeze. The Antarctic ice fish has no red blood cells. Its thinner blood contains a type of antifreeze. Its special blood helps it survive in the frigid waters beneath ice that would freeze the blood of most fish.
pages.brief: Beneath solid ice hundreds of meters thick, giant squid, Antarctic cod, and lion’s mane jellyfish live in water close to or below freezing. Many move slowly to save energy. The Antarctic ice fish has no red blood cells; its thinner blood contains a kind of antifreeze that helps it survive where most fish would freeze.

pages.text: What Did We Learn? Scientists learned that life is even more adaptable than they originally thought. Animals living in the deep ocean have found ways to survive in harsh environments that would be impossible for most other species to live in. The marine census counted more than 230,000 species in more than 30 million records. More than 6,000 new species had never been seen before! Some animals were see-through, or translucent. Some had warning lights that turn on and off so that they can see in the darkness. Others had long feelers instead of eyes to attract prey and learn what was around them. Some had teeth so long that they overlapped their jaws. Others made their own antifreeze to stay warm. This big-eyed squid lives in the cold, deep waters of the northern Atlantic Ocean.
pages.brief: In the cold, deep waters of the northern Atlantic Ocean, a big-eyed squid swims in darkness. Around it are deep-ocean animals with see-through bodies, warning lights that switch on and off, long feelers instead of eyes, and teeth so long they overlap their jaws. Some make their own antifreeze to stay warm.

pages.text: What else lives in the deep ocean? Scientists keep discovering new species and new facts. The more they look, the more they find. They think that only one quarter of all marine life has been counted. Not all the animals that have been discovered have been documented and described. There are many more surprises to come! Explore More To learn more about the Census of Marine Life, go to its website at www.coml.org. Each week, new discoveries are added to the marine census project map at www.comlmaps.org/census-on- google-earth. On the Internet, search terms such as deep sea species, blind lobster, or NASA oceanography.
pages.brief: Scientists continue exploring the deep ocean, where new species and new facts keep appearing. The more they look, the more they find. They think only one quarter of all marine life has been counted, and many discovered animals have not yet been documented or described. More surprises are still to come.

books.title: Electric Eels!
books.art_why: The book opens with an 1800 Humboldt expedition and scenes from before photographs existed.

pages.text: Legendary Shocker German naturalist Alexander Humboldt went to Venezuela to catch electric eels in 1800. He knew living electric eels could help him solve some mysteries about electricity. He knew not to touch the eels with his bare hands. Their shocks could cause great pain. He asked some fishermen if they could help.
pages.brief: German naturalist Alexander Humboldt stands by a Venezuelan waterway in 1800, keeping his bare hands away from electric eels in the water. He speaks with fishermen, asking them to help him catch eels. The fishermen listen near the water.

pages.text: The fishermen led about thirty horses into a shallow pond. The eels rose up and gave the horses hundreds of shocks. After the eels became tired and stopped shocking, the fishermen caught five of them. Humboldt learned much about the eels. Shocking Fish Story Not long ago, a scientist supported Humboldt’s report that eels rise up to protect themselves. Before that, some scientists thought Humboldt might have been stretching the truth, like any fish story. This picture was made from Humboldt’s writing about fishing for eels with horses. It shows how powerful electric eels are.
pages.brief: In a shallow pond, about thirty horses stand in the water as fishermen lead them in. Electric eels rise up and shock the horses. After the eels tire and stop shocking, fishermen catch five eels.

pages.text: It’s a Fish! Electric eels are long gray-brown fish with yellow or orange on their throats. These tube-shaped fish are more like catfish than other eels. The group they belong to is called knifefish. All knifefish can use electricity. Electric eels can grow as long as 2 to 3 meters (7–10 ft.). They can weigh as much as 20 to 22 kilograms (44–48 lb.). They can grow to about as big around as an average adult human’s thigh and four times as long. Male and female electric eels are alike in color and size. Electric Eel Facts Scientific Name Electrophorus electricus Animal Type Fish Diet Fish, crustaceans, and amphibians Length 2 to 3 meters (7–10 ft.) Weight 20 to 22 kilograms (44–48 lb.)
pages.brief: A long gray-brown electric eel with yellow-orange on its throat swims in water. Its tube-shaped body is shown next to an average adult human’s thigh for size, and it is four times as long. A male and female electric eel appear alike in color and size.

pages.text: Unlike most other fish, electric eels breathe air through their mouths. They have gills, but they mostly use their gills to help them breathe out. Electric eels open their mouths above the water to breathe air in through special organs in their mouths. The waste air they breathe out goes through their mouths and gills. Electric eels need air every few minutes. They can drown if they get trapped underwater.
pages.brief: At the water’s surface, an electric eel lifts its mouth above the water to breathe air through special organs in its mouth. Its gills help it breathe out waste air. The eel stays near the surface because it needs air every few minutes and can drown if trapped underwater.

pages.text: Like most other fish, electric eels have fins and a backbone. They have small fins on either side of their heads. They also have a long fin on their bellies from head to tail. Their backbones and fins help them move. Electric eels wave their belly fins in an S- shape to swim, which they do quite slowly. They move quickly only when they attack. Shocking Fact Electric eels can regrow the tail parts of their bodies if they’re cut off.
pages.brief: An electric eel swims slowly through water, waving the long fin on its belly in an S-shape. Small fins sit on either side of its head, and its backbone helps it move. It moves quickly only when it attacks. A cut tail part is shown regrowing.

pages.text: It’s Electric! An electric eel is the most electric fish on Earth. These eels can navigate, communicate, protect themselves, hunt, and stun or kill prey using their bioelectricity. Bioelectricity is the action of electric currents in a body. Other knifefish and some skates, rays, and catfish use bioelectricity, too. Those fish can navigate, communicate, or protect themselves. However, none can zap with as much power as an electric eel. Shocking Medical History Don’t try this at home! Ancient Greeks and Romans held live electric rays to people’s foreheads to cure headaches. A ray’s shock can cause numbness in humans, so it might have worked! Other Electric Fish.
pages.brief: An electric eel sends bioelectric currents through water as it navigates, communicates, protects itself, and hunts. Nearby knifefish, skates, rays, and catfish also use bioelectricity, but the eel is strongest. In an ancient scene, a Greek or Roman person holds a live electric ray to someone’s forehead to try to cure a headache.

pages.text: Three organs produce an electric eel’s shocks. The organs start just behind the eel’s head and make up two-thirds of its body. An eel’s body is like a battery. The positive end is at the head, and the negative end is at the tail. Shocking Fact If an electric eel curls its head toward its tail, the move increases the eel’s shocking power. Three Electric Organs.
pages.brief: Inside an electric eel’s long body, three electric organs begin just behind its head and fill two-thirds of its body. The eel is shown like a battery, with the positive end at its head and the negative end at its tail. The eel curls its head toward its tail, increasing its shocking power.

pages.text: An electric eel can shock prey with up to 650 volts of electricity. The shock can kill small animals and stun large ones. Anything in the water within 9 meters (28 ft.) of the eel can feel it. Electric eels have five times more volts than a typical U.S. wall socket—which can be dangerous to people. Electric eels can’t feel their own shocks, but scientists aren’t sure why. It might be because of their size or how the shock moves. It also might be because of some part of the eel that scientists don’t understand. Scientists do know that eels have special cells called electrocytes. These cells line up in long rows. They each produce a tiny shock at nearly the same time. Together, they create the electric eel’s stunning attack ZAP!
pages.brief: An electric eel releases a 650-volt shock in the water, stunning or killing prey and reaching anything within 9 meters. A typical U.S. wall socket is shown for comparison, with the eel’s shock five times stronger. Long rows of special electrocytes inside the eel each make a tiny shock at nearly the same time.

pages.text: Stunning Attack Before an attack zap happens, electric eels must find their prey. Dark, cloudy water and poor sight don’t help. Electric eels are also most active at night. They use small shocks instead of their eyes to see prey. They hunt much like some bats and owls, which bounce sound off objects. Electric eels send out small shocks of electricity—about fifty every second. These small shocks hit plants, animals, and objects. They help the eels sense what’s around them. When an electric eel senses prey is nearby, it sends out a group of two or three larger shocks. The shocks make the prey twitch. The animal can’t stop moving, so the eel senses where it is. Then the electric eel sends out its attack shock, which stuns or kills the prey. The electric eel quickly sucks the prey through its mouth into its stomach. Electric eels mostly eat small fish, crustaceans, and amphibians. Young eels also eat worms and insect larvae.
pages.brief: At night in dark, cloudy water, an electric eel sends out about fifty small shocks every second to sense plants, animals, and objects around it. When it senses prey nearby, two or three larger shocks make the prey twitch. Then an attack shock stuns or kills the prey, and the eel sucks it into its mouth.

pages.text: Don’t Swim There! Electric eels are top predators in the slow- moving rivers where they often live. Scientists have found them in the Amazon and Orinoco Rivers in South America. They also live in nearby freshwater swamps, creeks, ponds, and lakes. Because they breathe air, electric eels can live in water that might kill other fish. They can also live out of water for hours if their skin stays wet. Electric Eel Habitat ATLANTIC OCEAN Orinoco River Amazon River SOUTH AMERICA PACIFIC OCEAN.
pages.brief: Electric eels swim as top predators in slow-moving rivers, including the Amazon and Orinoco Rivers in South America. Nearby freshwater swamps, creeks, ponds, and lakes hold more eels. Because they breathe air, they can live in water that might kill other fish, and they can stay out of water for hours if their skin stays wet.

pages.text: Electric eels mostly mate in small ponds. Male eels build nests by making bubbles with their saliva. Female eels lay eggs in the bubbles. Males guard the nests and the baby eels until they are about 10 centimeters (4 in.) long. Then the babies have to live on their own. Because of their weaker shocks, young electric eels are more likely than adults to be prey for other animals, such as crocodiles. Black caimans are related to crocodiles. They are one of the few predators that try to eat electric eels.
pages.brief: In a small pond, a male electric eel builds a nest of bubbles made with its saliva. A female lays eggs in the bubbles, and the male guards the nest and baby eels until they are about 10 centimeters long. A black caiman, related to crocodiles, approaches the young eels as a predator.

pages.text: Future Energy Source Scientists now know more about electric eels than Humboldt did. Even so, there is always more to learn. Scientists at Yale University want to use electrocytes as a model to create cells that act like batteries. Some medical devices—such as pacemakers, which keep hearts beating—contain batteries that could harm a person if they break. Scientists want to create batteries that won’t be harmful and won’t run out of power. Humboldt wrote more than two hundred years ago, “We are, doubtless, very far from having discovered all the secrets of the electrical action of fishes.” What will electric eels help scientists understand next?
pages.brief: Scientists at Yale University examine electrocytes from an electric eel as a model for new battery-like cells. They want batteries for medical devices such as pacemakers that will not harm a person if they break and will not run out of power. Alexander Humboldt is shown from more than two hundred years ago, when he wrote about electric fishes.

books.title: Mysterious Caves
books.art_why: Caves, explorers, and formations exist in the real world today, so photos fit.

pages.text: A cave explorer stands by a gigantic flowstone column deep inside a Vietnamese cave. A New Underground World In 2009, a team of British cave explorers traveled to Vietnam. Vietnam is a long, narrow country that borders a portion of the South China Sea. It has many beautiful bays, large rock formations, forests, and rivers. These cave explorers, or spelunkers (spee-LUNK-ers), had already visited several large caves in the area. But this time, they were exploring a cave that was brand new to science. Only a local farmer, Ho Khanh, knew its location, and he had led them to the jungle-covered opening. They went in and walked for miles, into nothing but total darkness.
pages.brief: Deep inside a Vietnamese cave, a cave explorer stands beside a gigantic flowstone column. Nearby, a team of British cave explorers has entered through a jungle-covered opening, led by local farmer Ho Khanh, and walks for miles into total darkness.

pages.text: A shaft of sunlight helps an explorer see the wonders inside the Hang Son Doong cave in Vietnam. Suddenly, they saw light. A shaft of sunlight was cutting through the darkness ahead of them. As they moved closer, they could tell that part of the cave roof had collapsed long ago, leaving a hole that let in this patch of sunlight. The sunlight revealed the room’s amazing size. They soon realized that they stood in the biggest cave room known to exist. One single area of the room was over 90 meters (300 ft) wide, 180 meters (600 ft) high, and over 4 kilometers (2.5 mi) long. An entire city block of 40-story buildings could fit inside.
pages.brief: Inside Hang Son Doong cave in Vietnam, a shaft of sunlight cuts through darkness ahead of an explorer. The light falls through a hole where part of the cave roof collapsed long ago, revealing a huge cave room with a single area over 90 meters wide and 180 meters high.

pages.text: The entrance to the massive Hang Son Doong cave was hidden by dense jungle. This cave, called Hang Son Doong, or Mountain River Cave, is enormous. Where the roof collapsed, letting in sunlight and rain, dense hidden jungles grow. There is also a 60-meter (200-ft) cliff they named the “Great Wall of Vietnam.” The cliff stopped the cavers at first. They returned with equipment to scale the cliff, and continued their journey into the interior. This cave is the biggest yet found, but it may not be the biggest in the world. Adventurous explorers find new caves every year. In this book, you will learn about caves. You will read about how they form, the unusual formations and living things within them, and other caves that are just as wondrous as Hang Son Doong.
pages.brief: The entrance to Hang Son Doong, or Mountain River Cave, is hidden by dense jungle. Where the roof collapsed, sunlight and rain reach hidden jungles inside. A 60-meter cliff called the Great Wall of Vietnam stopped cavers at first; they return with equipment to scale it and continue deeper.

pages.text: What Are Caves? A cave is any natural hollow space in the earth. Usually when people talk about a cave, they mean a space big enough for a person to go inside, and deep enough so sunlight never reaches part of it. Caves can occur in rock, in ice, and underwater. Caves are found all over the world. Cave explorers want to see what’s inside. We may think of all caves as being dark and barren. But caves can be gorgeous, filled with amazing formations and unusual animals. Caves lure adventurous people who love the excitement and challenge of seeing a place no one has ever seen before. We know that humans lived in caves as long as 30,000 years ago.
pages.brief: A natural hollow space opens in the earth, with a dark interior deep enough that sunlight never reaches part of it. Around the opening are rock, ice, and underwater cave settings; cave explorers look toward the entrance, and a simple ancient human shelter suggests people lived in caves long ago.

pages.text: Montana’s Lewis and Clark Caverns contain some of the largest limestone formations in the United States. Types of Caves Caves can form in several ways. Nature uses basic tools such as rock, water, and heat to carve these chambers in the earth. Karst Caves The ground is made of different types of rock. Some types, such as limestone, can dissolve in water. Water from the surface seeps through the soil or trickles through cracks in the ground. If the water hits limestone underground, it slowly dissolves the rock, creating a hollow space. Over millions of years, the water eats away at the rock and creates a karst cave.
pages.brief: Inside Montana’s Lewis and Clark Caverns, large limestone formations fill a chamber. Water seeps through soil and trickles through cracks in the ground, reaches limestone underground, and slowly dissolves the rock. Over millions of years, the water eats away the limestone and creates a hollow karst cave.

pages.text: Molten lava spills into the sea from a lava tube at Kilauea, Hawaii. Primary Caves and Lava Tubes In karst caves, seeping water dissolves existing rock and eventually creates a hole. But in primary caves, the rock contained a hollow space from its beginning. The rock was born with a cave-sized hole in it. Another type of rock cave forms when liquid magma or lava in volcanoes cools and turns solid. In some volcanoes, liquid lava flows over the ground in a stream. The surface of the lava stream quickly cools and turns solid. But the lava underneath stays hot and liquid, and keeps flowing. The flowing hot lava creates long tunnels through the solid lava rock. These long tunnel caves are called lava tubes.
pages.brief: At Kilauea in Hawaii, molten lava spills into the sea from a lava tube. The surface of a lava stream cools and turns solid while hot liquid lava underneath keeps flowing, creating long tunnel caves. Other primary caves began with a cave-sized hollow space inside the rock.

pages.text: Sailors explore a vast sea cave on the island of Corfu, Greece. Erosional Caves and Sea Caves Moving water, such as rivers or ocean waves, can carry grains of sand. Ever so slowly, these tough little grains grind away rock in a process called erosion. Erosion creates caves called erosional caves. Erosional caves are different from karst caves in that water physically grinds away the rock. In karst caves, water chemically dissolves the rock. A common kind of erosional cave is a sea cave. Sea caves form when ocean waves continually crash against cliffs, eventually digging out a hollow space.
pages.brief: Sailors explore a vast sea cave on the island of Corfu, Greece. Ocean waves continually crash against cliffs, carrying grains of sand that slowly grind away rock by erosion. Over time, the waves dig out a hollow space, forming a sea cave.

pages.text: Inside a massive ice cave formed beneath the Mendenhall Glacier, in the state of Alaska Caves don’t always form in rock. Glaciers are enormous moving masses of solid ice. At the top of a glacier, the Sun can melt some of the ice, which becomes a stream of warm water. The warm water flows down through cracks in the glacier toward the soil layer beneath. As it runs, the warmer water melts the ice around it, forming a glacier cave. You can also find caves underwater. Most underwater caves formed in the same way as caves on land, except the rock was under a lake or ocean. Some underwater caves were once dry caves that flooded when the sea level rose in an area.
pages.brief: Inside a massive ice cave beneath Alaska’s Mendenhall Glacier, a stream of warm water from melted ice flows down through cracks. As it runs toward the soil layer beneath, it melts the ice around it and forms the glacier cave. Underwater caves also exist beneath lakes and oceans.

pages.text: Hikers have natural light at the entrance to Milodon Cave, near Puerto Natales, Chile. Inside Caves Caves are made up of three main areas: the entrance, the twilight zone, and the dark zone. The entrance to a cave may be large or small. It can be a doorway into a mountain, a hole straight into the ground, or a crack in a boulder. The twilight zone is any part of the cave where some sunlight still seeps in. If you can see without a flashlight, you’re in the twilight zone. This zone is often cool and damp, and you can find animals and some plants living there. As you might guess from the name, there is no light at all in the dark zone. No plants grow there, but some fungi, molds, and animals have adapted to the total darkness.
pages.brief: Hikers stand in natural light at the entrance to Milodon Cave near Puerto Natales, Chile. Beyond the entrance, some sunlight seeps into a cool, damp twilight zone where animals and plants live. Deeper inside is the dark zone, with no light at all, where fungi, molds, and adapted animals live.

pages.text: Karst caves are the most common type of cave, so let’s take a closer look inside one. Water and dissolved limestone create all kinds of fantastic formations in these caves. stalactite Many people are familiar with stalactites and stalagmites. These form when water drips from a cave ceiling to the floor. The drops contain dissolved limestone. When the water dries or evaporates, it leaves behind bits of limestone. Bit by bit, the limestone builds up, creating stalactites on the ceiling and stalagmites on the floor. These formations only grow about 2 millimeters (about 0.08 in) a year. But they can reach over 10 meters (33 ft) long. Sometimes a stalactite and a stalagmite join to form a column. Helpful Hint Do you forget which is a stalactite and which is a stalagmite? The word stalactite contains the letter c. Think of it as standing for ceiling. Stalactites hang from the top of the cave. Stalagmite contains the letter g, which can stand for ground. Stalagmites point up from the ground of a cave. stalagmite.
pages.brief: Inside a karst cave, water drips from the ceiling to the floor. Drops containing dissolved limestone leave bits of limestone behind as they evaporate. Bit by bit, stalactites hang from the ceiling and stalagmites point up from the floor; where a stalactite and stalagmite join, they form a column.

pages.text: Another rare shape is called a cave pearl. These round formations may start as a grain of sand. The grain gets wet with water that contains dissolved limestone. When the water evaporates, the limestone is left behind. Over time, the limestone deposits build up and form thin layers—just like a pearl. cave pearls It takes a very long time to build a formation, drop by drop—over many thousands of years. When water drops run down the sides of a cave, they leave behind trails of limestone. These trails can build up to form a drapery, or curtain of rock. Draperies can grow more than 3 meters (10 ft) long, and may be so thin that they are transparent. A soda straw formation is thin and hollow, like a straw for drinking soda pop.
pages.brief: On a cave wall, water drops run down and leave trails of limestone that build into a drapery, a thin curtain of rock. A soda straw formation is thin and hollow. Nearby, a cave pearl forms as a grain of sand is repeatedly wetted with dissolved limestone, then dries, building thin layers.

pages.text: Cave Inhabitants Creatures small and large make their homes in caves. Many scientists divide cave animals into three groups: animals that spend their entire lives in caves, animals that spend part of their lives in caves but can be found elsewhere, and animals that only visit caves. Some types of animals spend their entire lives in caves, and aren’t found anywhere else. They include certain millipedes, centipedes, spiders, insects, crayfish, salamanders, and fish. These animals have adapted to survive in total darkness. Many of them are blind, and some have no eyes at all. Crayfish salamander Other kinds of animals live both in caves and outside. A good example of this are bats. Bats may spend every night in a cave but must go outside to find food. Other examples are some beetles, millipedes, centipedes, and salamanders.
pages.brief: In a cave, small creatures make their homes. A blind crayfish and a salamander live entirely in total darkness, adapted to life without light. A bat spends every night in the cave but must go outside to find food. Other beetles, millipedes, centipedes, and salamanders live both in caves and outside.

pages.text: Ancient cave-dwellers used this doorway in the Great Hall of Bulls, Lascaux, France. Many animals spend most of their time outside but visit caves for shelter, to rest, or to hunt for food. This group includes bears, foxes, pack rats, snakes, raccoons, moths, groundhogs, vultures, crickets, and of course, humans. Many humans have found the enclosed space of a cave to be a good place to live. In Andalucia, Spain, hundreds of people live in caves, while northern China has millions of human cave dwellers. Other places where people live in caves include Turkey, North Africa, and France. Artwork on cave walls and the remains of campfires show that humans have used caves as shelter for tens of thousands of years.
pages.brief: At Lascaux, France, an ancient cave-dwellers’ doorway opens into the Great Hall of Bulls. Nearby, animals such as bears, foxes, snakes, raccoons, and moths use caves for shelter, rest, or hunting. In Andalucia, Spain, and northern China, people live in caves; wall artwork and campfire remains show humans have used caves for shelter for tens of thousands of years.

pages.text: Do You Know? In 1940, four boys accidentally discovered one of the most famous art caves, France’s Lascaux Cave. They squeezed into a small hole, entering a large cavern with beautiful paintings of deer and bulls. Luckily, the boys were not hurt, but entering a cave without an experienced cave explorer or guide is a dangerous idea. Later, one of the boys became the cave’s main guide.
pages.brief: In 1940, four boys squeeze through a small hole and enter a large cavern at Lascaux Cave in France. Beautiful paintings of deer and bulls cover the cave walls. The boys are unhurt, though entering a cave without an experienced guide is dangerous. Later, one of the boys becomes the cave’s main guide.

pages.text: Caves are very fragile habitats. Many have almost no contact with the world outside. If something new comes into a cave, it can cause trouble for the animals that live there. Bats hibernate in caves. During hibernation, a bat’s body slows down, allowing it to go months without eating. Recently, frightening numbers of hibernating bats have been getting sick and dying. Do You Know? Caves are too deep to be affected by seasons. Cave temperatures tend to be between 24 degrees C (75° F) and 1 degrees C (30° F). Animals that live in caves adapt to this unchanging environment.
pages.brief: A fragile cave habitat lies almost completely separate from the world outside. Inside, bats hibernate, their bodies slowing so they can go months without eating. Recently, frightening numbers of hibernating bats have been getting sick and dying. Cave temperatures stay between 24°C and 1°C, unaffected by seasons, and cave animals adapt to this unchanging environment.

pages.text: Bats with White Nose Syndrome Cave visitors first spotted the problem in 2006 outside Albany, New York. Bats there had a strange white fuzz around their mouths and noses. Instead of hibernating, they woke up and flew out of the cave. Waking up during winter is dangerous. Without food, the bats starve or freeze. Scientists call this condition White Nose Syndrome. Since 2006, it has spread across the entire eastern United States. White Nose Syndrome can kill over 90 percent of the hibernating bats in a cave in a single winter. Scientists have identified a fungus that causes White Nose Syndrome, but they don’t know how to cure it. Some scientists fear that even common types of bats may soon go extinct. They urge cave explorers to stay away from caves with bats in order to keep the fungus from spreading.
pages.brief: In 2006 outside Albany, New York, visitors spotted bats with strange white fuzz around their mouths and noses. Instead of hibernating, the bats woke and flew out, risking starvation or freezing. Scientists call this White Nose Syndrome. It has spread across the eastern United States and can kill over 90 percent of hibernating bats in a cave in one winter.

pages.text: Geologist studying the largest known crystals in the world Famous Caves Caves throughout the world are famous for their outstanding features. The Cave of Crystals in Mexico contains rooms full of gigantic sparkling crystals—the largest ever found. Some are 10 meters (33 ft) long! Mammoth Cave in Kentucky contains more than 480 kilometers (300 mi) of passageways, making it the largest known cave system in the world. The deepest cave found is Krubera Cave in the Eastern European nation of Georgia. It is over 2,000 meters (7,000 ft) deep, and spelunkers aren’t done exploring! One of the most world-famous caves is the Chauvet (shaw-VAY) Cave in France. Discovered in 1994, it contains over 300 of the world’s oldest paintings. Dated as approximately 30,000 years old, the paintings include horses, lions, and bears.
pages.brief: A geologist studies the largest known crystals in Mexico’s Cave of Crystals, where rooms hold gigantic sparkling crystals up to 10 meters long. Mammoth Cave in Kentucky has more than 480 kilometers of passageways, the largest known cave system. Krubera Cave in Georgia is over 2,000 meters deep. France’s Chauvet Cave contains over 300 paintings of horses, lions, and bears.

pages.text: Safety equipment, lights, and proper climbing gear are a must on any cave exploration. Exploring Caves Why do spelunkers go into caves? Some do it for the thrill of physically challenging themselves by climbing down ropes, crawling through tiny tunnels, or scuba diving in underground caverns. Scientists enter caves to learn more about Earth. Experienced cave explorers equip themselves with helmets, flashlights, warm clothing, rope, and kneepads. As the spelunkers go deeper, they may have to wriggle through tiny tunnels. They may wade through underground pools or rivers. In the cave, they hear water drip-drip-dripping, but no other sound. The only light is the glow of their flashlights.
pages.brief: Equipped with helmets, flashlights, warm clothing, rope, and kneepads, experienced cave explorers move deeper into a cave. They may climb down ropes, crawl through tiny tunnels, wade through underground pools or rivers, or scuba dive in underground caverns. They hear water drip-drip-dripping, with no other sound, and the only light is the glow of their flashlights.

pages.text: Lacey sprays of gypsum crystals are found only in the Lechuguilla Cave in Carlsbad Caverns Park, New Mexico. A cave is exciting, but it can definitely be dangerous. It is easy to get lost in the twisting, pitch-black tunnels or trapped in a narrow space. Cave floors can be steep and rocky, or slick with mud. It takes the skills of a hardy rock climber to explore many caves. Cave formations can be extremely delicate. Thoughtless cave visitors have broken off stalactite tips as souvenirs, destroying in a second something that may have taken 40,000 years to form. If you ever plan to visit a cave, take a guided tour. The guide can explain the many wonders of the cave and keep both you and the formations safe.
pages.brief: Inside Lechuguilla Cave in Carlsbad Caverns Park, New Mexico, lacey sprays of gypsum crystals cover it. The twisting, pitch-black tunnels can be dangerous, with steep, rocky, or muddy floors and narrow spaces. Cave formations are extremely delicate; thoughtless visitors have broken off stalactite tips as souvenirs. A guided tour helps explain the cave’s wonders and keep visitors and formations safe.

pages.text: An explorer admires the flowstone formations inside Carlsbad Caverns Park’s lower cave in New Mexico. Conclusion The world of caves is fascinating. Where else on Earth can you find unexplored land, discover otherworldly formations, and see artwork from thousands of years ago? As long as we treat them respectfully, we can continue to experience the wonder of caves indefinitely.
pages.brief: An explorer admires flowstone formations inside the lower cave of Carlsbad Caverns Park in New Mexico. The world of caves offers unexplored land, otherworldly formations, and artwork from thousands of years ago. As long as people treat caves respectfully, they can continue to experience the wonder of caves indefinitely.

pages.brief: A cave chamber shows a column where a stalactite and stalagmite meet, thin drapery hanging from the wall or ceiling, and narrow passageways. Nearby, a primary cave and a lava tube suggest other cave forms, while spelunkers explore carefully. The scene shows erosion and formations, with collapsed rock visible in the cave.

books.title: Route 66
books.art_why: The book covers 1920s–1990s history, so drawn scenes suit past events and changing roadside landmarks.

pages.text: Route 66 takes drivers across the entire American West. Introduction The year is 1957 and you’ve just taken the top down on your cherry-red convertible. Rock ’n’ roll music blasts from the speakers. Ahead of you lies nothing but open road. Could this drive get any better? You think not—until you pass a three-story- tall ice cream cone covered in sprinkles. Your mouth waters. Should you stop? Wait—there’s a cheeseburger the size of a bus. Time for a quick lunch instead! When it’s time to rest for the night, you park next to your teepee-shaped hotel room. What a spectacular day it was on the road! Who knows what tomorrow will bring? This was no imaginary road trip. You’ve just taken a real road trip down America’s favorite highway, Route 66.
pages.brief: In 1957, a driver in a cherry-red convertible with the top down cruises an open western highway, rock ’n’ roll blasting from the speakers. Ahead stands a three-story ice cream cone covered in sprinkles, then a bus-sized cheeseburger. For the night, the car parks beside a teepee-shaped hotel room.

pages.text: America’s Main Street Have you ever seen a road map of the United States? It looks a lot like an enormous spiderweb. Huge highways zigzag from coast to coast, connecting nearly every city in between. Getting around is easy: just jump in a car and hit the road! A hundred years ago, driving across the country wasn’t quite so easy. Most “roads” were just small dirt trails. Cars often broke down, got stuck in mud, or popped tires on jagged rocks. In the 1920s, the United States government created a new system of numbered highways to make driving cross-country easier. The first highway to be fully paved stretched 2,400 miles (3,862 km) from Chicago, Illinois, to Los Angeles, California. Its name was Route 66, but many fondly called it the “Main Street of America.”
pages.brief: A spiderweb of highways zigzags across the United States, with a car driving between cities. Beside it, an old dirt trail shows a stuck car with a popped tire among jagged rocks. A long paved road stretches from Chicago to Los Angeles.

pages.text: America’s Main Street was soon put to the test. In 1929, hard times hit the United States. Many banks failed, causing people to lose their savings. A great number of people lost their jobs and homes as well. The period that followed was known as the Great Depression. Meanwhile, a series of droughts—long periods without rain—destroyed many farms. The hardest-hit areas were in Kansas, Colorado, Oklahoma, Texas, and New Mexico. This historic time period was known as the Dust Bowl era. Suddenly, many people were forced to leave their homes to seek a better life elsewhere. Many believed paradise could be found in California. Thousands packed up their belongings and made the long journey west. How did they get there? On a new road named Route 66. The Dust Bowl in Literature The Grapes of Wrath, by John Steinbeck, is a classic novel published in 1939. It is about a family fleeing Oklahoma during the Dust Bowl era and making the long journey down Route 66 to seek work in California. Steinbeck described Route 66 as “the mother road” and “the road of flight.”
pages.brief: A farm family loads belongings onto a car beneath dusty skies, while dry fields stretch behind them. Other families travel west along a long road toward California. Empty buildings suggest lost jobs and savings during hard times.

pages.text: In the 1930s, 1.2 million people moved to California. More than half a million of them went because of difficult conditions during the Dust Bowl era. On December 8, 1941, the United States entered World War II. Soldiers, workers, and supplies needed to be quickly transported from around the country to military bases in the West. How did they get there? On Route 66, of course! Restaurants, gas stations, and hotels began to spring up along the route to serve these wartime workers. When the war ended in 1945, Americans celebrated. Soldiers came home, started families, and purchased cars. Many wanted to drive their new cars west to see sights like the Grand Canyon—by way of Route 66!
pages.brief: Soldiers, workers, and supplies move west along Route 66 toward military bases. Restaurants, gas stations, and hotels spring up to serve them. After the war, families in new cars drive west to see the Grand Canyon.

pages.text: Route 66 in Popular Culture The years after World War II were great days for Route 66. Shiny new cars and yellow Checker cabs cruised up and down the route. In 1946, a song called “Route 66” became a top hit. Its most famous line urged listeners to “get your kicks on Route Sixty-Six.” This song helped make the highway famous. In 1960, a new TV show called Route 66 followed two friends who drove across the country in a Corvette. They weren’t going anywhere in particular; instead, they were looking for adventures on the road. The original version of the song “Route 66” was performed by the Nat King Cole Trio in 1946. By 1970, most of the original Route 66 was bypassed by a new highway. However, Route 66 remained part of American popular culture through the end of the century. The popular television show Route 66 aired from 1960 to 1964.
pages.brief: Shiny new cars and yellow Checker cabs cruise the highway. A singing trio performs in a studio, while a television screen shows two friends in a Corvette driving cross-country. A newer multi-lane highway runs beside the older road.

pages.text: Fast forward to the year 2000: John Lasseter, the director of Pixar Animation Studios, was driving along Route 66 with his family. He fell in love with the imaginative buildings and colorful art he saw. He decided to turn his experiences into a Disney-Pixar movie called Cars, which was released in 2006. Lasseter sent a team down Route 66 to do research for the movie. Some of the roadside art they found inspired characters in Cars, and they also used Route 66 landmarks in the movie. For example, the Wigwam Motel in Holbrook, Arizona, became the Cozy Cone Motel. Cars was so successful that many families who saw it decided to take their own vacations along Route 66. This made the route popular again. This rusty tow truck (top) in Galena, Kansas, became the inspiration for the Cars movie character Tow Mater (bottom).
pages.brief: A family drives along Route 66 past colorful roadside buildings; a man looks out, inspired. A research team sketches a wigwam motel and a rusty tow truck. Later, families visit the route, and a movie scene shows a tow truck character.

Route 66 is also full of unique art, historic gas stations, and theaters. In addition, travelers can see live shows. For instance, you can see a Native American dance ceremony in New Mexico or a rodeo in Oklahoma. One thing’s for sure—you won’t be bored on Route 66!
pages.brief: Route 66 stretches across the country, lined with museums, motels, shops, historic gas stations, theaters, and quirky roadside art. In New Mexico, dancers perform a Native American ceremony; in Oklahoma, riders compete in a rodeo.

pages.text: Cadillac Ranch sits in a pasture where cows graze. Cadillac Ranch In 1974, some artists buried ten Cadillacs nose down in a field, rear bumpers sticking straight up toward the sky. Now the cars are every color of the rainbow because visitors have covered them with spray paint. At the nearby VW Slug Bug Ranch in Conway, Texas, five colorful Volkswagen Beetles stick out of the ground.
pages.brief: In 1974, artists buried ten Cadillacs nose-down in a pasture where cows graze; their rear bumpers point skyward, covered in rainbow spray paint. Nearby in Conway, Texas, five colorful Volkswagen Beetles stick out of the ground.

pages.text: Growing up, Elmer Long collected bottles and other items people had thrown away. Elmer’s Bottle Tree Ranch Folk artist Elmer Long built Bottle Tree Ranch out of recycled bottles, car parts, and other objects—including buffalo jawbones. When the desert wind blows through the open bottles, the air fills with music. Blue Whale What do you give the woman who has everything? Hugh Davis built his wife an 80- foot (24.4 m) blue whale for their anniversary. For many years, kids loved to slide and dive from the Blue Whale’s body into the swimming hole below. The Blue Whale of Catoosa, Oklahoma, has a boardwalk along its spine.
pages.brief: Elmer Long stands among bottle trees made from recycled bottles, car parts, and buffalo jawbones; desert wind blows through the open bottles. Nearby, an 80-foot blue whale with a boardwalk along its spine rises beside a swimming hole where children slide and dive.

pages.text: Paul Bunyon, Atlanta, IL Chicken Boy, Los Angeles, CA Gemini Giant, Wilmington, IL A Land of Giants Route 66 is truly a land of giants. A California factory built thousands of huge fiberglass statues. Businesses along Route 66 used them for advertising. The factory added costumes to turn them into cowboys, Native Americans, astronauts, and even chickens. Many of the biggest statues on Route 66 are food statues. Enormous oranges, donuts, cheeseburgers, and ice cream cones make for a mouthwatering ride. Look out the window near Collinsville, Illinois, and you may see the largest catsup bottle in the world! Brooks Catsup Bottle Water Tower, Collinsville, IL.
pages.brief: A California factory made thousands of huge fiberglass statues for roadside advertising: a cowboy, a Native American, an astronaut, a chicken, and enormous oranges, donuts, cheeseburgers, and ice cream cones. Near Collinsville, Illinois, the world’s largest catsup bottle towers over the highway.

pages.text: Dinny cost $300,000 to build and was made from roadside materials. Dinosaurs by the Dozen On Route 66, you can be greeted by prehistoric creatures of all shapes and sizes. Dinny is likely the largest concrete dinosaur in America. He is 150 feet (45.7 m) long and lives at a dinosaur park in Cabazon, California. Claude Bell built the park to attract visitors to his nearby restaurant, the Wheel Inn. The dinosaur park became famous. It was even featured in the 1985 movie Pee-wee’s Big Adventure. Mr. Rex, a three-story Tyrannosaurus rex, is a popular feature at Cabazon Dinosaurs.
pages.brief: Prehistoric creatures of all shapes and sizes greet travelers. Dinny, a 150-foot-long concrete dinosaur, stands at a California dinosaur park built by Claude Bell to draw visitors to his restaurant. Nearby, Mr. Rex, a three-story Tyrannosaurus rex, towers over the desert.

pages.text: Saving Route 66 With Route 66’s popularity came traffic— lots of it. Heavy traffic caused the highway to deteriorate. From 1956 through the 1980s, new interstates—high-speed highways with many lanes—were built around Route 66. As more travelers took interstates, businesses on Route 66 suffered, and many closed. Peeling paint, faded signs, and boarded-up windows became common sights. In 1999, the United States Congress passed a law to protect Route 66. The government offered money to help businesses and towns pay the cost of preserving important landmarks. Now Route 66 is growing popular again as many return to seek its amusing artwork and creative spirit. The best way to catch the spirit of Route 66 is to drive it. You’re sure to have an unforgettable American experience of your own! Route 66 Red Rocker, Fanning, MO.
pages.brief: Heavy traffic wears down the old highway. New multi-lane interstates draw travelers away, leaving closed businesses with peeling paint and boarded-up windows. In 1999, Congress passes a law to protect Route 66, and towns work to preserve landmarks. Drivers return to enjoy its artwork and creative spirit.

books.title: The Plague!
books.art_why: The Black Death of 1347-1351 happened long before photography and the book is about an event, not a named famous person.

pages.text: The Plague Ships The scene and smell must have been terrible. In October 1347, a dozen trading ships sailed into the port of Messina, Sicily—part of Italy today. The vessels had made the long trip across the Black Sea. The arrival of the ships likely caused excitement around the docks. Such ships often carried news and goods from faraway lands. Those who met them, though, got the shock of their lives and perhaps also the cause of their deaths. Most of the crew on the ships were already dead. The sailors working the ropes and sails were dying. Their skin oozed with open sores. People in Europe had heard rumors of a terrible disease in Asia. These ships and sailors now had brought the disease—the plague—to Europe. Later, it would be called the Black Death. It was the worst outbreak of disease Europe has ever experienced.
pages.brief: A dozen trading ships dock at the port of Messina, Sicily, in October 1347. Crowds gather excitedly along the docks. On deck, most of the crew lie dead, and the surviving sailors, their skin oozing open sores, struggle with the ropes and sails.

pages.text: The Fleas of Disease In the 1300s, no one had yet made the connection between germs and illness. The idea that bacteria or viruses could cause a cold, the flu, or other sickness was unknown. Many people at that time saw disease as a supernatural event. Some people blamed the plague on how the planets lined up. One doctor described how it could spread if a healthy person looked into an infected person’s eyes.
pages.brief: People in the 1300s watch the night sky, certain the line-up of the planets brings disease. A doctor leans close to stare into a sick patient's eyes, believing illness can pass that way. Around them, townspeople go about their day knowing nothing of germs.

pages.text: People also hadn’t made the connection between the plague and the fleas that were actually spreading the disease. These fleas most certainly had stowed away on the ships that docked at Messina. It was not until 1894— almost 550 years later—that scientists found the type of bacteria that caused the plague. These bacteria get into the gut of a type of flea that normally feeds on the blood of rats. The bacteria killed off the rats they normally lived with. The fleas were then forced to go looking for other animals to feed on, including people. How Rats and Fleas Helped Spread the Plague 3 The plague bacteria multiply in a flea’s gut.
pages.brief: A flea, magnified huge, clings to a rat's fur while plague bacteria multiply inside its gut. The rat lies dead, and the flea jumps to another animal, then to a person. In 1894, scientists finally identify the bacteria.

pages.text: Filthy people and cities did not help. In the 1300s, human waste and garbage were often dumped in the streets of overcrowded cities. Bugs were regular houseguests. Getting bitten by fleas and other pests was a fact of life. Not all investigators are convinced that fleas were the only source of the Black Death. Other diseases could also cause deadly outbreaks. However, the bacterium in the fleas remains the leading suspect, based on the kinds of illness that people reported. What seems clear is that humans began passing this deadly disease to one another. A person’s pus, blood, or spit could infect others. In other words, a simple cough could give the sickness to the next victim. At that point, the plague became all but unstoppable.
pages.brief: A crowded medieval city street where human waste and garbage are dumped in the road and bugs crawl everywhere. Fleas bite people as they walk. One person coughs near another, spreading pus, blood or spit, and the sickness moves on.

pages.text: Death Stalks Europe By 1348 the Black Death was spreading across Europe. Travelers and traders carried it to new areas. It often took weeks before an infected area knew something was horribly wrong. By then, it was too late to do anything about it. At the time, there was no treatment for such a serious disease. As the illness showed itself, victims experienced fever, vomiting, swelling, and strong pain. They might die quickly or live a few days. Historians think only one in five people who got the symptoms survived.
pages.brief: Along European roads in 1348, travelers and traders carry the plague into new towns. Inside a house, a victim suffers fever, vomiting, swelling and strong pain. Weeks pass before anyone understands something is horribly wrong, and no treatment exists.

pages.text: Bubonic Plague Symptoms The word bubonic comes from buboes. They are painful swellings of the lymph nodes in the neck, armpits, and groin. In plague victims, buboes can blow up to the size of a chicken egg. They can even burst through the skin. Other forms of plague could attack the lungs, causing a bloody cough, or the blood, causing areas on the face, hands, and feet to turn black. Bubonic plague bacteria start by attacking the lymph nodes in the neck, groin, and underarms. Lymph nodes are important organs of the immune system. They help the body fight disease. With plague, lymph nodes swell and blacken with poisoned blood and pus. They become boils called buboes. Plague can also infect the lungs, causing them to bleed. The disease soon reached France and England, spreading in every direction. By 1351, there was hardly a spot in Europe it had not reached. General: fever and lack of energy Head: headache Lymph nodes: swelling (buboes), oozing of pus, and bleeding Stomach: nausea and vomiting Joints: aches and pains.
pages.brief: A plague victim's body shows buboes, painful swellings the size of a chicken egg in the neck, armpit and groin, some bursting through the skin. Other victims cough blood from infected lungs, or their faces, hands and feet turn black.

pages.text: Panic and a Prayer Once people realized that plague had come to their community, many panicked. Frightened families abandoned sick loved ones. Doctors and priests fled the places and people they served. City folk left for the countryside, thinking it would be safer there. By fleeing, though, they often helped spread the disease. Few people had good ideas about how to stop the disease. Desperate people tried useless cures. Many burned incense or wore flowers to cleanse the air. If nothing else, the smoke and flowers may have covered up the awful smells around them.
pages.brief: A frightened family abandons a sick loved one and flees. A doctor and a priest hurry away from the people they served. City folk stream out toward the countryside. Others burn incense and hold flowers to their noses, trying to cleanse the awful air.

pages.text: Many people turned to their faith in hope of rescue. Bands of Christians walked from town to town, hitting their own backs with spiked whips. They prayed that they would be forgiven for their sins and spared. In some areas, Christian groups wrongly blamed Jews for causing the plague. Many Jewish communities were attacked and their people driven off or killed. A few cities instead used common sense to try to control the disease. Port cities soon realized that visiting ships were one of its sources. They began to block ships that came from plague-infected areas. A forty-day waiting period was used to confirm that the ship’s crew were plague-free. Only then could they come ashore. Officials in some areas also figured out that stopping the movement of people slowed the spread of disease. Infected families couldn’t leave their houses. Officials set limits on travel and trade to and from their cities. Work crews buried victims as soon as possible for fear that their bodies could infect others. In some areas, though, public order had broken down. This made it difficult to force people to follow such rules.
pages.brief: Bands of Christians walk from town to town, striking their own backs with spiked whips and praying for forgiveness. Elsewhere a Jewish community is attacked and its people driven off. At a port, officials block a ship, making its crew wait forty days offshore.

pages.text: The Aftermath Imagine half the people of your city gone. The shops are empty of food and other goods. That was the experience of many people who survived the worst period of the Black Death. Historians can only guess at the death count.
