There were about eighty million Europeans before the Black Death struck. Experts think that 40 to 60 percent of those people died, though the death rate varied greatly by location. Cities were usually the hardest hit. The disease spread easily in crowded, dirty neighborhoods. Nearly 60 percent of Londoners died, along with half the people of Paris. After 1351, the plague slowed for reasons researchers are still trying to understand. Survivors may have built up resistance to the disease. The bacteria may also have changed to a less deadly form. Plague outbreaks happened again and again for the next five hundred years. None, though, ever matched the deadliness of the Black Death. After the plague, Europe was left a very different place. There was a huge shortage of workers. The lack of skilled craftspeople and laborers caused big problems. Workers were able to demand better pay and treatment.
pages.brief: Empty shops with bare shelves stand in a half-deserted city. Survivors walk streets where most people are gone. Crowded, dirty neighborhoods suffered worst, and around half the people of London and Paris died. Remaining workers demand better pay and treatment.

pages.text: Fields were left unplanted or unharvested without peasants to work them. Farm animals died from a lack of care. Because of this, Europeans suffered food shortages and starvation. Survivors’ views about society and the meaning of life changed, too. Many began to question their belief in the church. Some challenged their rulers. The authority of these powerful individuals had proven useless in protecting the people they controlled. There were many examples of progress afterward. Farmers tried new practices to grow more food with fewer hands. Public health and medicine also saw changes for the better. More communities understood the importance of sanitation and cleanliness. They also put in place better ways to handle disease outbreaks.
pages.brief: Fields stand unplanted and unharvested with no peasants to work them, and farm animals lie dead from lack of care. Hungry survivors question their church and their rulers. Afterwards, farmers try new practices, and communities set up better sanitation and ways to handle outbreaks.

pages.text: Rebirth Modern medicine has made another outbreak of the Black Death all but impossible. Modern medicines can quickly cure most cases of plague. Better public sanitation and health programs also help control the spread of most forms of disease. Antibiotics: The Miracle Drug Antibiotics are a recent development in human history. Before the mid-1800s, some healers recognized that certain plant molds and other fungi attacked bacteria. In the 1800s, more research led to a better understanding of the link between microbes and disease. Then in the 1920s, Scottish biologist Alexander Fleming accidentally discovered a plant mold that destroyed a dangerous form of bacteria. Out of his research came the wonder drug penicillin, which is capable of killing many forms of bacterial infection. Fleming was awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1945 for his breakthrough work.
pages.brief: Modern medicine quickly cures most plague cases. In a laboratory, Scottish biologist Alexander Fleming studies a plant mold that destroys dangerous bacteria, leading to the wonder drug penicillin. He is awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1945 for the breakthrough.

pages.text: In the mid-1300s, the mystery and horror of the Black Death terrified Europe. Many people who lived through the Black Death believed it was the end of the world. In terms of death rates, it remains the most destructive event in European history. At the same time, some historians link the disaster to helpful changes that followed. From the late 1300s until the 1600s, Europe underwent big changes. This period, known as the Renaissance, was a time of great improvements in medicine, science, and art. Renaissance means “rebirth” in French. After the Black Death, a period of rebirth was exactly what Europe needed. The Peasants Rise England went through a period of economic shock in the aftermath of the Black Plague. Farmers and laborers were in such great demand that they saw their wages rise up to 40 percent from the 1340s to the 1380s. This big social shift so alarmed the upper classes and nobility that royal officials passed a law attempting to fix wages for peasants at the levels they had been before the Black Death. They passed another law to prevent peasants from leaving their home villages in search of better jobs. These crackdowns led to a major uprising known as the Peasants’ Revolt in 1381. King Richard II faces the peasant army in 1381.
pages.brief: Renaissance Europe: painters, scientists and doctors at work in a time of great improvement in medicine, science and art. King Richard II faces an army of peasants in 1381, after farm wages rose and new laws tried to hold them down.

books.title: Water Cities
books.art_why: Modern water cities exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Water Cities.
pages.brief: Venice, Italy, spreads across more than a hundred islands, with the Grand Canal as its main waterway. Bridges connect the islands, and boats move along the canals. The scene shows a famous water city built on and near water, one of many such places around the world.

pages.text: The Grand Canal is the main waterway of Venice. Living Near Water Each year, millions of people from around the world travel to Venice, Italy. This famous city of canals and bridges was built on more than a hundred islands. Venice is the world’s best-known water city, but it is certainly not the only one. Water cities are places that are built on or near a body of water. Some water cities are tiny, while others are huge. They are found near—or in— water on every continent except Antarctica. They exist for many different reasons, and each one has an interesting story to tell.
pages.brief: Venice, Italy, spreads across more than a hundred islands, with the Grand Canal as its main waterway. Bridges connect the islands, and boats move along the canals. Visitors arrive from around the world to see this famous water city built on and near water.

pages.text: Europe Amsterdam, Netherlands Amsterdam is another European city that is famous for its canals. It is the capital and largest city in the Netherlands. About one-third of the Netherlands is below sea level, and one-sixth is built on reclaimed land—land that was once underwater. The city of Amsterdam is about 2 meters (6.6 ft.) below sea level. The water was pumped out so people could build there. Pumping stations keep the land dry. Amsterdam was surrounded by a moat in the 1500s. More people moved there in the 1600s as the city grew. Workers drained swamps and built three new canals around the downtown area. EUROPE Amsterdam Amsterdam has more than 1,200 bridges over its canals.
pages.brief: Amsterdam, Netherlands, stands about two meters below sea level, with canals and more than 1,200 bridges. Pumping stations keep the land dry. In the 1600s, workers drained swamps and built three new canals around downtown as the city grew.

pages.text: Since that time, 161 other canals have been built. Amsterdam’s canals total over 100 kilometers (62 mi.) in length. They divide the city into almost 100 small islands joined by over 1,200 bridges. The canals were the city’s main transportation routes for centuries. Now they are mainly used by smaller boats. However, they are still an important part of Amsterdam’s character. Reine, Norway A tiny fishing village more than 100 kilometers (62 mi.) above the Arctic Circle has earned the nickname “The Most Beautiful Place in the World.” Reine, Norway, is located along the coast of one of the Lofoten Islands. The village offers fishing, kayaking, skiing, whale watching, hiking, and beautiful beaches. It’s also a perfect place for amazing views of the northern lights.
pages.brief: In Amsterdam, more than a hundred kilometers of canals divide the city into almost a hundred islands joined by over 1,200 bridges. Small boats travel the waterways. Far north above the Arctic Circle, Reine, Norway, sits on a Lofoten Island coast, with fishing, kayaking, skiing, whale watching, hiking, beaches, and northern lights.

pages.text: Singapore is one of the world’s busiest port cities. Singapore Singapore is the world’s only island city-state— an island that is both a city and an independent country. It is made up of about sixty-three islands. Singapore depends on goods from other places since it has few natural resources of its own. Singapore is much larger than it was before the 1960s. Like Amsterdam, it has grown by reclaiming land that was once underwater. However, instead of pumping out the water, Singapore has added land by dumping rocks and sand into the sea. A project begun in 2016 will use Amsterdam’s methods to increase its land area. ASIA Singapore Asia.
pages.brief: Singapore is a busy island city-state made up of about sixty-three islands, with ships bringing goods from other places. On the coast, rocks and sand are dumped into the sea to add new land. A project begun in 2016 plans to use Amsterdam’s methods to increase the land area.

pages.text: Dubai, United Arab Emirates Dubai is a modern city in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). One of its largest building projects is Palm Islands—three human-made islands shaped like palm trees. The islands are being built along the coast by piling up huge amounts of sand and rock. They are adding hundreds of miles of coastline to the city as well as thousands of homes. Construction began in 2001. The first island was finished in late 2016. Palm Jumeirah is one of the largest human-made islands in the world. A curved seawall protects the island from strong waves and storms. ASIA Dubai INDIAN OCEAN.
pages.brief: Dubai, United Arab Emirates, is a modern city where sand and rock are piled along the coast to build Palm Islands, three human-made islands shaped like palm trees. Palm Jumeirah, begun in 2001 and finished in 2016, adds homes and coastline, protected by a curved seawall from waves and storms.

pages.text: The village of Ganvié is sometimes called the Venice of Africa. Ganvié, Benin Ganvié (GAWN-vye) is the largest stilt village in Africa. The village is located in the middle of Lake Nokoué (NOHK-we) in the country of Benin. Ganvié has about twenty thousand people and three thousand buildings. Only the school and a cemetery are located on land. This water village began at least three hundred years ago. During that time, a powerful tribe called the Fon captured and sold members of other tribes into slavery. The Fons’ religion did not let them pursue people who lived on water. Another tribe, the Tofinu, escaped to Lake Nokoué to avoid capture. They built the stilt village and set up a way of life that continues to this day. The name of their village means “we survived.” Ganvié AFRICA Africa.
pages.brief: Ganvié, Benin, is the largest stilt village in Africa, with about twenty thousand people and three thousand buildings in Lake Nokoué. Most buildings stand over the water, while the school and cemetery sit on land. Long ago, the Tofinu escaped capture by moving onto the lake and building this water village.

pages.text: Most villagers make their living by fishing. They keep and breed fish using underwater fences. They also keep chickens and goats on patches of grass that grow in the water. People travel in long, narrow canoes. Fadiouth (Shell Island), Senegal The people of Fadiouth (fad-YOOT), Senegal, live on an island made of clamshells. For over three hundred years, they have been eating clams and recycling the shells. The shells are held in place by the roots of trees and reeds. The island’s buildings and streets are also made of shells.
pages.brief: In Ganvié, villagers fish and breed fish behind underwater fences. Chickens and goats stay on patches of grass in the water, and people travel in long, narrow canoes. At Fadiouth, Senegal, an island made of clamshells has shell streets and buildings, with shells held by tree and reed roots after three hundred years of recycling.

pages.text: The Uru people make reed canoes for transportation. South America Uros Floating Village, Peru Like the Tofinu, the people of Uros Floating Village moved to water for safety. The Uru people escaped to Lake Titicaca over five hundred years ago when other people took over their land. About two thousand Uru now live on about seventy floating islands made of reeds. The islands, which are 1.2 to 2.4 meters (4–8 ft.) thick, break down from the bottom. New reeds must be added on top all the time. The Uru people also use the reeds to make canoes, homes, and furniture. Uros SOUTH AMERICA.
pages.brief: On Lake Titicaca in Peru, about two thousand Uru people live on about seventy floating islands made of reeds. The thick reed islands break down from the bottom, so new reeds are added on top. The Uru use reeds for canoes, homes, and furniture, traveling by reed canoe as their ancestors did for safety.

pages.text: NORTH AMERICA Mexcaltitán Mexcaltitán sits on a long sandbar off the coast of Mexico. North America Mexcaltitán, Mexico The Aztec people ruled large parts of Mesoamerica between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries. A story says that they came from an island near the Pacific coast of Mexico. The story also says that their gods told them to find a new place to live. After looking for two hundred years, they founded a city that is now known as Mexico City.
pages.brief: Mexcaltitán sits on a long sandbar off Mexico’s coast. The Aztec people ruled large parts of Mesoamerica between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries. A story says their gods told them to find a new place to live, and after searching two hundred years, they founded the city now known as Mexico City.

pages.text: Some historians think that Mexcaltitán (mes-kahl-tee-TAHN) is where the Aztec people came from. This small human-made island is in the same place as the Aztec island shown on a 1579 map. Also, the early people used small canoes almost exactly like the ones used there today. Mexcaltitán is home to about eight hundred people. This water town is sometimes called the Mexican Venice. In summer, during the rainy season, boats are the only way to travel through the streets. Children play “water soccer” on the island’s underwater soccer field. Locals boat and swim in the streets during the flood season in Mexcaltitán.
pages.brief: Historians think Mexcaltitán may be the Aztec homeland. About eight hundred people live on this small human-made island. In summer, rainy-season floods make boats the only way through the streets. Children play water soccer on an underwater field, and locals boat and swim in the flooded streets.

pages.text: Auckland is New Zealand’s largest city. Oceania Auckland, New Zealand This city of 1.5 million people is on the North Island of New Zealand in the South Pacific Ocean. It is located between two large harbors on an isthmus less than 2 kilometers (1.24 mi.) wide at its narrowest point. Auckland’s nickname is the “City of Sails.” About one-sixth of its residents own a boat. The city has thousands of beaches. Water-related activities include swimming, surfing, fishing, diving, kayaking, and beach horseback riding.
pages.brief: Auckland, New Zealand, is the country’s largest city, with 1.5 million people on the North Island. It lies between two large harbors on a narrow isthmus in the South Pacific Ocean. Residents sail boats, swim, surf, fish, dive, kayak, and ride horses on beaches; about one-sixth own a boat.

pages.text: California Italy Aircraft carrier People and Water Many kinds of water cities exist besides the ones you’ve just read about. For instance, Italy has a tiny fishing town with brightly colored homes built on steep cliffs. Northern California has a floating community made up of houseboats. People in the military may spend months living on aircraft carriers. Water means different things to different people. For residents of water cities, it may mean fun, work, safety, a connection with nature, or a way of life. The world’s water cities are proof that people can make a home for themselves just about anywhere.
pages.brief: Other water cities include an Italian fishing town with brightly colored homes on steep cliffs, a Northern California floating community of houseboats, and aircraft carriers where military people live for months. For people in water cities, water can mean fun, work, safety, nature, or a way of life.

books.title: Slithery Snakes
books.art_why: Snakes are real animals that exist today.

pages.text: Introduction Snakes are unusual animals. They are reptiles, a class of creatures that also includes lizards and turtles. Long and limbless, snakes come in many lengths, patterns, and colors. To date, scientists have identified several thousand species of snakes. They live in oceans, in trees, and on land, and they have adapted to survive in many unusual ways.
pages.brief: A long, limbless snake slithers across land while another rests in a tree, and a lizard and turtle appear nearby to show reptile variety. Snakes of different lengths, patterns, and colors are shown in ocean, tree, and ground settings.

pages.text: Where Snakes Live Snakes are found on every continent except Antarctica. Some places, however, are snake-free zones. For instance, no snakes live in the wild on certain islands, such as Ireland, New Zealand, and Iceland. Depending on the species, snakes in the wild may live up to twenty-five years. Biggest and Smallest One of the largest snakes is the green anaconda. A full-grown green anaconda can be close to 10 meters (33 ft.) long and weigh more than 230 kilograms (507 lb.). By contrast, one of the smallest snakes is the thread snake. It is only about 10 centimeters (4 in.) long.
pages.brief: A huge green anaconda lies coiled in a wetland, its long, heavy body filling the scene, while a tiny thread snake rests on a leaf nearby. The background shows varied land and island settings where snakes do and do not live.

pages.text: Snake Traits Like all reptiles, snakes are cold-blooded, meaning their body temperature changes as the temperature around them changes. If a snake needs to warm up, it basks in the sun. If the snake needs to cool down, it rests in the shade. Snakes become much less active in winter. Some snakes that live through cold winters do not hibernate; instead, they find a place underground or beneath a rock pile or log to stay warm. Another way snakes remain warm in winter is by gathering in a group and looping around each other to share body heat.
pages.brief: A snake basks on a sunlit rock, then rests in cool shade beneath leaves. In a cold winter scene, several snakes loop around each other in a group, sharing body heat, while another disappears underground beneath a rock pile and log.

pages.text: A snake’s skeleton is made up of a long backbone, ribs, a skull, and a jawbone. Its hard, bony skull protects its brain. Snakes can have from about 150 to more than 400 vertebrae. Their many vertebrae allow them to move in a multitude of ways. A very limber snake usually has more vertebrae. Like all reptiles, a snake has scales on its body. In addition to providing protection, scales are nearly waterproof, helping keep the snake dry. Scales grow from the snake’s skin. Some scales are colorful. Other snakes have scales for camouflage, which helps them blend in with their surroundings. Since snakes have no arms or legs, they use their muscles and scales to move. The scales on their belly tightly grip the surface beneath them. Their muscles help them move from side to side, or slither, along the ground. Some even use their muscles and scales to climb trees.
pages.brief: A snake’s long skeleton is visible with many vertebrae, ribs, skull, and jawbone. Close views show colorful and camouflaged scales gripping the ground as the snake slithers from side to side and uses its muscles to climb a tree.

pages.text: Snake scales look like a single sheet of skin. Snakes don’t actually shed skin. Instead, they shed the outer layers of their scales. Snakes usually shed up to four times per year. This is called molting. During molting, a snake rubs against a hard object such as a rock or log. Rubbing helps its skin stretch and split. Then the snake crawls out and leaves it behind. Snakes shed for several reasons. Young snakes shed more often than mature snakes because they are still growing. Unlike the skin of other animals, a snake’s skin does not stretch as the snake grows. Another reason snakes shed is to get rid of parasites that may have attached to their old skin.
pages.brief: A snake rubs its head against a rough rock, its old outer scale layer splitting and peeling away. A complete shed skin lies curled on the ground. A smaller young snake is shown beside a larger mature snake.

pages.text: Scales protect a snake’s eyes, as well as its body. Unlike many animals, snakes do not have eyelids, and their eyes do not move. Instead, each eye is covered with a clear scale that protects the eye from drying out. Because of this, snakes can’t blink. Another difference between snakes and other animals is their ears. Snakes do not have ears on the outside of their skull. Instead, they listen through their jawbone. Sound vibrations pass through the jawbone to the inner ear, which sends a signal to the snake’s brain.
pages.brief: A close view of a snake’s head shows clear scales covering its unmoving eyes, with no eyelids. Sound vibrations move toward its jawbone, and a signal reaches its inner ear and brain. The snake stays still, unable to blink.

pages.text: Another important feature of a snake is its tongue. A snake uses its forked tongue to smell. When its tongue is out, scent particles stick to it. The snake pulls its tongue back and touches the roof of its mouth where a special organ identifies the scent particles. Certain snakes, such as pythons and boas, are able to sense the heat of warm-blooded animals nearby. Pits near a snake’s eyes can sense even the slightest change in the temperature around them. Other snakes, known as pit vipers, use two sensitive pits to send a heat image to their brain. The snake can “see” its prey through the heat given off by the prey’s body. This adaptation helps them judge distances while hunting in the dark.
pages.brief: A snake flicks out its forked tongue, catching scent particles in the air. A cutaway view shows the tongue touching the roof of its mouth. Pits near another snake’s eyes sense the body heat of a small warm-blooded animal in the dark.

pages.text: Hunting and Eating Snakes are carnivores, or meat eaters. They eat other animals in several ways. Some snakes inject venom, which is a type of toxin, when they bite prey. Other snakes, called constrictors, squeeze prey to death. Some snakes sneak up on their prey, grab it with their powerful jaws, and swallow it alive. Most snakes’ upper and lower jaws are loosely connected. This allows a snake to spread its jaws and open its mouth wide enough to swallow large objects. Snakes’ teeth are mainly designed for catching and holding prey. Their fangs and regular teeth are curved backward, which pushes the food toward their throat. They are even able to push their breathing tube out of their mouth so they can breathe as they swallow their prey whole. Once prey has been swallowed, a snake uses its powerful muscles to move it into the stomach and intestines. Strong acids produced by the walls of the stomach dissolve the prey into a liquid-like mass for easy digestion.
pages.brief: A carnivorous snake opens its loosely connected jaws wide to swallow large prey, curved teeth holding the food and pushing it toward its throat. Another constrictor squeezes prey in its coils. Inside the snake, stomach acids dissolve the swallowed meal.

pages.text: How Snakes Are Born Most snakes that live in cold areas mate in late spring or early summer. Snakes that live in warmer areas may mate at any time of year. Once they mate, the male snake usually leaves. About two-thirds of all female snakes lay eggs in a safe place and then leave. Snake eggs have soft, leathery shells. Baby snakes grow inside the eggs, and most develop sharp teeth to cut through the egg to hatch. Once a baby snake hatches, it must survive on its own. It is not easy to survive because birds, some mammals, and other snakes eat baby snakes. Some types of female snakes, such as rattlesnakes, hold their eggs inside their body until they hatch. Others, such as common garter snakes, also give birth to live young.
pages.brief: A female snake lays soft, leathery eggs in a safe hiding place and leaves them. Inside one egg, a baby snake develops sharp teeth to cut its way out. A rattlesnake holds eggs inside her body, and a common garter snake gives birth to live young.

pages.text: Venomous Snakes Some, but not all, snakes produce venom. Venom is injected through fangs, which are located on a snake’s jaws. Venom is produced in sacs behind a snake’s eyes. Some fangs are hollow so the venom can flow through them from these sacs.
pages.brief: A close view of a venomous snake’s head shows fangs on its jaws and venom sacs behind its eyes. Hollow fangs carry venom from the sacs, ready to inject it through a bite. The snake’s mouth is slightly open, revealing the sharp fangs.

pages.text: Snakes use venom for both defense and attack. They usually inject more venom when they bite in defense. Snakes’ venom paralyzes their prey. Some inject the prey with venom and let it go. Then they use their sense of smell and heat sensors to track the prey until it dies. Other snakes use their teeth or body to hold on to the prey until it dies. Then they eat it. Fewer than half of venomous snakes have venom that is strong enough to kill humans. Venom versus Poison Venom and poison are not the same thing. Poison is absorbed, eaten, or breathed in, while venom is injected into the victim through a bite or sting. Other animals, such as scorpions and certain insects, inject venom by stinging.
pages.brief: A snake strikes in defense and then follows a bitten prey animal, using smell and heat sensors to track it. Another snake holds its prey with teeth and body. Nearby, a scorpion and an insect sting, showing venom injected through a bite or sting.

pages.text: Conclusion Snakes are among the animal kingdom’s fiercest predators. Snakes have survived in most environments because their senses have adapted to the natural world in specific ways. Whether they are long or short, large or tiny, venomous strikers or constrictors, snakes are fascinating animals that play an important role in Earth’s natural environment.
pages.brief: A powerful snake moves through a natural environment as a fierce predator, its senses alert. Around it appear a long snake, a tiny snake, a venomous striking snake, and a constrictor wrapped around prey, showing varied forms that survive in nature.

books.title: Acadia National Park
books.art_why: The keyword check points to drawing for this book, which mixes ancient Wabanaki history with the park's story.

pages.text: National P ark ACADIA.
pages.brief: A wide view of Acadia's granite shoreline, where pink-gray rock slopes down into the cold blue Atlantic. Dark spruce forest stands behind it and a rounded mountain summit rises in the distance, with low morning light spreading across the water and the wet stones.

pages.text: The Sun rises on Acadia’s rocky coast. First to See the Sun Acadia National Park is one of the first places in the United States to see the Sun rise. Look on a map and you’ll understand why. Maine stretches farther east than any of the other forty-nine states. Acadia sits on Maine’s eastern edge, facing out into the Atlantic Ocean. The park is less than 50,000 acres (202 sq km). Compared to many national parks, that’s small. Still, the bits and pieces that make up Acadia make for a beautiful park.
pages.brief: The Sun breaks over the horizon and lights Acadia's rocky coast, shining on the ocean swell and the wet stone. The shoreline faces east into the Atlantic at the far eastern edge of Maine, so the first light of the day reaches the park before most of the country.

pages.text: Land That Meets the Sea Today, Acadia is one of the most popular national parks in the United States. More than two million people visit each year. The park includes beautiful coastline, islands, forests, lakes, mountains, and rocks. It packs a lot of variety into a small space. Acadia’s water, rocks, and vibrant fall colors make for a lovely combination.
pages.brief: A sweeping look across Acadia: a jagged coastline, small islands offshore, thick forest, quiet lakes and bare rocky mountains, with red and orange fall colours in the trees. Water, stone and autumn leaves sit close together inside one small, varied park.

pages.text: The largest part of Acadia National Park is on Mount Desert Island. More than twenty mountains rise from the sea here. At 1,530 feet (466 m), Cadillac Mountain is the tallest. Because of its early sunrise and amazing view, it’s also the most crowded. Acadia has more than 40 miles (64 km) of coastline. Because Acadia’s coast is young, sandy shores are rare. Waves shift around what sand there is, along with rocks and other material. President Barack Obama and his family hike Cadillac Mountain in 2010.
pages.brief: Mount Desert Island, where more than twenty mountains rise straight from the sea. Cadillac Mountain, the tallest at 1,530 feet, stands above a coastline of coves and stone. On the open granite summit, President Barack Obama and his family hike together in 2010.

pages.text: During low tides, the ocean leaves behind pools of water. Inside these pools live sea stars, sea cucumbers, hot pink seaweed, and other living things.
pages.brief: At low tide the ocean pulls back and leaves shallow pools between the rocks. Inside one clear pool, sea stars cling to the stone, a sea cucumber rests on the bottom, and clumps of hot pink seaweed spread out among the other small living things in the water.

pages.text: Tide pools come and go—after all, they are created by tides, which also come and go. Acadia’s tide can rise and fall 12 feet (4 m) during a day. It’s best to visit tide pools when the tide is going out. You’ll have more time to explore them.
pages.brief: A visitor crouches beside a tide pool on the rocky shore as the water drains away, stepping carefully on the wet stone. The tide here can rise and fall twelve feet in a day, so the pools come and go, and exploring as it goes out leaves more time.

pages.text: Wildlife Acadia is one of the best bird-watching spots in the country—338 kinds of birds have been sighted there. Each autumn, strong winds push thousands of raptors south as they migrate from Canada to warmer areas for the winter. Cadillac Mountain offers a close look as these hawks and kestrels fly overhead.
pages.brief: Autumn on Cadillac Mountain: strong winds blow and thousands of migrating raptors stream south overhead. A bird-watcher stands on the rocky summit with binoculars raised, watching a hawk and a kestrel glide low over the ridge on their way from Canada to warmer country.

pages.text: Return of the Falcon Peregrine falcons are one of the fastest animals on Earth. Long ago, they nested on Acadia’s Mount Desert Island. Their speed didn’t save them from humans, though, whose activities killed many of them. By the 1960s, peregrine falcons had disappeared from Acadia. In 1973, the park began efforts to bring the falcons back. Since 1991, falcon chicks have been born in the park every year.
pages.brief: A peregrine falcon folds its wings and dives fast above the cliffs of Mount Desert Island. Long ago falcons nested on this island, but human activity killed many and by the 1960s they were gone from Acadia. Since 1991 falcon chicks have been born here every year.

pages.text: American mink porcupine Other parts of Maine have lots of black bears and moose. Acadia has a few of these, but it mostly has smaller mammals, such as foxes, mink, and porcupine. Why small? Because Acadia is not a big park, and that limits the size of animals found there.
pages.brief: Small mammals of Acadia among the undergrowth: two baby foxes tumbling near a den, an American mink slipping along a streambank, and a porcupine waddling over fallen leaves. Black bears and moose live in other parts of Maine, but this park is small, so its animals are small.

pages.text: A Park Made Piece by Piece The most amazing fact about Acadia may be that it became a national park at all. Native people, called the Wabanaki, lived on the land that is now Maine for 12,000 years. Wabanaki means “People of the Dawnland.” Five different tribes united to be the Wabanaki. They made canoes out of birch trees, and fished, hunted, and gathered plants around the area known today as Acadia. In the 1600’s, French settlers arrived and took land from the Wabanaki. When British settlers began moving north in the 1700’s, there was much conflict between the French and British. These conflicts, and diseases brought by European settlers, killed many Wabanaki people and forced others to move away. Although much of Maine was taken by these settlers, the Wabanaki remained in smaller numbers.
pages.brief: Wabanaki people paddle a birch-bark canoe and gather plants and fish along the shore of what is now Acadia. Later, French settlers arrive and take land, British settlers move north in the 1700s, and conflict and European diseases kill many Wabanaki and force others away.

pages.text: After Maine became a state in 1820, rich people from big, Eastern cities came to the rocky coastline. The Wabanaki sold baskets, handmade from sweetgrass and birch. The rich people who came to buy land and build fancy summer homes bought them. The Wabanaki Today Five separate tribes joined together to become the Wabanaki. These tribes, or nations, can be found today in Northern Maine and parts of Canada. Those who live near Acadia continue the traditions of their ancestors by building canoes and baskets. They also act as guides for hunting tourists, sell smoked shellfish, and educate people at the yearly Native American Festival and Basket Makers Market.
pages.brief: Wabanaki basket makers sit with sweetgrass and birch splint, weaving baskets for the wealthy summer visitors who came to Maine's rocky coast after 1820. Nearby, Wabanaki guides lead hunting tourists, sell smoked shellfish, and show canoes and baskets at the yearly Native American Festival and Basket Makers Market.

pages.text: By the early 1900s, a few rich landowners had the idea of buying land in order to protect it. A man named George Dorr and others began to donate land to create a park that would preserve the area. By 1913 they had acquired 5,000 acres (20 sq km), which they gave to the government. In 1919 all that land became a national park. The Story of Dorr George Dorr lived alone in a grand house on Mount Desert Island. By the time he died in 1944, he had spent all his money buying land, then turning around and donating it. But Dorr had made his dream come true: Acadia had become a national park. After his death it kept growing, piece by piece, like a patchwork quilt. Even today, landowners continue to donate land around Acadia.
pages.brief: George Dorr, an older man living alone in a grand house on Mount Desert Island, stands over a map of land he has bought and given away. By 1913 he and other landowners had donated 5,000 acres to the government, and in 1919 that land became a national park. He died in 1944.

pages.text: Two young visitors walk on Sand Beach after a hike in Acadia. Conclusion Acadia National Park is a place where sea and mountain meet. People come to see them meet, to breathe the salty air, and, of course, to watch the Sun rise. After greeting the new day, there is plenty more to see and do in Acadia. Visitors can hike, climb, fish, or ride a bicycle. If you ever get the chance to visit, do!
pages.brief: Two young visitors walk along Sand Beach after a hike, the ocean surf rolling in behind them and a rocky, forested headland closing the sand. Further off, other visitors climb the trails, cast fishing lines and ride bicycles, breathing the salty air where sea and mountain meet.

books.title: Grasslands
books.art_why: It includes 1800s explorers and wide natural-history scenes suited to illustration.

pages.text: Some people feel small and unprotected in grasslands, as if the wind could pick them up and carry them for miles. A Sea of Grass When Meriwether Lewis and William Clark explored the West, they were shocked by what they saw. Both men were from Virginia and were used to seeing forests when they were in nature. When they found themselves on the Great Plains, however, endless grass spread out in every direction. The Great Plains area covers about one-third of the United States and reaches well into Canada. It is one of the world’s largest grasslands, and there are many others. These mostly flat areas with grasses and few trees have a character all their own.
pages.brief: On the Great Plains, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark stand amazed in a vast flat sea of grass. Endless grasses stretch in every direction with few trees, reaching far into Canada. Wind bends the grass as the two explorers from Virginia look out over the open land.

pages.text: The Grasslands Biome Different types of environments cover Earth’s surface. These regions and the communities of plants and animals that live there are called biomes. Deserts, rainforests, oceans, and tundra are examples of biomes. So are grasslands. Many factors play a part in creating Earth’s biomes. One is latitude, or how far a location is from the equator. Another is elevation, or height above sea level. Both help determine how warm or cool a place is. Climate, land, and water are also important building blocks of biomes, as are plants and animals. Grasslands are huge open plains where grasses are the main vegetation. Some have scattered trees, while others are treeless. Grasslands don’t have forests mainly due to fires as well as low and unpredictable rainfall. Grassland Fires Lightning often causes grassland fires. Some grassland plants need fire in order for their seeds to sprout. Plants that burn help to make the soil healthy. Grasses can survive fires because they grow from their roots, which do not get damaged. Trees and shrubs with bark that resists fire also survive.
pages.brief: A wide grassland plain shows grasses as the main vegetation, with only scattered trees or none. Nearby, a lightning strike starts a fire on the grass. In the burned area, grasses survive because they grow from roots, while trees with fire-resistant bark remain standing.

pages.text: Earth’s Grassland Regions Grasslands stretch over much of Earth’s land. Although many exist, the two main types of grasslands are tropical and temperate. Grasslands cover about one-fourth of Earth’s surface land and close to half of the land not covered by ice. Every continent besides Antarctica has grasslands, which are mainly found between deserts and forests. Various types of grasslands exist because of differences in temperature, soil, and rainfall, but there are two main types. Tropical grasslands are in hot tropical climates between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn. The main plants are grasses and other short nonwoody plants. Some shrubs and trees are also present.
pages.brief: A broad view of Earth shows grasslands spreading across continents except Antarctica, lying mainly between deserts and forests. In a hot tropical grassland between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn, grasses and short nonwoody plants grow among some shrubs and trees.

pages.text: Temperate grasslands are found in cool temperate climates outside the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn. By far the most common plants are grasses and other similar plants. Trees and shrubs generally only grow along rivers and other permanent water sources. Grasslands have grass of different heights, depending on rainfall. Drier grasslands have shorter grass. Wetter grasslands have taller grass—up to 4 meters (13 ft.) tall in some places. Some grasslands are home to huge herds of grazing animals.
pages.brief: In a cool temperate grassland outside the tropics, grasses of different heights cover open land. Taller grass rises where rainfall is heavier, while shorter grass grows in drier places. Along a river, a few trees and shrubs stand, and a huge herd of grazing animals moves across the plain.

pages.text: Animals must be careful when gathering at water holes. They are more vulnerable to predators there. Tropical Grasslands Tropical grasslands are located in large areas of Africa, India, Australia, and South America. By far the largest is in Africa. Almost half of Africa is grasslands. Tropical grasslands in Africa as well as some other areas are called savannas. The climate in tropical grasslands is usually warm or hot year-round. Average rainfall is 51–127 centimeters (20–50 in.) a year. Summer often has frequent thunderstorms. Plants benefit from the water and grow fast, turning everything green, and rivers and water holes fill up. Animals breed in summer, when there is plenty of food and water. During the dry season, usually in winter, rivers and water holes often dry up. Vegetation turns brown, and many fires happen.
pages.brief: At a tropical savanna water hole, animals gather carefully because predators are near. Warm air and summer thunderstorms bring rain; rivers and water holes fill, plants turn green, and animals breed. In the dry season, the same water hole shrinks, vegetation turns brown, and fires burn the grassland.

pages.text: Trees in tropical grasslands have important adaptations that allow them to survive the long dry season. Some store water in their thick trunks. Others have long taproots that reach down to where water is always present. Thick bark allows some trees to survive fires. Tropical grasslands differ widely in how much rainfall they receive, and rainfall affects how many trees grow. The wettest grasslands are nearly 40 percent trees, while the driest grasslands have none. Along with rainfall, soil quality plays a role in the kinds of vegetation that grow. Heavy rainfall tends to wash nutrients from the soil, leaving only a thin layer of humus. This top layer of soil is made up of decomposing organic material, which provides most of the nutrients. With little humus, the soil is generally not very rich in these areas. Baobab trees store water in their thick trunks (left). Kans grass can grow up to 3 meters (10 ft.) in height (right).
pages.brief: In a tropical grassland, a baobab tree stands with a thick trunk holding stored water. Other trees send long taproots down to water and have thick bark that resists fire. Nearby, tall Kans grass grows high, while trees are fewer where rainfall is light and soil has little humus.

pages.text: Many different kinds of animals live in tropical grasslands, and each region is different from the others. In Australia, bats, rodents, and kangaroos are common. Big cats and hoofed mammals abound in Africa. Capybaras, the world’s largest rodent, live in South American grasslands, along with monkeys, marsh deer, and giant anacondas. Indian grasslands are home to leopards, rhinos, and crocodiles. Birds live in all of these grasslands, along with billions of insects. Many animals in tropical grasslands migrate during the dry season to find food. On the African savanna, each species of hoofed animal is adapted to eat slightly different kinds or parts of plants. This allows them to live together without competing for food. Spotlight on the Serengeti Perhaps the best-known tropical grassland is Africa’s Serengeti Plain, in Tanzania. The Serengeti is home to elephants, giraffes, lions, cheetahs, hyenas, ostriches, and many other animals. Poaching— the illegal hunting of animals—is a major threat to Serengeti wildlife, even though much of the area is a national park. Black rhinoceroses and African wild dogs are endangered. Elephants and cheetahs are also in serious trouble.
pages.brief: On the African savanna, elephants, giraffes, lions, cheetahs, hyenas, and ostriches share the grassland. Hoofed animals feed on different plants so they avoid competing. In other tropical grasslands, kangaroos, capybaras, leopards, and rhinos live. Many animals migrate in the dry season, while poaching threatens wildlife such as black rhinoceroses and African wild dogs.

pages.text: Some temperate grasslands, like this one in Turkey, have explosions of wildflowers. Temperate Grasslands Temperate grasslands have few trees. These cooler grasslands go by different names in different parts of the world. They’re called prairies and plains in North America and steppes in Europe and Asia. In Southern Africa they’re known as veldts. In South America they’re called pampas. The climate in temperate grasslands varies with the location. Closer to the tropics, hot summers and mild winters are typical. Areas farther north or south have warm summers and cold, windy winters, often with snow and ice. Rainfall also varies. Closer to deserts, temperate grasslands may only get about 25 centimeters (10 in.) of rain each year. Areas near forests may get 89 centimeters (35 in.) of rain. Rainfall is most common in spring and early summer. In late summer, the soil dries out and grasses turn yellow.
pages.brief: In a temperate grassland in Turkey, a burst of wildflowers covers the open land. Few trees grow in this cool grassland, which has warm summers, cold windy winters with snow and ice, and rainfall mostly in spring and early summer. In late summer, the soil dries and the grasses turn yellow.

pages.text: Grasses in temperate grasslands have long, dense roots. The roots hold water and help keep the soil from washing away. The difference between summer and winter in temperate grasslands is often much greater than in tropical grasslands. Summer temperatures can be above 38°C (100°F), while winter temperatures can fall as low as –40°C (–40°F). Another difference is the smaller amount of rainfall. Lighter rains wash away fewer soil nutrients, so these nutrients build up. This creates a thick humus layer. As a result, the soil tends to be very rich. Plants and animals in temperate grasslands must cope with less rainfall and colder winter temperatures than those in tropical grasslands. Many plants only grow during the warmer months. Because there is less food in winter, animals are less diverse. They are also less diverse because few temperate grasslands around the world remain in their wild state. Most have been turned into farms and ranches. Smaller animals have survived more than larger animals. Hunting has had a significant effect on larger animals as well.
pages.brief: In a temperate grassland, long dense grass roots reach through rich soil, holding water and keeping soil from washing away. Summer heat is intense, while winter can be bitterly cold. Many plants grow only in warmer months. Most of the land has become farms and ranches, and smaller animals have survived better than larger ones.

pages.text: In North America, rabbits, foxes, coyotes, snakes, and small rodents are common. Owls, hawks, and ground-nesting birds also live in these grasslands. Rodents, hares, wolves, lynxes, and foxes live on the European and Asian steppes. Foxes, skunks, bush dogs, and many bird species live on the South American pampas. Some larger animals in these regions live in protected areas. However, leopards and zebras survive in the wild in some parts of the South African veldt. Other veldt species include hyenas, badgers, weasels, crocodiles, and pythons. Spotlight on the North American Tallgrass Prairie Most of North America’s tallgrass prairie has been converted to farmland and ranchland. Today, tallgrass prairie is mostly found in eastern Kansas. A small portion of that region is now protected as a United States national preserve. The tallgrass prairie existed in balance for thousands of years, thanks to a perfect combination of rainfall, fire, and grazing. Bison, the largest grazing species, were almost hunted to extinction in the 1800s. Bison were reintroduced to the preserve in 2009. Other animals include coyotes, badgers, lizards, gopher snakes, greater prairie chickens, and monarch butterflies.
pages.brief: On the North American tallgrass prairie in eastern Kansas, bison graze in a protected preserve. Coyotes, badgers, lizards, gopher snakes, greater prairie chickens, and monarch butterflies also live here. The prairie stays in balance through rainfall, fire, and grazing. In other temperate grasslands, rabbits, foxes, owls, wolves, lynxes, zebras, and leopards find homes.

pages.text: People and Grasslands Native peoples thrived in grasslands for thousands of years. These included Plains Native Americans, Australian Aboriginals, and the Hadza people in the Serengeti region. The arrival of European settlers had a significant impact on these peoples’ traditional lifestyles. Today, much of the land is used for farming and ranching. Grasslands—particularly temperate grasslands, with their rich soils—are ideal for growing crops and grazing livestock. An estimated 20 percent of the world’s grasslands are used to grow wheat and other cereal crops. Over 40 percent are used for grazing livestock. People could not live without grasslands because of the quantity of food they provide. These activities also provide livelihoods for large numbers of residents.
pages.brief: Plains Native Americans, Australian Aboriginals, and the Hadza people live in grassland regions, where their traditional lifestyles changed after European settlers arrived. Today much grassland is used for farming and ranching. People grow wheat and cereal crops and graze livestock, providing food and livelihoods for many residents.

pages.text: Some of the beauty of grasslands lies in how big the sky looks. The Humble Grass Plant On first look, one might not think that grasslands are very interesting. The flat, grassy land has very little variety compared to some other biomes. However, grasslands are special and fascinating for other reasons. Take a moment to think about grasses— humble plants that few people would consider special. They cover vast areas of land, moving gently like a living sea when the wind blows across them. They survive fires, droughts, intense summer heat, and below-freezing temperatures. Grasses provide food for an amazing variety of animals, from insects to bison. They also add nutrients to the soil, so much so that this biome has become the world’s main source of grain. The wonder of grasslands lies in the fact that such humble plants are so important to life’s balance on Earth.
pages.brief: A wide grassland stretches under a huge sky, with wind moving the grasses like a living sea. These humble grass plants survive fire, drought, intense heat, and freezing cold. They feed animals from insects to bison and add nutrients to the soil, making grasslands the world’s main source of grain and important to life’s balance.

books.title: Natural Wonders of the World
books.art_why: Keyword check points to drawing for this wide-ranging natural wonders book.

pages.text: Natural Wonders of the World.
pages.brief: A calm opening scene shows a wide view of Earth’s natural world: land, water, and sky with no people. The mood is inviting and grand, preparing readers for a journey across remarkable natural places around the planet.

pages.text: Natural Wonders Natural Wonders of the World of the World.
pages.brief: A sweeping natural-world scene continues across the page, showing a broad landscape of mountains, water, and open sky with no people. The view feels calm and majestic, suggesting the variety of natural wonders that will be explored.

pages.text: Arizona’s Barringer Meteorite Crater shows how space rocks colliding with Earth create amazing landforms. Introduction What makes something a natural wonder? A wonder is an amazing and beautiful natural structure. It makes you think about how it was formed. Natural wonders are landforms that have been created by nature, not by humans. Our planet is home to many natural wonders. In this book, we will learn about five of them: • A young volcano that took over a village • An immense coral reef.
pages.brief: A wide Arizona desert view shows Barringer Meteorite Crater, a huge bowl-shaped hole in dry land under open sky. The crater shows a landform made by a space rock colliding with Earth. No people are visible.

pages.text: Grand Canyon Between five and six million years ago, the Colorado River wound through a large plateau (pla-TOE), or an area of raised ground. Over time, the river picked up small pieces of the plateau and carried them as it flowed to the sea. This process is called water erosion (e-RO-zhun). Different kinds of rocks factor into water erosion. Some rocks are soft and break easily. Other rocks are hard and resist breakage. As the Colorado River flowed downstream, it carried pieces of the softer rocks and left behind the harder rocks. Over millions of years, this process carved deep canyons in the rocks. UNITED STATES Grand Canyon Arizona The Colorado River slowly carved the rock of the Grand Canyon into the wondrous structure we see today.
pages.brief: The Colorado River winds along the bottom of the Grand Canyon, cutting between high rock walls in Arizona. Layered rocks of different hardness line the canyon. A small locator view places the Grand Canyon within the United States and Arizona.

pages.text: Colorado River Layers of rocks form the Grand Canyon’s walls. They tell the story of what happened in the area over a period of two billion years. These rocks make up the layers in the canyon walls. The top of the canyon, where most visitors enjoy their first view, is the youngest layer of the canyon. The bottom layer, near the river, is the oldest. Scattered rocks located at the bottom of the canyon date back as long ago as two billion years. The Grand Canyon is a great place to study rocks and the Earth’s history because the rock layers are so easy to see and reach. Geologists often visit the site. One of the first geologists to visit was John Newberry. He traveled to the canyon in 1858. Newberry was the first scientist to record the canyon’s layers, although he wasn’t the first to see them.
pages.brief: The Grand Canyon’s layered rock walls rise above the Colorado River. A geologist stands on a rocky ledge, studying the visible layers. The top layers are younger, and the bottom layers near the river are older, including scattered rocks dated as far back as two billion years.

pages.text: Rattling Reptiles More than forty-seven different kinds of reptiles live in the Grand Canyon. While most of these reptiles are harmless, visitors should keep an eye out for snakes. Although they rarely bite humans, the rattlesnakes are venomous. In the winter, rattlesnakes hibernate in dens. Hundreds of rattlesnakes may live in one den. This is one of the only times rattlers live together. In the spring when the weather warms up, the snakes come out of their dens and go their separate ways. In late summer, females give birth to live babies. The babies only stay in the area where they were born for about seven to ten days. Then they shed their first baby skin, add their first rattle, and move on in search of food. As a rattlesnake grows, it sheds its skin at least once a year. It adds a new rattle to its tail with each shed. A mature diamondback rattlesnake may grow to be 2 meters (about 6.5 ft) long. It may weigh up to 6.8 kilograms (15 lb). Rattlers can live to be 25 years old.
pages.brief: A diamondback rattlesnake rests among rocks in the Grand Canyon, its rattle visible at the tail. Nearby, several rattlesnakes share a winter den. In another part of the scene, a female rattlesnake is with newborn babies before they shed and move on.

pages.text: Native Americans lived in and around the Grand Canyon for more than four thousand years before European explorers arrived. By 1150, most of the original tribes had moved away. Only one group remained. Some of them still live and work in the canyon. Every year, millions of people travel to Grand Canyon National Park to hike, raft, and see this majestic wonder of nature.
pages.brief: Native American people are shown living and working in and around the Grand Canyon. One group remains in the area. In the distance, visitors hike and raft in Grand Canyon National Park, coming by the millions each year to see the majestic natural wonder.

pages.text: Paricutín Many of nature’s creations are millions of years old. They began forming long before humans lived on Earth. Other creations have formed in modern times. The Paricutín (pah-ree-koo-TEEN) volcano in Mexico is one such formation. Paricutín began forming in 1943 in a field. A farmer discovered a fissure (FISH-ur), or opening in the ground, in his cornfield. The crack was about 1.8 meters (6 ft.) long. Soon more fissures appeared. Black smoke came from the holes, and ash piled up on the ground, forming a cone. In about twelve hours, the cone had grown to 10 meters (33 ft.) high. After a day, it had grown to 50 meters (164 ft.). The volcano continued to grow. In just a week, it reached a height of 100 meters (328 ft.). UNITED STATES GULF OF MEXICO MEXICO Paricutín PACIFIC OCEAN Paricutín volcano erupts in 1943.
pages.brief: In a Mexican cornfield in 1943, a farmer stands near a long crack in the ground. Black smoke rises from new fissures, and ash piles into a growing cone. A locator view places Paricutín within Mexico between the Pacific Ocean and Gulf of Mexico.

pages.text: A church steeple is all that can still be seen after ash and lava covered the town of Paricutín. The people of Paricutín hoped that their village would be safe. After a few months, however, the cone had grown so large that lava started to reach their town. The villagers had to evacuate, leaving behind their homes and farms. Over a nine-year period, lava and ash eventually covered the entire village of Paricutín and most of the nearby town of San Juan. In the end all that was left of Paricutín was the church steeple rising out of the black rock as a reminder of nature’s power.
pages.brief: A church steeple rises alone from a field of black volcanic rock where the village of Paricutín once stood. In the background, villagers evacuate with their belongings, leaving homes and farms as lava and ash spread across the land over nine years.

pages.text: Volcanoes such as Paricutín are called cinder cones. They are the simplest type of volcano. Lava is under pressure inside Earth. Cinder cones form when lava shoots out from a central vent in the ground. As the lava explodes into the air, it cools and breaks into small pieces. They harden and fall as rocks and ash, or cinders, around the central vent to form a cone. Most cinder cones have a bowl-shaped crater at the top. Because Paricutín volcano is young, scientists have been able to observe its growth since it first appeared. Today, the volcano stands about 424 meters (1,391 ft.) tall. It covers 26 square kilometers (10 sq mi.). cinder cone crater rock fragments central vent.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of a cinder cone volcano shows lava rising through a central vent. The lava shoots into the air, cools, and falls as rock fragments and ash around the vent, building a cone with a bowl-shaped crater at the top. Paricutín stands in the background at its present height.

pages.text: AFRICA Zambia Victoria Falls Zimbabwe INDIAN OCEAN Victoria Falls, like the Grand Canyon, was formed by water. Victoria Falls Victoria Falls is the largest mass of falling water on the planet. The water drops 108 meters (354 ft.) into a deep pool. The people of Zambia call the falls Mosi-oa-Tunya (MOH-see wah TOON-yah) (the smoke that thunders). It’s a perfect name. The thunder has to do with the booming sound created of water crashing over the falls into the pool below. The smoke has to do with the water vapor, or mist, that comes up from the bottom of the falls.
pages.brief: Victoria Falls sends a huge sheet of water over a cliff into a deep pool below. Mist rises from the bottom like smoke, and the crashing water suggests a booming thunder. A locator view places the falls between Zambia and Zimbabwe in Africa.

pages.text: Victoria Falls is located on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe in Africa. The falls began forming millions of years ago when a shallow crack in the rock appeared across the path of the Zambezi River. The crack was caused when parts of the earth shifted about 150 million years ago. Over the years, the river flowed over the rock. Eventually, the water wore down the soft rock, forming a cliff over which the river now falls. The pool into which the water falls is called a plunge pool. The Scottish explorer David Livingstone visited the Falls in 1855. He was probably the first person from outside of Africa to see the wondrous formations. He named the Falls after Queen Victoria of England. But many people think that Mosi-oa- Tunya is a more accurate name. Victoria Falls is now part of two national parks, one in Zambia and one in Zimbabwe. cliff hard rock soft rock plunge pool.
pages.brief: The Zambezi River flows over the cliff at Victoria Falls, with hard rock and soft rock shown in cross-section. Water drops into the plunge pool. Nearby, Scottish explorer David Livingstone views the falls, which he visited in 1855 and named after Queen Victoria.

pages.text: Victoria Falls Fun Facts • Victoria Falls is actually divided into six waterfalls: Devil’s Cataract, Armchair Falls, Horseshoe Falls, Main Falls, Rainbow Falls, and the Eastern Cataract. • A bridge at the Falls is a popular site for bungee jumping. • During a full moon, the park stays open late so people can enjoy the rainbow that is made when moonlight shines through the water vapor. • People go rafting and kayaking on the water below the Falls. They can even surf on the rapids below.
pages.brief: Victoria Falls is divided into six waterfalls. A bridge spans near the falls, where a bungee jumper leaps. Below, people raft and kayak on the water and surf on the rapids. At night, a full moon shines through water vapor, creating a rainbow while visitors stay late in the park.

pages.text: CHINA Mount Everest NEPAL PACIFIC OCEAN Mount Everest Mount Everest, the tallest mountain in the world, is one of the most amazing sites on Earth. Called “Forehead in the Sky” by the Nepali people, this magnificent landform in the Himalaya mountain range reaches a height of 8,850 meters (29,035 ft.). The snowcapped Himalayas might appear old. In fact, they are quite young for mountains. The mountains were formed millions of years ago when two parts of Earth’s crust hit each other. Over time, the pressure of the two parts rubbing against each other caused the ground to crumble and rise above the sea. Since Mount Everest is a young mountain, its peaks are still sharp and steep. They haven’t yet been smoothed down by endless years of wind, ice, and snow.
pages.brief: Mount Everest rises as a sharp, steep, snowcapped peak in the Himalaya mountain range. A locator view places it between China and Nepal, near the Pacific Ocean. The surrounding Himalayas are shown as young mountains, their peaks not yet smoothed by wind, ice, and snow.

pages.text: Although Mount Everest is beautiful to look at, it’s a bitterly cold place to be. The average temperature is about −36°C (−33°F) and can drop to −60°C (−76°F). Even in July, the warmest month, the temperature only reaches −19°C (−2°F). It never gets above freezing. As a result, the ice and snow at the top of the mountain never melt. Mount Everest’s summit Storms dump more snow on Mount Everest every year.
pages.brief: Mount Everest’s summit stands in bitter cold beneath storm clouds. Snow falls heavily, adding more snow to the already frozen peak. The ice and snow at the top never melt, and the mountain’s average temperature is far below freezing even in the warmest month.

pages.text: The fierce cold on Mount Everest makes it hard for animals and plants to survive. One of the only animals that can live on the mountain is the wild yak. This large animal can weigh more than 454 kilograms (1,000 lb.) and grow up to 1.8 meters (6 ft.) tall. The yak can survive in part because its blood can take in more oxygen than the blood of other animals. This adaptation is a lifesaver on Mount Everest, where the air contains little oxygen. Wild yak grazing The people who first settled in the Himalayas believed that the gods made their homes in the peaks. As a result, no one tried to climb Mount Everest until explorers arrived in the early 1900s. The earliest climbers quickly learned about the harsh conditions on the mountain—freezing temperatures, powerful winds, changing weather, and rough terrain.
pages.brief: A wild yak grazes on the cold, high slopes of Mount Everest. The large animal has thick fur and can take in more oxygen from the thin air. In the background, early climbers face freezing temperatures, powerful winds, changing weather, and rough terrain on the mountain.

pages.text: Mountaineers Hillary and Norgay accept awards for their achievement. The yeti (YEH-tee), or Abominable (a-BOM-in-a-bal) Snowman, is a legend of Mount Everest and the Himalayas. Sherpas tell stories about seeing large footprints and chewed yak bones in the mountains. Hillary’s team took what was said to be a yeti scalp and skins to Europe and the United States. Scientists there agreed that the scalp was from a goat and the skins were from a bear. To this day, no one has been able to prove the existence of the yeti. Despite all the obstacles, mountaineers continued to come to Mount Everest, hoping to be the first to make it to the top. No one was successful until 1953. That year, Sir Edmund Hillary (from New Zealand) and Tenzing Norgay (a Sherpa from Nepal) became the first men to successfully climb the mountain. Since then, many climbers from all over the world have risked their lives to get to the top.
pages.brief: Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay stand together after their successful 1953 climb of Mount Everest, accepting awards for their achievement. In the snowy mountains behind them, a shadowy yeti legend is suggested by large footprints and chewed yak bones, though no proof of the yeti exists.

pages.text: AUSTRALIA Great Barrier Reef A diver explores coral formations on the Great Barrier Reef. Great Barrier Reef The Great Barrier Reef is really a collection of many reefs. It is more than 2,300 kilometers (1,429 mi.) long and is located off the northeast coast of Australia. It is full of amazing sea creatures, from sea slugs and urchins to dolphins, whales, and sharks. A reef is a chain, or range, of rocks that lies at or near the surface of the water. The Great Barrier Reef is a coral reef.
pages.brief: A diver swims among colorful coral formations on the Great Barrier Reef off Australia’s northeast coast. Sea slugs, urchins, dolphins, whales, and sharks share the reef waters. A locator view shows the long reef stretching along the coast of Australia.

pages.text: Coral reefs are found in all tropical oceans of the world. However, none is as large as the Great Barrier Reef. Most established coral reefs are between five and ten thousand years old. At first glance, the Great Barrier Reef might look like a rock, but it’s not. It’s made from the skeletons of millions of animals called polyps (POL-ips). As the polyps die, new ones grow on top of the old skeletons. The many layers of skeletons form the limestone base of a coral reef. Other kinds of plants and animals also help make up the reef. They include algae, sponges, and shellfish. But the tiny polyp is responsible for most of this natural wonder’s structure. The life and death of coral polyps are responsible for the formation of coral reefs such as the Great Barrier Reef.
pages.brief: A close view shows coral polyps living on the Great Barrier Reef. New polyps grow on top of the skeletons of dead polyps, building layers of limestone. Algae, sponges, and shellfish share the reef. The reef may look like rock, but it is made mostly by the life and death of tiny coral animals.

pages.text: Reefs are made from animals, and they supply food and shelter for other animals. Thousands of species live on the reef. They include 1,625 kinds of fish, more than 30 kinds of marine mammals, 500 kinds of seaweed, and 6 kinds of marine turtles. The reef is also an important breeding area for animals, including birds, sea turtles, and the endangered humpback whale. As one of the most interesting and beautiful places on Earth, the reef is popular with scientists, scuba divers, and tourists. Today, environmentalists are working with these groups to protect the reef so future generations can learn from it and enjoy its beauty. Look, But Don’t Touch! Reefs are alive and full of delicate creatures. Responsible snorkelers and scuba divers should always follow these important rules: • When snorkeling, float over the reef. Never stand on it. • Take pictures, not coral souvenirs. • Stock saltwater aquariums with fish that are raised in captivity, not those taken from a coral reef. • Always pack out your plastics and other trash. • Learn more about coral reefs and how you can help protect them.
pages.brief: Scuba divers and snorkelers float above the Great Barrier Reef without touching it. Fish, sea turtles, seaweed, and a humpback whale are nearby. Scientists and tourists visit the reef, while environmentalists share rules: take pictures, not coral, pack out trash, and help protect the delicate living reef.

pages.text: Wonders Everywhere From Arizona to the coast of Australia, natural wonders are everywhere. Whether they were formed millions of years ago or within the span of a lifetime, they are all special. These amazing landforms are some of the largest, highest, and most breathtaking places on Earth. Travelers, scientists, and adventure seekers will continue to visit these special places for generations to come. The Grand Canyon, Paricutín, Mount Everest, Victoria Falls, and Great Barrier Reef are only five of the many wonders that surround us. Other well-known natural wonders include: • The Northern Lights, a light show that brightens up the skies in the Northern Hemisphere • The Barringer Meteorite Crater, a massive hole in the Arizona desert that is almost a mile wide and 174 meters (570 ft.) deep • Ayers Rock, the world’s largest solid rock, rising 862.5 meters (2,830 ft.) above sea level in Australia Do you live near an amazing and beautiful natural wonder—an incredible mountain, a majestic river, a mysterious cave? These are all examples of wondrous sites you can visit, learn from, and enjoy every day.
pages.brief: A wide montage shows the Grand Canyon, Paricutín, Mount Everest, Victoria Falls, and the Great Barrier Reef. Above, the Northern Lights brighten the sky. In the Arizona desert, Barringer Meteorite Crater forms a massive hole, while Ayers Rock rises in Australia. Mountains, rivers, and caves hint at wonders near home.

books.title: The Magic of Migration
books.art_why: Science and nature book about real animals and habitats that can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Some animals wing their way across the skies for hundreds or thousands of miles. Others thunder across great plains. Others make their way through strong ocean currents. They travel far to find food, water, warmer climates, or a place to raise their young. All are taking part in the magic journey of migration.
pages.brief: Birds wing across a bright sky, a herd thunders over a wide grassy plain, and marine animals swim through strong ocean currents. The scene shows animals traveling far to find food, water, warmer climates, or a safe place to raise their young.

pages.text: What Is Migration? Migration is the word scientists use to describe these long animal journeys. Many different types of animals migrate. These include birds, bats, whales, sea turtles, large grazers such as caribou and wildebeests, salmon, and some kinds of insects.
pages.brief: A wide landscape and seascape show many kinds of migrating animals together: birds and bats in the sky, whales and sea turtles in the ocean, caribou and wildebeests on land, salmon in a river, and insects in the air.

pages.text: Some animals migrate at the same time every year and follow the same path. Others follow more irregular patterns. Their movement depends on local conditions, such as the weather. There are also some animals that only migrate one way. Locusts migrate when their numbers get so big that they need to find a new feeding ground. They stay in a new field until they need another source of food.
pages.brief: A large swarm of locusts moves into a green field, darkening the air above the crops. Nearby, other animals follow a familiar seasonal path across the land, while the locusts settle in the new field to feed until they need another food source.

pages.text: Migration is one of the most dangerous journeys an animal can make. Migrating animals face many dangers along the way. These include hungry predators, strong winds, ocean currents, hunters, and fishers. But migrating to find better living conditions is important for survival.
pages.brief: Migrating animals face dangers on their journey: a predator chases a smaller animal, strong winds buffet a flock, rough ocean currents swirl around swimmers, and hunters and fishers stand along the route. The animals press on to find better living conditions for survival.

pages.text: The Search for Food and Water The most common reason why animals migrate is to find food and water. One of the most spectacular examples can be found in Africa. Every year more than a million wildebeests, which are large, grazing animals, migrate because of drought. When hot weather dries up grass and water in one place, wildebeests travel in huge herds to find food and water. As these large mammals travel, hundreds of thousands of zebras and gazelles join them on their journey.
pages.brief: On a dry African plain, a huge herd of wildebeests travels in search of food and water. The hot weather has dried up grass and water. Hundreds of thousands of zebras and gazelles move alongside the wildebeests on the same journey.

pages.text: Many birds also make amazing journeys to find food. Warblers, flycatchers, storks, pelicans, terns, and all kinds of other birds migrate every year.
pages.brief: A great flock of birds flies across the sky, including warblers, flycatchers, storks, pelicans, terns, and other kinds of birds. Their wings spread wide as they travel together over land and water on an amazing yearly journey to find food.

pages.text: Finding a Place to Nest Another reason animals migrate is to find a place to lay their eggs or to raise their young. Many fish, such as salmon and trout, migrate to spawn, or lay their eggs, in freshwater streams. And some, such as freshwater eels, do the opposite. They leave their freshwater homes and migrate to the open sea to spawn.
pages.brief: In a clear freshwater stream, salmon and trout swim upstream to spawn and lay their eggs. In another scene, freshwater eels leave their freshwater home and move toward the open sea to spawn. The water connects the different journeys.

pages.text: How Do They Do It? How do animals find their way when they migrate? Scientists are still learning about this. Some animals, such as salmon, use their sense of smell to find the stream where they were born. Others, such as indigo buntings and other night-flying birds, use the stars to guide their way. Day-flying birds use the sun. They also watch for special landmarks, such as coastlines and mountains, to stay on course.
pages.brief: At night, indigo buntings and other night-flying birds fly beneath the stars. By day, birds use the sun and watch coastlines and mountains to stay on course. In a stream, a salmon swims using its sense of smell to find the place where it was born.

pages.text: Scientists are still exploring other ways that animals navigate. They think some animals are able to sense Earth’s magnetic pull to guide them. Magnetic Brains Think of Earth as a giant magnet. Scientists think that many species of birds navigate by sensing Earth’s magnetic north and south poles. They have found tiny bits of a magnetic substance, magnetite, in some birds’ brains. They think these tiny bits are pulled by Earth’s poles, helping guide birds as they migrate.
pages.brief: Birds fly through the sky as Earth is shown like a giant magnet with north and south poles. A close-up shows tiny bits of magnetite inside a bird's brain. Scientists think these bits are pulled by Earth's poles and help guide the birds on their migration.

pages.text: Insects, Whales, and Turtles One of the most interesting yearly migrations is that of monarch butterflies. These bright orange and black butterflies travel from the northern and eastern parts of North America. They go to Mexico and southern parts of the United States. They spend the winter on certain trees in the mountains. In the spring, the adults return north. They breed along the way. The adults die after the females lay eggs. The eggs grow into young butterflies that complete the journey back home.
pages.brief: Bright orange and black monarch butterflies cluster on trees in the mountains of Mexico and the southern United States. In spring, adults fly north and breed along the way, then die after females lay eggs. Young butterflies continue the journey back home.

pages.text: Many marine creatures migrate. These include huge humpback whales, lobsters, sharks, sea turtles, and tuna. Some, such as many of the sea turtles, follow ocean currents to get from one part of the ocean to another. But scientists still don’t know how these animals find exactly the right beach to lay their eggs. They must find the same one they hatched on years before.
pages.brief: In the ocean, humpback whales, sharks, sea turtles, tuna, and lobsters travel through the water. Some sea turtles follow ocean currents toward a beach. Scientists still do not know how these turtles find exactly the right beach where they hatched years before.

pages.text: Every year, millions of animals move far away to find food, water, better weather, or a place to nest or raise their young. Some travel alone. Others travel in huge flocks or herds. But no matter how they travel, they all take the magical journey of migration.
pages.brief: Millions of animals move across land, sky, and sea, traveling far to find food, water, better weather, or a place to nest and raise their young. Some travel alone, while others move in huge flocks or herds, all taking part in the magical journey of migration.
